S. must go out— he cannot stand another election— He was told in large parties— "Sir you shall be turned out" Rd.— "you cannot turn him out"— Yes— was the answer Col<sup>o</sup> Howard or Ille can do it— As my professional engagements render it impossible for me to engage in any representative office I have peremptorily declined. I will not suffer myself to be polled— if Col<sup>o</sup> Howard can be prevailed on to serve He will of course be our next delegate—

I have heretofore thought the Treaty a bad one— and have acted under that impression. But from inability to form a correct opinion, have never endeavored to make a Convert to a subject I did not fully comprehend— But on one Question I have no doubt— The Legislature possess neither expressly or incidentally any authority to give effect to or oppose the operation of Treaties. The making a treaty is not a legislative function. It is not strictly an executive Power— They depend on [underline: Contract] and their obligation is the Consequence of good faith.— But whether this opinion is just or not— Every consideration which can attach a man to his Country unite to press giving efficacy to the Treaties.

I am D<sup>r</sup> Sir
with sincere Esteem
Y<sup>r</sup> obed Ser

J. Winchester

Dear Sir

Finding no such paper as the Cohnawaga's now call for, I [strikethrough: found] from my house to examine once more at my office: but no such paper appears: and I am confident I never saw any paper purporting to be a power from the Chief to M<sup>r</sup> Louis and others; for when by themselves they declared they were impowered to make a final agreement for their nation, I recollect that the idea was perfectly new to me.

I think however, that the final settlement may be made in the way I suggested. I am disposed to believe the present deputation to have been empowered, as they declare. The negotiation then may be held with them, and the terms agreed on. They may then return to their nation, and the State of New York suspend the payments stipulated until agents, duly empowered [strikethrough: and properly authorized], shall come to receive them. To make the transaction still more satisfactory, New York might send an agent with the deed or treaty which the present deputies shall conclude, and obtain a formal ratification by the signatures of all the Chiefs of the Seven Nations.

respectfully yours

E. Pickering

[The Secretary of War]

James McHenry Esq
Secretary at War
Philadelphia

Balt<sup>o</sup> May 1796

My dear friend

Since my last We have had no change in the public opinion except that animosity is increased for the want of approbation and additional resentment exists against our member for his speech on the Treaty business. — It may be politic for aught I know for him to count on [strikethrough: members] since he has so openly relinquished all claim to support from orderly and "respectable" Citizens — The Committee have found it necessary to renew their correspondence calling on him to explain the Reason of suppressing the true number of his instructions — regretting his attempt — to create jealousies between the Town & County and explicitly declaring that he does know the opinion of Balt<sup>o</sup> to be opposed to his Conduct, and that resolutions expressive of Confidence in the H<sup>se</sup> of Rep<sup>s</sup>. would never have been started but [strikethrough: for] for his declaration that by such means he could influence nine members of Congress. — You know what an Egotist the man is — It is right the Public should also know the means he has adopted to puff himself off. —

I will attend to the business of M<sup>r</sup> Marburgs letter — but perhaps he might wish some other Person to be chosen when I inform him that I shall decline going to the Legislature — If he does I will write you

I am with sincerity
Y<sup>r</sup>. Ob<sup>t</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup>

J Winchester

War-Office of the United States.

May 4, 1796,

The following RULES, explanatory of those published the 15th February, 1789, are to be observed by all persons entitled to lands in pursuance of Resolves of Congress.

EVERY certificate of the acknowledgment of a Deed, or Power of Attorney, either before a Notary Public or other Magistrate, must, in addition to what is usual, set forth that the person making the acknowledgment is known to the Notary or other Magistrate; for which purpose words of the following import must be inserted in the Certificate.

"And I do moreover certify that the said A. B. making this acknowledgment, has been for                                              personally known to me."

If the Notary or other Magistrate has reason to believe that he is the person he represents himself to be, he will also certify it.

And if the proof be made by a witness or witnesses, he or they must swear to some general state of their knowledge of him, which matter must be set forth in the Certificate; and the Notary Public or other Magistrate before whom the acknowledgment is made, must also set forth that the witness or witnesses have been for upwards of                                              personally known to him.

If a Justice of the Peace is employed, the clerk of the court of the corporation or county must certify that such person is a justice of the peace of the county or corporation, as the case may be, and that full faith is due to his acts as such.

James M<sup>c</sup>Henry,

Secretary of War.

[1796 May]

To Jeremiah Wadsworth Esquire.

The President of the United States having nominated, and by and advice and consent of the Senate appointed you a Commissioner to hold a treaty with the Cohnawaga Indians, stiling themselves the Seven Nations of Canada, respecting a claim or right set up by the said Indians to a parcel of land lying within the limits and jurisdiction of the State of New-York, you are therefore and hereby authorized to hold a treaty with the said Indians, their deputies or Chiefs, at such time and place within the State of New-York, as may be fixed on by the Governor of the said State.

The sole object of this treaty is to enable the State of New-York to extinguish by purchase the right to the land in question; you will take care therefore, that the negociation for this purpose, between the Agents of the State of New York, and the said Indians or their Deputies, be conducted with such candour and fairness as to preclude all reasonable ground of complaint hereafter on the part of those Indians. The compensation and all expences connected with the Treaty, are to be paid and satisfied by the State of New York.

In negociating this business you will conform to the rule laid down in the Act intitled "An Act to regulate trade and intercourse with the Indian tribes passed the first day of March 1793, particularly the eighth section of the said Act.

Given at the War Office of the United States this fifth day of May 1796 —

James McHenry
Secy of war.

Sir,

When I had the honor to address you on the 4<sup>th</sup> of December last I did expect that the Mathematical Instruments then mentioned to be in forward=ness would have been completed within a short time but notwithstanding almost daily Solicitation on my part and as repeated Promises to finish them on the part of the Workman they were not sent me till within these few days, and which is the reason that your Order has not been long since complied. The desire too to send you the Articles perfect in their kind made me engage the first Artist in that line (Ramsden) and the Multiplicity of his Engagements added not a little to the Delay; I hope however you will now soon receive them and that they will give Satisfaction. They are under the Care of M<sup>r</sup> R. Bird who will be the Bearer of this Letter. — I doubt whether the Plan of the

Water Level made part of the Theodolite or was meant to designate a different Article induced me to order a Telescopic Level there being no Instruments under the two Names. The Theodolite I understand is a complete one for the purposes for which you want it. With respect to the Cost of these Articles I am necessarily obliged to trust in a great degree to the Workman himself. Some of them appeared to me high priced but on Inquiry of other Officers I have no reason to think them charged extravagantly or at more than the customary Prices. — I now send you Muller's Practical Fortification & Elements of Mathematics which have been procured after some Search. I believe I have exceeded your Order in sending the whole of Muller's Works but as the last of them Viz those more expressly on Artillery was inconsiderably I ventured to send them with the rest as they are reputed of good Authority on their respective Subjects and being scarce might

not be easily procured at a future day if you were desirous to have the whole. — With respect to the Payment for these Things as Bills are not to be had on Philad<sup>a</sup> it has been judged the better mode to take Payment here from the Funds of the Department of State which will accordingly be done as soon as Remittances shall arrive on that Account.

Sir,

Your most obed<sup>t</sup> Servant,

Don<sup>l</sup> Allen Peal.

I have the pleasure to enclose you a return of all the articles received into the Navy yard at this Port, and on which I have distinguishing each particular as to what of as yet remain on hand some of the materials have been used expended in [strikethrough: erecting] the Store be mentioned in the return, and also in [strikethrough: erecting] some of the buildings as well as in repairing the Wharf, and fencing in the yard —

As the articles that are of a perishable nature contemplated in the line art of Coopery, perhaps it would easy to contain many articles might perish in length of time if exposed, which would be preserved if properly taken care of. I am clearly of the opinion that all kinds of lumber used in the construction of a Ship may be preserved and for any time, and greatly improved by being sunk in salt water, what the worm will not take hold — It appears to me it would be for the Interest of the united to preserve from all the Materials mentioned in the return, as such as ought to be kept for future use. They are mostof at the yard have been preserved at much trouble and expense, and some of them are so good can now be had and at the Market, when any are sold they will not fetch one half their value. They demonstrate being so widely different from any thing that are wanted for Private use — I have received the thanks from Georgia — If the live Oak that are in the yard and which are being offering every one are wanted at other yards they ought to be sent on [strikethrough: thither] but I have inserted them among the articles that I thought may should be sold, as they are bad, or not good of their kind being raised very short and great scarcity of that size has been must long been cut and laying [strikethrough: to] were taken on board to make Stiges, and they are as bad our Georgia pieces are a better blank of the kind in this State and at one third the expence as those from Georgia —

So fine are the Sticks that compose the keel and so great has been the expence of preserving them and puting them together that I am of opinion [strikethrough: it will be best to] in case of the Timber is not to sole the keel ought to be preserved as it may be Sunk under water with the rest — I have indeavor'd to comply with your directions by being Particular in the return and I am persuaded there is no material error therein. Fort Johnson May 12<sup>th</sup> 1796

I received your favor of the 8<sup>th</sup> of April last, and now enclose to you the Returns for the Months of January February, March & April, also a copy of Barrack account for the Months of June July & August which you informed me had not come to your hands. — I hope these Returns will give you satisfaction, and clear up every accommodation. if there should be any still wanting, and is in my power to give you any information, I shall be done with pleasure —

I must observe that the duty of the Post is so multifold and requires great attention — all Vessels coming with the Tide on, you by the laws of the State, obliged to send their boat a shore at the Post the Captn likewise demanded on deck at the place he came from, if any stock on board, and what persons of Colour are on board — in both of said matters to call with the Governour, in case of People hoping or attempting to People — We are to fire at them, and to bring them too — This with collecting between Vessels and settle the cases — Celebrating on the fourth Proof July, and the Presidents Birth Day expences much powder &c —

I must also beg leave to observe that in the months of June, July and August, I was confined by a sickness, and afterwards obliged to go to the G<sup>t</sup> Court on Public business, and did not return until the 1<sup>st</sup> of December —

I hope this circumstance you will not be found to be blame worthy, if there should be any mistakes, for I shall take every possible care to find them out of force — Clothing for the Men are much wanted, as I wrote with precision by the last Returns transmitted to you, which I hope you have received, and will forward what is necessary as soon as possible —

I am with esteem & Respect

Sir

your most Ob<sup>t</sup> Hble Serv<sup>t</sup>

West Point May 10<sup>th</sup> 1796.

[Private]

Sir

The Situation of the Regiment in which I have the honor to Serve is Such, that after the most mature deliberation, I think the Means which I Shall produce to relieve it, calls on the Subject of the unhappy, differences which exist between its Agent & the Officers.

I hope my motives for taking the liberty to address you in private, will be my apology, when I declare that without entering into the Merits of advanced Statements or opinions, meant to bear a [undecipherable] observation directly or particularly, with no other view than to endeavour to propose means by which the welfare of the Corps may be promoted & the unhappy Necessity of an [undecipherable: Eclat] avoided.

Passion & prejudice may often lead men out of the Path which on cool reflection they would come to follow — a little time brings us to be an object, under a different light from what it appeared at first view. & the thought of having attacked the honor of an Officer without having certain facts to support the motion, & the consequence has sometimes occasioned cruel reflexions, particularly if the challenge is designed as a preliminary to ensure, leads to a Suspicion that nothing growing out of it, can be entirely without Sin.

Matters have gone so far that they cannot rest where they Stand, both for the good of the Service, as well as for the attainment of truth. I think that a Court of Inquiry, would be preferable to a Court Martial it would be conceived more calmly; it would lead further than to a mere investigation of a particular charge, for it would comprehend the chain of circumstances & events from which originate all the unhappy Situation in which we unhappily find ourselves

It will probably be pleasing to you to hear the situation of the British at Niagara.

I had occasion in the course of my business to find M<sup>r</sup> Parrish the Interpreter for the Six Nations and to Buffalo Creek & Niagara on business with the Senecas — He informs me the British are making every preparation to leave the Garrison & have already dismounted their cannon & moved some of their Military Stores on their own side of the River into their new Magazines which they have built.

The British he says expect the Americans there about the time stipulated by the Treaty and heard much said respecting the Command which was coming to occupy the same place. It is now commanded by a Major and as they understood a Captains command was to relieve the Fort was a little degrading British pride. M<sup>r</sup> Parrish's business was in some measure to see the Indians relative to the Connecticut company going forward, since some while they were strongly oppose to it. [To A. Wayne]

Sir

The President has received information that certain emissaries are employed and paid, to gain a knowledge of our military posts in the Western country; and to encourage and stimulate the people in that quarter to secede from the union, and form a political and separate connexion with a foreign power.

The persons more particularly named for this employment are a Powers, [strikethrough: De] Collot & Warin. It is said also that these men have received written instructions for their government, and letters to influential citizens in the district of country that has been designated as the field for their operations.

Powers is about thirty five years of age; of Irish descent, born in one of the Canary Islands, educated at S<sup>t</sup> Omers; bred a physician; a man of science; seemingly sensible; and speaks the Spanish and English fluently, and as some other languages.

De Collot is a French man; has commanded as a general officer in the West Indies; full six feet high; about 50 years of age and speaks English very well.

Warin is also a French man; was lately a civil engineer in the service of the U.S. which he resigned for his present employment & speaks English tolerably; about 30 years of age; about six feet high, black hair, sallow complexion and easy mannered. He was added as adjutant general in [undecipherable].

The route of these emissaries (at least one or more of them) as by Pittsburgh down the Ohio to the old Shawanee town; thence across the Ohio thro the lower parts of Kentucky and South Western territory; thence to the rapids of [undecipherable]; thence to Fort Vincennes; thence to S<sup>t</sup> Genevieve; and thence down to New Orleans. It is also intended that one, if not two of them, shall visit our lined posts from Washington to Fort Defiance inclusive, and if permission is obtained go from the latter by way of Detroit and the [undecipherable] down to Louisiana.

But as these emissaries were at Pittsburg on the [undecipherable] and were to remain at that place or in its neighbourhood about a fortnight it may perhaps be in your power on your arrival there, to ascertain their route with more certainty

from going abroad that you suspect the country to be visited by Spies. M<sup>r</sup> Brackenridge will perhaps call upon you and may give you some information respecting them. If he does, receive it as from a [undecipherable]; and a thing that you will attend to without coinciding absolutely in opinion with him that they are emissaries, should he be of that way of thinking. You will therefore thank him civilly for it, and tell him that you will keep an eye upon them should they come within your reach and manifest traiterous intentions.

Should the information respecting these men be founded & which there is no reason to doubt, and their suspicions in no ways alarmed, circumstances will necessarily emerge at every post they may visit that must betray their traiterous errands and justify their arrest and seizure of their papers for examination. Of this you will judge; and take measures to prevent their being destroyed or concealed.

And yet it may happen, in order to guard against a discovery of the fact which would criminate them most in case of their arrest that they may have left their instructions with some person or in a place of safety. Should they have used this kind of precaution, and should their traiterous intentions have been sufficiently indicated by other circumstances they may perhaps be disposed to discover them in the hope of procuring for them a mitigation of their punishment. You will not however understand by this that either rigorous or unlawful [strikethrough: measures] means are to be employed to obtain them, for tho the crimes of traitors affect a whole people, it is nevertheless proper to respect the rights of humanity in their chastisement.

I have no doubt, therefore, but that you will observe a line of proceeding in this business conformable to the exigencies of the case. You know the powers of a commander, the measures which the safety of the posts he is intrusted with, exact and require, and how far the military laws apply to spies and emissaries found within their jurisdiction in time of peace. On this point it is unnecessary to remark.

I would observe only in general, that should either of the before named persons be arrested, and papers be found upon them shewing unlawful designs, copies of them are to be taken and certified by some of the officers present; and with the originals certified in like manner, sent to the Sec<sup>t</sup> of War by separate and trusty persons. You will also inform minutely of every thing touching their detection arrest and communication.

Opinion concerning
attaching the pay due
to a discharged Soldier]

Philadelphia 30<sup>th</sup> May 1796

The Attorney General understands by the letter of Constant Freeman bearing date the 6<sup>th</sup> december 1795 that Cap<sup>t</sup> Armstrong made advances of necessaries to a Soldier in the army of the United States while in actual service, who has since been regularly discharged and who has certain arrears of pay in the hands of the deputy paymaster which have been by legal process attached by Cap<sup>t</sup> Armstrong for the purpose of satisfying the debt so contracted and remaining due by the soldier to him. Can this suit be maintained or not [strikethrough: is the question proposed] and in what manner is the deputy paymaster in cases of this sort to act, appear to be the questions arising out of the case.

The Attorney General is of opinion that Cap<sup>t</sup> Armstrong may attach by process from a court of equity the arrears of pay due to a [underline: discharged] soldier in the hands of the paymaster of the army to satisfy his claim if it be just. A Soldier [underline: in service] cannot assign his pay but when [underline: discharged] he may assign his arrears of pay — So the 4<sup>th</sup> Section of the act entitled "an act making alterations in the Treasury and War departments, has been and is to be understood. If indeed the arrears of pay due to a [underline: discharged] soldier were not assignable either in law or equity, there would be some ground for an opinion that they could not be attached in equity. The contrary however has been determined — 2 Black. reports 1137—

When the justice of the claim shall be established either by the agreement of the debtor and creditor, or by the sentence of a competent court, the paymaster after deducting the amount of the [underline: costs of suit] if any shall have occurred out of the arrears of pay in his hands, is to pay the balance according to the direction of the proprietor or of the court — The paymaster is not liable to costs for standing suit but they are payable out of the attached effects in the first instance, for without an order of [strikethrough: the proprietor] or the sentence of the court he would not be warranted in paying those arrears to any individual.

Charles Lee
Attorney General.

New London June 3<sup>d</sup> 1796

Since I wrote to you on the 9<sup>th</sup> of April I have made some progress in the examination of the Musket Cartridges & many of them. I have found entirely damaged. They were generally found damaged than Saltpetre received in that State. At the same time I have discovered that a number of those returned as good are also unfit for service and even in the same Cartridge a Section of the Powder to Wit that next to the life of it has been found to be good while the cover fixed next to the Ball was in a decayed State, this circumstance has suggested to me the Propriety of Making a general and thorough examination of the State of them, And am deterred from that pursuit only on account of the loss of the Skafer made use of which will I think in general be unavoidable. I have, however it may be of greater importance to maintain the quality of the Powder with precision supposing the total loss of the Skafer in doing it, to the consequence than to remain in a great degree ignorant of its state for the sake of preserving the Skafer — In this particular Sir I must beg to be favored with your instructions how to Act. — I am all present engaged in dusting and sorting the Powder in Barrels and also emptying the Powder out of the Cannon

Cannon Cartigns unconnected with Ball which I treat in the same manner and have the whole put away in Barrels — I am at a loss to know what to do with the fixed Cannon Cartiges. Most of the Flannel is considerably injured by the Moth, the quality of the Powder I cannot fully ascertain without unfixing them, and am unwilling to do it without your directions — If on the whole you shall think it best that there be a general and renewed handling of all the Powder, and that it be put into Barrels I will proceed as soon as I shall receive your instructions — I shall be employed in the business for — I am now engaged for perhaps two or three Weeks, and have to beg you will please to favor me with an answer to this letter as soon as Possible

I have the honor to be Respectfully

Sir

Your Obedient Servant

[W<sup>m</sup> Bolls]

Samuel Hodgson Esquire

Sir,

West Point, June 7<sup>th</sup> 1796

Sir,

Your favors of the 20<sup>th</sup> & 28 ultimo I have received. I have drawn on the Se- cretary of the Treasury for the two thousand dollars agreeably to the advice you gave me in yours of the 20, and have received a considerable part of the money for my draft. The receving the remainder will, but in part diminish my want of money for public purposes, if the repairing of the powder magazines & [strikethrough: military] storehouses should have to be continued.

The money business has, for a great many months, been the source of a great deal of embarrassment & uneasiness to me on several accounts. When I have the pleasure of seeing you I will mention them to you.

June 11. A confluence of business that required immediate attention prevented my finishing this letter until today. And now I have only time to mention, that I enclose Col<sup>o</sup>. Conard's requisition for one hundred & fifty four dollars, & the Officers & Doctors receipts for the same — and to add, that I have vouchers for about two thousand dollars, but time will not permit my arranging them to go by this mail.

I have received your favors of the 30 ultimo & 11 instant. Tomorrow I will write receipts & send them to Col<sup>o</sup>. Bird for the April pay of the ordnance detachment. I furnished Col<sup>o</sup>. Conard with a copy of your favor to me of the 11 instant.

I am, with great respect,

Sir,

P.S. I also enclose a pay roll for the pay of the ordnance detachment for the month of May.

Your most obedient, humble servant,

Geo. Fleming.

[William Simmons Sec<sup>y</sup> War]

(Sir,)

By the act to ascertain and fix the military establishment of the United States passed the 30<sup>th</sup> May 1796 (a copy of which is enclosed) you will perceive that after the last day of October next only two Companies of Dragoons are to be continued in Service.

53971:
To M<sup>r</sup> Edward Price

Sir, War Office, June 14<sup>th</sup> 1796

I have received your letter of the 9<sup>th</sup> of April on the 10<sup>th</sup> Instant.

To enable the Secretary of War to exhibit to the President, from time to time, the actual situation of the Indian trade, and state of the Stock employed to carry it on, it will be necessary that each factor should lodge with this department a copy of his day book, which should contain all entries of goods received for the Indian trade, all goods sold to the Indians, and entries of all furs and Pottery received in exchange therefor, with every expence and transaction relating this business, So that regular accounts may be raised from the Same.

You will, therefore, be pleased to make out a copy of your day book down to the present time, which you will transmit, and keep this department regularly furnished with a copy of each successive months transactions.

I am Sir &c.

[Signed]

James McHenry

War office 17 June 1796

My dear Sir

Indeed I am truly sorry at the situation in which you found Mrs Murray on your return. I did hint that the [undecipherable] indisposed before leaving this city; but I cannot but ascribe her getting worse to [undecipherable] absence from her, seeing as I can very well conceive how your presence might have added to her consolation. You and I have long thought of your wife the best friend in the world. I am not therefore surprised at your alarm, and hope that this very circumstance has served to increase it more than any real danger she may be exposed to.

It is not easy to determine whether, the sea voyage or going to the Springs, ought to be preferred. You might prefer the former. This being the case I would give it a trial; because if the springs should not have [undecipherable], she might resort, and you also, that her own [undecipherable] had been neglected.

I send you annexed two of your acts respecting western land. The operation of these acts will be to raise the value of the land warrants. I believe they have already had that effect.

I put your Worcester friend in a way of getting a clue to his case. I sent him to the brokers to ascertain the selling price of deferred three and six per cents. This obtained he had only to divide the fund into three component parts, and buy the current price for each with or without an interest as he could make his bargain.

Things have varied but little since you left us. The Flying fish has made a capture as you have seen by the papers, and Mr Adet has given a severe answer as you have not seen by the papers.

I have not got into my House and I miss you very much.

Yours affectionately
James McHenry

[for France]     War Office June 20 1796

[M<sup>r</sup> William Pennock
Norfolk]

As there are again many live Oak knees in the Navy yards at Gosport that are suitable for the Frigate building here, and of which M<sup>r</sup> Humphreys is in immediate want, endeavour to request you will be pleased to send such of them to Philadelphia as may be seized by the first favourable opportunity.

[for]     War Office June 30 1796.

[Ass<sup>t</sup> of the Treasury]

As there is a prospect of a considerable progress being made towards compleating the Hulls of the Frigate building at Boston this Summer, and a sufficient quantity of Hemp will be required for manufacturing the necessary Cordage for the Rigging &c which I am anxious to have in readiness for [use] immediately after the Vessel is launched, and as considerable time will be necessary to go through the various branches of manufacturing and preparing the Rigging; I there therefore request you will be pleased to give the necessary directions proper for procuring the same quantity of Hemp for that Frigate as was furnished for the Frigate at this place —

Should there be a difficulty of purchasing at [or] near Boston I have been informed a quantity may be procured in this City.

Know all Men by these Presents, That I Samuel Chapman Late Soldier in the Amnuetician Line

in the service of the United States of America, for a valuable and full consideration to me in hand paid, at or before the execution hereof, by John Brady

the receipt whereof, is hereby acknowledged, have, and by these presents do sell, release, transfer and assign unto him, his heirs, executors, administrators and assigns forever, all my right, title, interest, property, claim and demand, which I [strikethrough: now have or] may have or hereafter claim, or my heirs, executors, or administrators, may at any time hereafter have, to all and singular the lands, pay, arrearages of pay, cloathing, rations, rewards, bounties, gratuities, prize-money and other demands, due and owing to me from the United States, or from any particular State. And do hereby for me my heirs, executors, and administrators covenant and agree, to and with the said John Brady

his heirs, executors, administrators and assigns, that they being reasonably aided and abetted, shall, and may, at any time hereafter, in our name, and at the costs and charges of him, his heirs, executors, administrators and assigns, make, seal, execute and deliver, or cause, or procure to be made, sealed, executed and delivered, any and every such instrument, deed and other thing or things, conveyances, evidences, powers, and assurances in the law, for the perfect granting, conveying, releasing, transferring and assigning, all the right, title, interest, property, claim and demand, which I now have, or which my heirs, executors, or administrators, shall, or may have after my decease, in, to, all and singular the lands and other the premises hereby granted and assigned unto him, his heirs, executors, administrators and assigns, as by him, or their counsel, learned in the law, shall be reasonably advised, devised, or required. And I do hereby make, constitute and appoint the said Brady

my true and lawful attorney irrevocably, to ask, demand, recover and receive, of and from the United States, or from any particular State, or from any person or persons, acting by, from, or under them, or either of their authorities, all and singular the lands, pay, arrearages of pay, cloathing, rations, rewards, bounties, gratuities, prize-money, and other demands, due and owing to me, and also to ask demand and receive, of from and by any manner of ways or means whatsoever, and, upon receipt, thereof, to execute and deliver sufficient and requisite releases, recitals, and acquittances for the same, and by good and sufficient conveyances and assurances in the law, to grant, bargain, sell, release and confirm the said lands to the purchaser or purchasers thereof, his, her, or their heirs and assigns forever. And also to fill, sign and transfer, all certificates, and registered or other stock, now, or hereafter, standing in my name

in the books of the treasury of the United States, or of any particular State, for or in consequence

of services as aforesaid, with power of attorney, or attorneys under him, for the purposes aforesaid to make and substitute, and with all lawful acts to do and to effectuate the premises as fully and effectually, to all intents and purposes, as might or could do, by being personally present, and to have and hold the same, hereby absolutely ratifying and confirming all, and whatsoever his said attorney, or his substitute or substitutes, shall, or may do, or cause to be done therein, by virtue hereof. War Office 23. June 1796.

Sir,

I do myself the honour to inclose you a duplicate of my letter of the 20. instant forwarded by express to which permit me to intrest your attention.

As the frontiers of the State of Tennessee may occasionally require the protection of militia, it may not be improper to mention; that no claims for Militia services, which have not been authorized by the President can be admitted or paid agreeably to existing laws. And, that altho a State may call out its militia or any part thereof, without the consent of Congress or the President, when invaded or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay; yet no pay can be allowed them, or remuneration made to the State till the whole circumstances of the case be laid before Congress and have received their decision and approbation.

Should you conceive the services of any part of the Militia to be requisite for the defence of the frontiers you will be pleased to mention it to me, with the circumstances which induce the opinion and the number deemed necessary, that it may be submitted to the President for his consideration and orders —

I am Sir
with the highest Respect
Your obed Servant
James McHenry

54121:
[The Secretary of War]

Sir,

Your letter of the 27<sup>th</sup> Ult: by Post, with its enclosures (the originals of which, I return) came to my hands on Wednesday — and your other letters of the 27<sup>th</sup> & 28<sup>th</sup> by Express, was received about five oclock yesterday afternoon.

The accounts brought in the latter are very pleasing indeed, inasmuch as they will serve to remove the doubts of the credulous, with respect to the Western Posts; and when realized, be productive of that tranquillity, and peace with the Indians which, in itself, is so desirable and has been so much wished and longed for, by every real friend to his Country.

It is my desire that the charges exhibited against General Wayne or Brigadier Wilkenson, with the letters of crimination on both sides, should be laid before the heads of Departments; and your and their opinions reported to me on the measures

measures necessary to be pursued to do justice to the Public; — the accused; — and the accuser; — as also where, and by whom, the enquiry is to be made; — with the preliminary steps necessary thereto. —

There are no Officers, I conceive of sufficient rank to constitute a Court before whom the Commander in chief can be brought. — Is the matter then to come before Congress? — In what manner? — My first impression relative to this business (though not maturely, or distinctly formed) is, that General Wayne ought, immediately, to be furnished with a copy of all the charges exhibited against him by the Brigadier, in order as many of them are of old standing, he may have time allowed him to recollect circumstances; and to see what counter evidence can be produced, or what satisfactory explanations can be given; that he may not be unprepared for trial when so ever he is called upon. —

It may be well, by discreet impressions, to stimulate the present Governor of

of Tennessee to an effectual repression of encroachments on Indian Territory secured to them by Treaties; — but the honor of the government, and the Peace of the Union, require that if he is not decisive, the Laws relative thereto be not suspended, or trifled with; — but promptly, and energetically, with temper & prudence, enforced. —

I shall not speak upon the new model of the Army now, but shall take more time to consider the scheme for resolving the Legion into four Regiments, on the plan you have suggested. —

In speaking of the Generals, Wayne & Wilkinson, I omitted to add, as my opinion, that the latter (if leave has not been given already) ought to obtain the furlough he has asked; and as soon as the former joins the Army, — for no good can result from both being with it in the irritable temper they are in, at the same time. —

Mount Vernon 1<sup>st</sup> July 1796.

G<sup>o</sup> Washington

Sir

I here herein inclosed, you a return of ordnance Stores at this post, also a return of cloathing both for the months of June and July. on my former letter the ninth of May 1796. I acquainted you with the want of cloathing for the Soldiers under my Command — which you may see by the returns I have sent you. and by the one I now send you. Coats. Vests. Hats. Linen Overalls are much wanted — the Soldiers haveing none. but old wollen rags to put on this hot weather. which causes great murmering and discontent.

The two brass field pieces are also much wanted here for the use of the company. I hope you will send them by the first opportunity — (if not already sent) none can be got here —.

Department of State July 8. 1796.

Dear Sir

The President, in two letters I have received this week, mentions three points for consideration.

1.<sup>st</sup> How soon & "in what manner" the Cherokee boundary can and ought to be run & marked, agreeably to the treaty of Holston.

2. What can be done relative to the appointment of an Indian agent [superintendent] in the room of Governor Blount; and the Agents for carrying on the Indian trade.

He will expect a report as soon as our opinions are formed.

I have conversed with M<sup>r</sup> Wolcott: We are both of opinion that the first step towards building the frigate, is to send M<sup>r</sup> Fox to the different Navy yards, to take an account of the timber, and to converse with the principal builders, to see on what terms & within what time they will, any of them, undertake to have her completed. We think it ineligible and fruitless to advertise for a contract. The explanations which M<sup>r</sup> Fox can give to the master builders will

enable them to state their terms, which he will bring back with him, & then a choice may be made. I am convinced that it will be in vain to seek a substitute for M<sup>r</sup> Fox; & I beg you to decide thereon that his instructions may be prepared to enable him to start by furthest on Monday.

respectfully yours
T. Pickering

[The Secretary of War]

Sir

I arrived at this place on the 5<sup>th</sup> Instant &found that the man Powers had been with G— M— or at Greeneville for several days, but returned I descended the Ohio about the 20<sup>th</sup> ultimo for the rapids, where he probably would be delayed a week or more, he shewed certain instructions from General Wilkinson to put a suit of interrogatories, to a certain Newman, &if he answered them to Satisfaction, he wou'd reward him Powers with One Hunn.d red Dollars, either for them or the person of Newman,

Powers had a number of lette.rs &c &c — on &paroled that his object in visiting Greeneville, was to obtain materials for writing a history of this Country &c

On or about the 29<sup>th</sup> ultimo De Collet &c came a croft by land from Lexington to this place, he immediately waited upon the commandant, and enquired where he find G — M— was, he was informed that he had marched from Greeneville some days since for the rapids of the Miamis, & that I was uncertain where he then was, De Collet appeared greatly disappointed &said that he wanted much to have an interview with

that great & popular General, if he had a certainty of overtaking him he wou'd follow; that he had a great number of letters for him, which he wished to present with his own hands, but must be the present content himself by enclosing them, & request them to be forwarded by an immediate & safe express; & that he De Collet wou'd proceed to the rapids of this where he shou'd have occasion to wait a week or ten days; a very large packet was placed in the hands of the Commandant by De Collet early next morning addressed to G — M— with reiterated injunctions of dispatch & safety;

De Collet immediately descended the river & was met on this side the rapids, by A<sup>dj<sup>t</sup></sup> S<sup>t</sup> Clair, (who has been appointed to command in the Militia and Prothonotary of the Illinois Country by Gov<sup>r</sup> S<sup>t</sup> Clair,) They had a few moments conversation De Collet said that he shou'd wait at the rapids several days, in order to see the country & to transact some business of consequence after which he probably wou'd accompany S<sup>t</sup> Clair to The Illinois;

Not knowing the character of S<sup>t</sup> Clair & from some other circumstances, I did not think it prudent to make any confidential communications to him respecting De Collet.

S<sup>t</sup> Clair said he waited upon me in behalf of the inhabitants of the Kashaskias or Illinois who were anxious for a small post in that Quarter. That the troops cou'd be supported by the produce of that Country to a certainty, & on more moderate terms, than at this place; that a post at that place wou'd have a happy effect &give energy to the laws & respectability to Government. That the Spaniards in that Quarter were infusing improper ideas into the minds of the People, & imposing them with the apathy & imbecility of the United States,

I requested him to give me a particular statement in writing upon the subject matter upon which he was speaking, which he promised to do as soon as he returned to that Country; That he was now ready to descend the River, with a cargo of merchandise & that it was probable he wou'd be accompanied by De Collet. That his intention was to land at Rapace & proceed on horseback to the Kashaskias &to send his boat around by the Mississippi; That he expected De Collet wou'd accompany him, & that his boat wou'd also go around to that place;

I then communicated to him the complaint made against Cap<sup>t</sup> Pike for a supposed insult offered the Spanish Flag, & that I was in the act of preferring

that Officer demanding of him a true state of facts relative to that subject. M<sup>r</sup> S<sup>t</sup> Clair said he had heard of the complaint, & that Cap<sup>t</sup> Pike had only done his duty — that the insult was offered to him by the Spanish Officer in attempting to pass his post. I then requested him to be so obliging as to take charge of my letter to Pike & the printed Acts of Congress for carrying into effect the Treaty with Spain &c<sup>c</sup> and to assure the Spaniards of the friendly disposition of this Government towards that Nation; that my dispatches wou'd be ready in an half an hour, & embraced that opportunity to enclose in the packet a private Note to Cap<sup>t</sup> Pike a copy of which is now transmitted;

In addition to this I shall immediately give orders to Cap<sup>t</sup> Pasteur the commandant of Fort Knox, similar to those forwarded by Cap<sup>l</sup> Taylor to Cap<sup>t</sup> Pike, so that I trust the nefarious machinations of the enemies of our Country, will be fully discovered & the prime movers receive the punishment due to their demerits; with the above wishes and Sentiments I have the honor to be

Your Most Ob<sup>t</sup>
Hum<sup>ble</sup>
[signed] [undecipherable] [signed] Anty Wayne

To Josiah Fox,

you will be pleased forthwith to proceed to New York Portsmouth in New Hampshire and Boston.

The general objects of your Journey to those Towns are

1. To examine a sort and arrange, into several parcells the Ship timbers and planks the property of the United States in the different yards in New York Portsmouth, and Boston —

2 To examine into the state of the Naval Stores at those places and procure for them greater protection and security where wanted.

3 To obtain from the principal Shipbuilders of New York Portsmouth, and Boston upon what terms and within what time they will agree to build a 36 Gun Frigate of the dimensions described in sketch A.

You will arrange the Ship timbers and Planks according to the following Classes

Class N° 1. will comprehend the number of pieces of live Oak at the respective yards fit for the Frigates whose building have been suspended, and exclusive of the pieces requisite for those under construction.

In this Class as well as in all the other Classes you will report the Timbers or planks agreeable to their names

and use N° A from [undecipherable] September, likewise specifying the exact number of each

Class N° 2 will comprehend the number of pieces of live Oak unsuitable for the Frigates building or suspended but which may be used in the construction of Frigate sketch A.

Class N° 3 will comprehend the number of pieces of live Oak unsuitable for any of the Frigates including those A by reason of defects or other causes, noting those causes

Class N° 4 will exhibit 1° The number of pieces of [undecipherable] suitable and wanted for Frigate sketch A. 2 The number of pieces unsuitable and not wanted for the Frigates under construction, or for Frigate sketch A

Class N° 5 will exhibit a statement of the plank in each Yard arranged according to their thickness, lengths and kinds N° the kind and quantity wanted for Frigate sketch A exclusive of the quantity necessary to compleat the Frigate at Boston 2 the surplus assorted into its kinds

Class N° 6 will exhibit the number, figure, and kinds of Masts, and Spars —

It being contemplated to dispose of the Timbers assorted under Class N° 3, those under 2 Class N° 4, and the plank under 2 Class N° 5, and such of the Masts and Spars as may not be wanted, or would be injured by keeping, you will therefore endeavour to form an Opinion of what those would probably sell for at the places where deposited, and report the same

The timbers ordered from New York for the

Frigates building at Philadelphia and Baltimore are to be excluded from your estimates

You are to see the timbers received for future use carefully piled up as well as the timbers appointed for Frigate sketch A and the whole protected against the weather by proper Sheds and against Thefts by enclosures.

A person by the name of W<sup>m</sup> Wedderburns now comes forward and demands of me a formal Power of Attorney from his Alex<sup>t</sup> Scott in justification for what I have done, and threatens me with a prosecution — Will you therefore be so obliging as to send me a Copy of the Order upon which the proper Officer of the Department issued the Certificates — It is an unpleasant thing to be now troubled, and exposed to the expense of Law suits, particularly when I reflect on the purity of my motives — and, this case may not be the only one, for if a precedent be set, I may be exposed to perpetual law squabbles, let me lived as long as I may — I anticipate your ready disposition to serve any person, and will therefore only add, that a compliance with much obliges —

Your Ob<sup>t</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup>

Recruiting Instructions
For Captain William Preston of the 4<sup>th</sup>
Sub Legion
in the Service of the United States.

SIR,

YOU are immediately to commence the recruiting service in the State of Virginia ————— The principal rendezvous will be at Lynchburg —————
A contractor will be appointed who ————————————————
—————————————————— will furnish your recruits with rations, barracks, barrack-utensils, straw and fuel; and also obtain such necessary medicinal assistance as your recruits may require.

The recruiting service is sometimes abused, both as it respects the individuals recruited and the public at large,—That is, recruits are unwarily and unworthily entangled, contrary to their intentions: such men generally desert the service, at some critical moment, or serve grudgingly; and set bad examples to others; or, unsuitable persons are engaged, who are constitutionally defective and unfit for the hardships incident to a military life.

Although the character of a recruiting officer may require peculiar talents, yet it is in the power of every officer to conduct himself with candor, integrity and industry.

In order therefore to avoid the errors of this business, the following instructions are to serve as the general rules and principles of your conduct:

1st. The recruits are to be inlisted for [strikethrough: three] lives years, unless sooner discharged.
as particularly mentioned in the Act of the 30 May herewith inclosed
2d. Each Recruit is to receive a bounty [strikethrough: of Eight Dollars];—but no part of this sum is to be advanced until the recruit shall have been fairly inlisted and sworn before a Magistrate, according to the form herein prescribed, and then only the said sum is to be advanced in such proportions as the judgment of the recruiting officer shall dictate, until experience shall in some degree have ascertained the fidelity of the recruit. Any money advanced contrary to this direction, will be at the risque of the recruiting officer.

3d. Every recruiting officer will be allowed the sum of Two Dollars, for the trouble and expence of inlisting each recruit.

( 2 )

4th. The utmost fairness is to be used by the recruiting officers in engaging the recruits; no individual therefore is to be inlisted in a state of intoxication, or be sworn until after he shall have been inlisted for the space of twenty-four hours.

5th. Each recruit (musicians excepted) must be five feet and six inches in heighth, without shoes:—he must also be healthy, robust, and found in his limbs and body, in all respects; and to ascertain which he must be thoroughly examined, previously to inlistment.—But if, notwithstanding this direction, a recruit should have any secret disease, at the time of his inlistment, the expence of his cure, if retained in service, shall be deducted from his pay.

6th. Each recruit, before he is sworn, is to have distinctly read to him the rules and articles of war against mutiny and desertion, and relative to the administration of justice; and the act of Congress of the 30th of [strikethrough: May] April, 1796, establishing the pay, rations, clothing, and compensation in cases of disability; and also the act providing for raising and organiz- [strikethrough: ing corps of artificers and docompanies,] after which he is to take the following oath, before a Magistrate, to wit:

"I A. B. do solemnly swear (or affirm, as the case may be) to bear
" true allegiance to the United States of America, and to serve them ho-
" nestly and faithfully against all their enemies or opposers whomsoever,
" and to observe and to obey the orders of the President of the United
" States of America, and the orders of the officers appointed over me
" according to the articles of war."

7th. Each recruit (musicians excepted) must be above eighteen and under [strikethrough: thirty-five] forty five years of age.

8th. No negro, mulatto, or indian, to be recruited.

9th. All the recruits, to be natives of fair conduct, or foreigners of unequivocal characters for sobriety and fidelity, and who have been at least five years in the country. Any recruiting officer inlisting a vagrant, or transient person who shall desert before marching from the place of rendezvous shall reimburse out of his pay the loss sustained by such desertion. It is therefore important that the officers be attentive on this point.

10th. As soon as the recruits shall be assembled at the rendezvous, they are to be taught, by gentle methods, regularity of conduct, as it shall respect cleanliness of their persons, diet and rooms, and also due subordination, and they are to be exercised at least four hours in every day in the attitudes, and other first principles of a soldier.

( 3 )

11th. The commanding officer at each place of rendezvous must make out, on every Saturday, a return of the number of recruits under his command, and of the number joined during the course of the week, and transmit the same to the War-Office by the next post; and also such information as he may possess, of any officers out on the recruiting service.

12th. You, or the commanding officer at Lynchburg are to sign returns for the issues of all rations, and other necessary supplies for the troops; and on the Saturday of each week the returns made in the course of the week are to be taken up and one general return made out and signed for the rations received in the course of the week, noticing the daily issues.

13th. No allowance is to be made for the expences of a recruit, until he joins at the rendezvous, the bounty being considered as adequate for that object.

The recruits will be mustered and inspected previously to their marching from the place of rendezvous.

14th. The utmost industry and vigor must be observed in the recruiting service agreeably to the foregoing rules.

[strikethrough: 15th. The officers who are to be inlifted in purfuance of the law are to enliſt for the following branches: Two Wheelwrights. Two Blackſmiths and Two Coopers. The pay and allowances to the artificers muft be confidered as ſlightly liberal perſons, are to be engaged, but who have ſerved a regular apprenticeſhip to their trades and who can produce in writing a good character from two reſpectable freeholders for ſobriety and induſtry.]

You will observe by the law the liberal pay established for the non-commissioned officers; this will be a good reason that you should not place any man in the quality of a Serjeant or Corporal but of a most excellent character.

Greensburg July 18.<sup>t</sup> 1796

Sir,

I am at present laid up at this place, and am much afraid I shall not be able to prosecute my Journey with the expedition I intended, having been confined to my Bed these two days before. — The Person you know of has left Pittsburg, where, I learn from a confidential Person, he has not been so guarded as might have been expected. The Rout he proposed was to follow General Wilkinson from Cincinnati — to return to that Place after having seen him to make the Tour of Kentucky — proceed from thence to the Illinois Country, and then descend the Mississippi to New Orleans. He reports that the ratification of the Treaty with Spain will be delayed, and that the Stipulation in that Treaty with great Britain respecting the Navigation of the Mississippi will be made the pretext, and that Measures to produce that Effect have already been taken by the present Directory of France. — He has been on great intimacy with Judge Inness who was at Pittsburg when he arrived there, and it would not surprise me if he had entered into his Views — I may wrong him, but my suspicions arise from the connexions I know he had with the Persons most opposed to the Government —

I hope to be at Cincinnati before his return to that Place and well follow or precede him to the Country below. Measures have been taken to get possession of the Correspondence that may take Place between the French Minister and him, but they cannot be effected without Money, and I do not yet know the price — I have fixed on the Expectation that it shall not be wanting, and I request you to inform me, by the return of the Post, how far it may be engaged, the manner of obtaining it. As soon as I am able to ride, I shall proceed to Pittsburg from whence I hope to give you more explicit information.

With great respect I have the honor to be

Sir
your obedient Servant

A. S<sup>t</sup> Clair

War Office, August 13. 1796.

Sir,

M<sup>r</sup> Stephen Hillis having been appointed with the approbation of the President of the United States, deputy Pay Master and Storekeeper of the public property in Tennessee, I here annex a Copy of his Instructions, and Powers.

With respect to his powers as Storekeeper you will perceive, That he is accountable for all public property placed under his Superintendance, and that no part or parcel thereof is to be drawn out of the public Store, but by an order signed or countersigned by the Agent of the department of War. War Office August 23. 1796

Sir

The Agents appointed by the State of Georgia to attend the meeting of the Representatives of the Creek Nation at Coleraine, have no doubt informed you of their refusal to sell any part of their lands.

I am directed by the President to express on this occasion, his sincere regret, that a conference which he had flattered himself would have obtained the object for which it was principally projected, has failed of success.

As he felt in this manner, he could not but read with surprize, the protest of the Agents against the proceedings of the Commissioners of the United States, and lament that regulations calculated to inspire the Indians with confidence in the fairness of the intended negociation, should have worn to those Gentlemen a different aspect.

Neither could he ascribe the refusal of the Indians to sell to the State to any other cause, than that which they have assigned; in as much as his invitation described the land to them, which it was the wish of Georgia to purchase, and requested that they should send their Representatives to the meeting, charged with the sense of the Nation: and in as much as the Commissioners of the United States had his instructions to facilitate the purchase.

To remove however every cause for doubt on this subject, the President has determined to have ascertained in the most unequivocal mode, whether the mind of the Nation has undergone any change relative to the land in question, and if it has, the terms upon which they will sell it. Should this enquiry turn out favourably, the President has directed me to say, that he will readily concur to open another negociation.

The Creeks, as you will see by the Treaty, (a copy of which is inclosed) have among other things agreed, that Military and Trading Posts may be erected within their boundary line, and that all animosities for past aggressions, shall henceforth cease, with an exception to the violators of the Treaty of New York, now under arrest who are to abide the decision of the laws.

These circumstances which evidence the sincerity of the Indians, and their disposition to peace, offer as you must perceive, the fairest opportunity of leading them by degrees to grant whatever is reasonable and does not involve their ruin. It is therefore to be presumed, that the Citizens of Georgia will patiently wait their operation, and avoid whatever might disturb the tranquillity thus re established.

You no doubt in particular will duly appreciate the blessings of peace, and heartily co operate with the President in every measure calculated to perpetuate its continuance.

With this view, the President has directed such an arrangement, and use of the Troops of the United States, as ought to satisfy the Indians that their rights will be protected; and the Inhabitants of the frontiers, that they have nothing to apprehend from the Indians.

These arrangements rendering it unnecessary to keep up the Militia Corps of Infantry and Cavalry, the Agent of the Department of War in Georgia, will be directed to settle their Muster and Pay rolls up to the 18<sup>th</sup> September ensuing, after which time they will be considered as discharged.

With the greatest respect

I am Sir —

your obed<sup>t</sup> Servant

signed James McHenry
Sec<sup>t</sup> of War

His Excellency
the Governor of Georgia.
54701:
[Copy of a letter from the Secretary of War to Lieutenant Colonel Commandant Gaither, commanding the Troops of the United States in Georgia.]

War Office, August 25<sup>th</sup> 1796.

Sir,

The President has received the Treaty entered into with the Creeks at Coleraine and information from the Commissioners of the disposition of the Indians to live in peace with and cultivate the friendship of the United States. So far the meeting has issued favorably. There are however circumstances relative to it which ought not to be disregarded.

It cannot be ascertained at this time, what may be the consequence of the refusal of the Creeks to sell their land to the State of Georgia; or whether the desire to intrude upon it may not be encrease by the light in which the Agents of that State have unfortunately viewed or may represent the measures taken by government to obtain it, or in what manner the civil decision in the case of Harrison and others may affect the Indians.

In this state of things the President has deemed it adviseable to give such an arrangement to the military force within the Indian line, as may on the one hand, prevent the Indians from coming into effect harming or hostile incursions on the frontier Inhabitants of Georgia, and on the other hand, the Citizens of the United States from intruding on the Indian land contrary to Treaty and Law.

54744:
To Silas Dinsmoor, Temporary Indian Agent in the Cherokee Nation

Sir,

You will be pleased to have the annexed talk to the Cherokee Nation from the President carefully distributed, translated and explained in their respective Towns and Tribes; you will also consider it as forming a part of your standing instructions, at least, so far as you may have it in your power to facilitate the accomplishment of the objects to which it has relation.

It is to be lamented, that the experiments, heretofore made, with a view to civilize the Indians, have issued so unsuccessfully. Notwithstanding the pains that have been taken on this subject, the Indian differs but little at this day from what he was when first known to the Europeans. Neither the time which has since elapsed; nor our intercourse with them; nor our establishments among them, seem to have rendered them more civilized or less savage. We still find them characterized by the same habits and manners; the same pursuits and pleasures, varied only by certain incidental vices derived from the outcasts of Society.

What is it that can have perpetuated such an uniformity of character, and acted as a barrier against the different attempts that have been made to civilize them?

Is not the cause to be found in their mode of life? Is it not hunting and trapping which continues them indolent, savage and warlike, and must not this practice be broken in upon before they can be made to approach civilization? To trap and hunt for subsistence amidst immense deserts and wilderness would gradually approximate civilized Man to the Savage. To Benjamin Hawkins Esquire principal temporary Agent for Indian Affairs, South of the Ohio

The President of the United States has and by these presents constitutes you Principal Temporary Agent for Indian Affairs, within the Indian Nations South of the Ohio, and North of the territorial line; and confiding in your judgment, discretion and integrity, charges you with the execution of the following instructions and such others as you may from time to time receive relative to the nature of your appointment.

It appearing from the conferences between the Representatives of the Creek Nation and Commissioners of the United States at the meeting at Coleraine that the former have required, and the latter promised, that the President would send into their country, within four months from the date of the Treaty, there entered into, a person instructed upon the following points.

1. To assist in designating and fixing upon proper sites for trading houses and posts; and to explain to the Nation by Towns and Tribes, the reason for having them established within their boundary line.

2. To explain the plan of Trade to the different Towns or Tribes.

3. To confer with and advise the Nation, how it ought to conduct itself, in the case of the Murderers of the Indians, should they escape without being punished —

4. To explain the object for running the boundary line between Spain and the United States. —

War Office, *September* 13*th*, 1796.

Sir,

THERE will be wanted for the frigate defined for the Mediterranean, twenty-four nine pounders, and twelve fix pounders; and for the three frigates now under conſtruction, forty twelve pounders; it is requested therefore, that a contract may be entered into for the delivery of this number of cannon, on or before the firſt of April enſuing.

To obviate as much as poſſible diſpute with the perſon who may engage to furniſh them, it may be proper that the contract ſhould compriſe the following conditions:

1. That the guns be caſt in the ſolid, and bored.

2. That the twenty-four nine pounders, and twelve fix pounders, conform exactly in weight, bore, caliber and length, to Britiſh ſhip guns of the ſame dimenſions now in uſe.

3. That the forty twelve pounders, be formed agreeably to the dimenſions laid down in the annexed drawing.

4. That the guns, after having been bored, and before undergoing any proof, ſhall be examined by one or more perſons, to be appointed by the Preſident of the United States, in the preſence of ſuch other perſons as ſhall be named by the owner of the works. That this examination ſhall commence by a verification of the diameters of the different parts, and aſcertainment whether there are more internal and external cavities or defects than are ſpecified in the annexed table, exhibiting the defects which are to be tolerated. That in all caſes where the bore or caliber is found to be leſs, than the diameter preſcribed, and the defects not greater than thoſe tolerated, the cannon will be returned to the boring machine, to be enlarged, before being proved; and in all caſes where the defects are greater than thoſe tolerated, the examination ſhall ceaſe and the cannon be rejected.

5. That the inſtruments commonly employed to aſcertain dimenſions and diſcover cavities or holes, in the external and internal parts of guns, ſhall be uſed on ſuch occaſions.

6. That the touch hole ſhall end in the cannon, at the middle of the rounding of the axis of the bottom of the bore. That ſhould any defect be found in the touch hole, deeper than the twentieth of an inch, the cannon cannot be admitted to proof. The inner diameter ſhall here be of well beaten iron.

7. That the trunnions ſhall be perpendicular to the verticle plane, which is ſuppoſed to paſs through the touch-hole, and to cut the bore into two equal parts. That the upper part of the trunnions ſhall be level with the centre of the caliber, or bore, and that the ufual relative weight be preferred between the breeech and chace.

8. That the proof by powder, ſhall be as follows—viz. Each cannon ſhall be proved by two ſucceſſive diſcharges. The charge of the powder for the firſt diſcharge, ſhall be equal to two-thirds of the weight of the ball; and for the ſecond, equal to half the weight of the ball. The cannon ſhall be firſt rammed down, with a wad over it; two balls ſhall be placed over that, with a wad in between, another wad laid over, which ſhall be well rammed down; the balls to be meaſured, ſo as to allow a ſufficient windage, and approved of by the officers who ſhall make the inſpection, and the owner of the works, or any perſon whom he may appoint for that purpoſe.

9. That to aſcertain the ſtrength of the trunnions, the cannon muſt be placed on two pieces of wood, having indentions large enough to receive two-thirds of the trunnions, and with the hinder part at a ſufficient diſtance from where the trunnions lie, ſo as that the breeech may be elevated in any direction, but never ſo as to reſt on the ground. The proof by powder, muſt be made on theſe pieces of wood.

The necessity of the Sub Pay Masters settling their accounts more frequently is experienced here daily, you will therefore continue to put them in mind thereof.

If the forming an Estimate would meet with so much difficulty as your mention— it must be suspended and I as usual must form them from Fort Wayne's Returns— I proposed it to you thinking that you could forward an Estimate the same time the return is forwarded, and as you are on the Spot that you were possess'd of Information which it would be difficult for me to obtain, such as Soldiers being discharged, others inlisted, Officers on furlough, others joining &c. Corps of Artillerists & Engineers
Commandant of
Fort Johnson]

Fort Johnson,
29<sup>th</sup> Sept. 1796

Dear Sir

The Hospital being now separated from the Barracks, it becomes necessary that some one should be appointed to take care of the rooms, & administer to the sick such Medicines as I may direct.— For this duty, I should give the preference to a man, who could use more authority than a woman, & whose orders would be more attended to.—

Permit me to recommend Charles Murphy to you for this appointment. He has discharged this duty since the 1<sup>st</sup> inst. to my very great satisfaction— as well as to the Satisfaction of the sick.— He is an old Soldier, and is capable of feeling for the distresses of those, whom sickness obliges to go into the hospital— he is indefatigable in his attention— he regards the wants of the sick, night or day— he is perfectly sober— and in short is just such a man as I wish.—

As a recompense for this extra and fatiguing duty, permit me to request you to add 4 dollars to his monthly pay.— It will then only equal the sum allowed to the Nurses of the hospital, by the Act of Congress— And I assure you, no man in the Army, earns his pay with more fidelity.—

Accept my esteem
[underline: Fred.<sup>k</sup> Dalcho]

[Capt. M. Halteisen.]
55072:
[Mr. Jacob Sheafe]

Sir,                              War Office September 21. 1796.

I have been favoured with your letter of the 13 inst.

You will be pleased to send such pieces of live oak and plank, whether oak or pine to Boston as may be pointed out by Mr Fox and deliver such pieces of timber and oak or pine plank to Mr. Hacket as shall be selected by Mr Fox for the new frigate to be built by that Gentleman having the same previously valued.

The idea is that the timber previously destined for the new frigate be immediately separated from that which is to be reserved in future use, and the whole of it valued, after which it is to be at Mr. Hackets dispose. To be calling upon persons to value any piece as they should want it would be to give them, you and the public officers a great deal of unnecessary trouble. You will therefore be kind enough to notify Mr. Hacket to attend to make the selection and to appoint a person on his part to value upon the valuation.

Bedame who arrived at this Garrison under Lieut. Talman and was transferd to the Company of which I have the Command — and being order'd to Oswego I was induced to advance him the additional Bounty and for which you will find his receipt. I have charg'd the two Dollars upon those only who were recruited by myself being twelve in number, as will appear by the Certificate of the Comd't as having been duly mustered at this Garrison — I have never met a Desertion among those recruited by me except in one instance and that was a waiter taken by Capt. Morris to Nyork.

I will thank you to transmit the Balance of my Acc't. upon adjustment to this place

The Touch holes will be stopped with a wooden peg covered with tallow the Cannon will then be raised, and the chace surrounded with linnen, so that any water which may fall down the sides on filling the bore shall not be confounded with the drops that may filter through the mettle, and with the same view the water will be poured into the cavity by means of the spout of a watering pot. The water will be then pressed upon by a rammer covered with thick cloth, so as to fill exactly the muzzle of the Cannon. During this operation the exterior will be attentively watched to see whether any water passes through the mettle. If the least filtration appears the cannon will be refused.

War Department June 4. 1796

Sir,

I have the pleasure to inform you of your having been nominated by, and with the consent of the Senate appointed Quarter Master General to the Legion of the United States, and to request in the event if your accepting the Office, that you will forthwith join the Army, and enter upon its functions —— Permit me to suggest that as the Service will require that you should reside with the Army, so your absence from it (unless in the discharge of some indispensable duty of which the Officer Commanding the Army is to judge) will necessarily call for a new appoint— [strikethrough: ment] — and therefore, that you can consistently, with your private affairs devote your whole time and talents to the Department.

It may perhaps be proper to mention to you as you may not have seen the late law making certain modifications in the Military Establishment, that after the first of next March, the Quarter Master General must be an Officer in the line of the Army.

You will be pleased to favour me with an answer.

War Office 10<sup>th</sup> October 1796

Sir

The President has lately given activity to certain measures calculated to introduce among some of the Indian Nations, South of the Ohio, a more improved state of agriculture, a greater attention to cattle-raising, and by means of their women, the art of spinning and weaving.

To favour this plan I have been directed to have medals struck emblematic of these objects and the end in view, to be bestowed, instead of war-medals, upon such as may appear to deserve them.

It was my intention to have had these medals struck at our mint; but upon enquiry I am induced to prefer having them done in England, as well on account of the workmanship, as cheapness, and have therefore taken the liberty to request your kind Offices on the occasion.

I believe it would be some satisfaction to the President, were the assemblage of figures for the medal to be by M<sup>r</sup> Trumbul; and were the workmanship to correspond with the design. Will you therefore be so kind, at a moment of leisure to mention the thing to that Gentleman, and the ideas to be presented by

by the medal, or in case he should be absent, to some artist in his walk of Genius. I should wish to have the legend, or on some part of the medal, the words, "Presidency Geo Washington — 1796."

As these medals may be used for the chiefs of all the Indians in friendship with the United States, you will oblige me by ordering seven hundred to be struck by Bolton of Birmingham who has reputation in that line; five hundred of which to be of silver, somewhat larger than a dollar in circumference and about the thickness of half a dollar, the remainder to be of copper and if it will add to their beauty, thicker.

You will be pleased to direct them to be shipped to the Secretary of Wars and draw upon him for the amount, and to believe me to be very sincerely

The Construction of the Limitation Acts has fixed an established rule in the Office which cannot be deviated from short of an Act of Congress.

My dear McHenry

[undecipherable] That I have been remiss in not writing you before, I do admit, I have frequently determin'd it, & have been as often prevented. I presume You have heard the Issue of the Election between M<sup>r</sup> Wright and Myself, I had a Majority in the District of 698, (a Majority) in Talbot & Caroline, He was 45 Votes a Head in Queen Anne, where I am convinc'd He was fairly beaten, as one of his Men had the Effrontry to declare, that He had voted five Times for M<sup>r</sup> Wright under different Names. — My Friend M<sup>r</sup> Edw<sup>d</sup>. Wright voted for Me, the only One of that Name; this has increased my Sollicitude for his obtaining some satisfactory Office, & I must beg You not to forget Him. — I am afraid M<sup>rs</sup>. Sedgwick & Goodhue's Successors are not found Men. —

I find We are on the Point of loosing that best of Men, our amiable President, a Loss never to be repaired, I wish not to anticipate Evil, I cannot however help dreading the Consequence — God send Us a Federal Successor. —

I sincerely pray that little Swanwick [undecipherable] be overthrown — I lament much that Murray declin'd; it is however said that almost every Man in his District is Federal, if so, We must have a good Man — M<sup>r</sup> Bernis who was in the House of Delegates I hear is his Successor. — I have not heard whether Christie is reelected, I hope his Defeat much at [undecipherable] — I [have] been confin'd for nearly four Weeks with the Bilious Ague & Fever — [undecipherable]

Y<sup>rs</sup> Sincerely &c
[undecipherable] Henderson
