[Extract of a letter from the Secretary of State to the Secretary of War, dated]

Philadelphia. October 14, 1796.

D<sup>r</sup> Sir,

"When I was at Oneida in 1794, I considered it as an evil that the person (Wemple) employed and paid by the United States as a Blacksmith to work for the Oneida & Stockbridge Indians, should be engaged in a private concern that occupied most of his time; but especially that he should keep liquors for sale, in the very heart of the Oneida Settlement, and when they were resorting daily to their Grist-Mill, and frequently to get tools made or repaired. It was much complained of by the Indians, that it was extremely difficult to get the Smith to do their work; and not without such delays as rendered his services of trifling value. The Superintendent, Captain Chapin, removed him, and appointed his Brother, whom he represented as being a much better Character. But I am lately very satisfactorily informed that the Brother is treading in the same Steps. The father of these Men also lives there, and from his familiar knowledge of the Indian tongue and manners, and his own disposition, can promote all their vices, without contributing any thing to their improvement in the useful arts of civil life.

"Considering then how little service is rendered by Wemple, the present Smith, and the real mischiefs produced by his residence and keeping a dram shop in the midst of the Oneidas, I cannot with-hold from you my opinion, that the interest of the Indians and of the United States will be promoted, by dismissing the Smith altogether; and instead thereof to direct the Superintendent to employ, periodically, a faithful Smith from some neighbouring [village]

55267:
West point October 16<sup>th</sup> 1796.

Sir,

I received your letter of the 5<sup>th</sup> Inst<sup>t</sup>. respecting the officers who have Some accounts to settle with your Department and who have neglected to this day to do it. I have requested them, in order, to fulfill that Duty as soon as possible.

Captain Thompson being namely mentioned, I Sent him your letter to procure him the perusal of it.

As to Lieu<sup>t</sup>. Dayton, he has been absent from the garrison for Some time previous to my receiving your letter, and from Elisabeth Town the Secretary of War has ordered him on to Oswego where he will pass without passing to this Garrison, I will not therefore be able to communicate to him what relates to him in your letter.

I wish you could do Justice to the non comd officers & Privates who have been enlisted by Capt. Lee and others who have been prevented by Death or otherwise, from giving a proper account of the public Money trusted to them. They have just claim against the U.S, by what I can collect from other officers who are acquainted with the men, and it is not right they Should Suffer for the misconduct of the officers who Enlisted them.

respectfully I am, Sir, your ob<sup>t</sup>. Sew<sup>t</sup>.
J. Hy: Rochefontaine
D. Col. Comd<sup>t</sup>. of the Corps
of Art<sup>r</sup>. & Eng<sup>rs</sup>.

Pittsburg 15<sup>th</sup> October 1795.

Sir,

My being under a necessity of setting off on the 22<sup>d</sup> Ultimo to visit the posts of Fort Franklin, Le Boeuf, & Presque isle. Your letters of the 18<sup>th</sup> & 23<sup>d</sup> Ultimo arrived at Pittsburg in my absence & also that of the 3<sup>d</sup> Instant on the day of my return, but so late that I had not then the pleasure of acknowledging the receipt of it.

I find your letter of the 18<sup>th</sup> Ultimo enclosed two thousand Dollars in Post Notes, that of the 25<sup>th</sup> Eighteen Hundred Dollars & that of the 3<sup>d</sup> Instant one thousand Dollars also in Post Notes, the whole of which has come safe to hand & I find that M<sup>r</sup> Park has agreeably to my Orders advised you of the receipts of the two former sums.

Several Waggons with Hospital Stores have lately arrived, and generally in good order, but on inspecting a load delivered by Matthew Daiton Barrell N<sup>o</sup> 23 said to contain 179 lbs Coffee was found to contain Rice only — and Barrel N<sup>o</sup> 6 of James Hamiltons load said to of 31 Gallons Spirits & to weigh Cst 2-3-9<sup>oz</sup> is marked on the Cask Cst 2-2-9<sup>oz</sup> which is precisely the weight at this place the Cask being nearly full. —

I am much obliged to you for the attention you have paid to my business with M<sup>r</sup> Grier & have to request you to continue your attention until the business is compleated.

The Quarter Master General is on his way from Head Quarters & expected on Saturday next at this place, he is retiring from public business & will [undecipherable] you shortly in order to compleat a settlement of his public Accounts.

My Return up to the 1<sup>st</sup> October will be ready & transmitted by next Post.

I am at a loss to know whether any separate appropriation of Medicine & Hospital Stores for the upper Posts on the Ohio has been made or and to take a proper supply for those Posts from the Quantity now here & coming forward — I presume it would be improper to delay the transportation of all the Stores at this place for your answer as the season for Navigating the Ohio is far advanced & Boats now waiting I shall therefore in a few days, ship the greater part of the Stores for Fort Washington.

Have had expectation of a barrel of Sugar arri-ving for family use in some one of the late Waggons. — Your letter of the 9<sup>th</sup> Instant is this moment come to hand, together with the Packet of Newspapers.

You will find enclosed James Hamiltons Note for twenty Dollars, which sum please to retain at settlement of his Waggon Account & place to my Credit.

I am

[undecipherable] obt
H[is] Servant

Samuel Hodgdon Esq<sup>r</sup>          Isaac Craig

New London, Virginia 17<sup>th</sup> October 1796

Sir

When I engaged with you in Philadelphia, to come to this place to work in the United States Armoury, for the term of one year, it was agreed, that if I should be at any time unable to work owing to Sickness, that my pay should go on in the same manner as if I was at Work.

By a rule entered into by M<sup>r</sup> Perkin in May inst, by which the pay and Subsistance of every person employ'd in the public Works here [strikethrough: is stopped] should be stopped for every hour he is not at Work. I consider myself as injured; having had some time past a very Severe Fever and Ague, which disabled me so much as to prevent my being able to do my usual Work for nearly a month, and in consequence of the rule enters into by the Superintendant my pay was stopped. —

After the expiration of the term for which I was engaged, I shall cheerfully agree to be put upon the same footing with the other hands employ'd here, but trust, that until that time, you will direct that no stoppage shall be made from my pay, in absence from Duty occasioned by Sickness, as being contrary to bargain. —  I am Sir

Your obliged Hum Serv<sup>t</sup>

Adam Bowser

War Office, October 21, 1796.

Sir,

I have received your letter of the 14<sup>th</sup> instant.

It appeared by your former letters that the order given by General Knox in June 1794 for a supply of powder, lead &c. for the Six Nations had not been complied with, & therefore directed that M<sup>r</sup> Houdin Storekeeper at Albany should forward to your address the five hundred weight of best musket or rifle powder, one thousand weight of lead and two thousand flints which were mentioned in that order, provided they were not already sent on.

M<sup>r</sup> Houdin not recollecting the order or that he had sent on the Articles agreeably thereto, I find has forwarded to you a supply equal to that directed by General Knox in 1<sup>st</sup> 94 which it was by no means my intention to have done.

You will therefore inform the Nation to whom those last Articles may be delivered, that the amount of them together with the charges of transportation will be deducted from the next years annuity.

I am Sir,
with respect
Your obed<sup>t</sup> Servant
James McHenry

Israel Chapin Esq<sup>r</sup>.

War Office 24<sup>th</sup> October 1796

Sir,

I have had the honour to receive your letter of the 23 of September last on the 22 instant.

I find that my letter of the 23 of August had not arrived at that time; a copy of which I here inclose. Be assured that it is the sincere wish of the President to give tranquility to the frontiers, and that every thing tending to disturb it, whether proceeding from acts of our own bitigens or the Indians will claim his immediate attention.

With a view to that peace which he is so desirous to preserve, the following arrangements have been entered into.

A Company of Dragoons have been ordered to join the regular troops on the frontiers of Georgia, and such a disposition to be given to the whole force in that quarter, as may appear best calculated to cover our bitigens from predatory parties, and the Indian land from intrusion.

An Agent of known influence and capacity M<sup>r</sup> Benjamin Hawkins has been appointed to reside in the Creek nation, who will use his best endeavours to arrest their thieving expeditions, or make the nation feel in such a manner as may induce them to take effectual measures to prevent them.

And that compensation be made to the bitigens who may suffer in the mean while by those Banditti, should it be refused by the Indians, the Agent for the department of War has been authorized to give notice to all concerned that he will receive all complaints arising under the 14. Section of the Act to regulate trade and intercourse with the Indian tribes and to preserve peace on the frontiers, with the proper documents to substantiate the loss or offence, and to transmit the same to the President that measures may be taken to indemnify the injured.

These measures which disburthen the United States from an heavy expence, and which provide at the same time for the due execution of the laws, the President flatters himself will render it wholly unnecessary to keep up any Militia beyond the period mentioned in my letter of the 23 Ultimo. Should it however be found in experiment that more troops will be required to secure the frontiers, a further detachment will be ordered for that purpose as soon as the fact shall be ascertained, on which subject the President will be always happy to have your opinions.

Advice had been received previous to your letter of the attempt to murder on the Oconee, and that the Cussetaw Chiefs were highly incensed at the young men who had committed it, and who it would seem were stimulated to it by the continual haranguing of the Mother of the two young Cussetas killed the last summer by some of our Citizens.

M<sup>r</sup> Hawkins has been written to respecting it, and there is reason to believe that the measures which may be taken will prevent further attempts at retaliation for blood.

With great Respect
I have the honor to be
Sir
Your obedient Servant
James McHenry

His Excellency
The Governor of Georgia

Sir,

You will be furnished by the Superintendent of retailing Stores with an Invoice of goods for the trading house at Coleraine, which you will dispose of agreeably to your instructions.

The mode of keeping your accounts, and the person to whom you are to address your remittances, and from whom you are to receive returns hereafter, will be pointed out to you in a future letter; till which time, you will be governed by existing orders.

You have stated that you are sometimes pressed by Officers of the United States, in garrison in Georgia, and by frontier Inhabitants to sell to them articles in store; & that it would be a great convenience to both both, were you permitted to yield to their solicitations. The institution of the trading house, you will observe, being for different purposes, it would be wrong to divert from the Indians goods already purchased for their use. However, should there be more of any article on hand than the Indians may call for, till it can be replaced; and the want of the above description of persons for that article are pressing; and there should appear to you to be no other way in which they could be supplied; you may, under such circumstances, sell to them for ready money; but, in no case whatever, upon credit.

It being intended to remove the trade from Coleraine to the principal post to be established within the Creek Boundary, you will be pleased to furnish Lieut. Col. Gaither immediately upon your arrival, with the dimensions and plan for a Store proper for your business, that he may take measures to have it erected in a [undecipherable] situation.

You will also, as soon as it is ready to receive the goods, have them transported thither.

The goods which are to go under your care addressed to Benjamin Hawkins, principal temporary Indian agent south of the Ohio, are to be forwarded agreeably to such instructions as he may send you. Those for the Creeks are to be stored in the trading house, and held in like manner subject to his orders.

With respect to the latter, you will open an account for the Creeks; in which you will credit them with the amount of the goods annually sent them, and charge them with the orders that may be given by the Agent for their delivery.

As the views of the Government extend to Cattle Rearing and Agriculture among the Indians, as a mean of approaching them to the civilized State, it becomes an object to find for their Cattle and grain a ready and profitable market. I wish you, therefore, to ascertain and report to the Secretary of War, how far it would be proper for the Store to give goods for the one or the other; that is, whether the Store could readily, and without loss or risk, dispose of either, if received in exchange. Good horses, it is presumed, might be cheaply conveyed to market; and perhaps grain or beef could be [undecipherable] to the Contractor for supplying the troops, or transported to a Sea Port and [undecipherable] to advantage,

or, rather without a loss. All this you will enquire into, which includes a knowledge of what transportation will cost from the place where received to where they may be sold.

You will be pleased, immediately on your return, make out an Inventory of all the goods on hand, the debts, if any, due to, and by the Factory, and remit it to the Secretary of War; and will, every six months, make out and transmit a similar return, that the same may be laid before the President.

I am Sir &c
Signed  James McHenry

Sir,

I received your letter of the 27<sup>th</sup> Ulto enclosing extracts of M<sup>r</sup> Flemming's communication to you on the subject of his Account of which I suspended that part relating to Expences in pursuit of Deserters until the Items were more fully explained. —

On the account of Cap<sup>t</sup> Mitchell, I have to remark that it has not been customary at this Office to allow Officers their expences when on direct ordinary duty, which is the light in which I view the business. Cap<sup>t</sup> Mitchell was sent on — whether he went in pursuit of deserters or for other purposes relating to his duty as an Officer is immaterial. The Charges are in my opinion very extravagant. His Subsistence is allowed him for the time, and which is thought to be sufficient, and there are a number of advances he made to pursuers as he calls them for which the particulars are not stated. Sergeant Henry Hannah and others without noting the particulars, they charge 16 <sup>Dol</sup>/<sub>100</sub> for expences in pursuing Deserters, these are matters which ought to be particularly stated, as this mode leaves it too much in the power of the person to sport with public money. The objections may be obviated at present by stating the particulars of the expenditures, if this cannot be done the accounts must pass as they are as the payments have been made and it would be difficult to have any part reformed —

But I have particularly to request that in future, you will cause the persons to keep an accurate & descriptive list of their expences, and also to the account which must in all cases be forwarded to this Office for examination before the payment is made, this will prevent any objections to the accounts of the Pay Masters after the payment is made. — The necessity of being thus particular must appear obvious to you. I shall therefore conclude by requesting your attention thereto

November 5 1796—

Sir.

Adjutant Lovel has officially informed me that the command: of the corps (by permission of the d<sup>t</sup> of War) has ordered 25 of my men left at West, to be transfered to other companies: and 10 of this detachment, belonging to other companies, to be transfered to mine: that the 24 of M<sup>c</sup>Ken's detachm<sup>t</sup> with me are considered as his company under the command of Lieut. M<sup>c</sup>Lellan: But as nothing is said about W<sup>m</sup> Parr fifer, Eliot Raines artificer, and Ph<sup>s</sup> Swelland, I hope mention'd a conjecture they were forgot, or cou'd also, have been transfered. I have, therefore, mustered them as such; also J<sup>as</sup> M<sup>c</sup>Connill a deserter from Cap<sup>t</sup> Keltigun — who gave himself up to serve until August next to make up his lost time, and to obtain a proper discharge; but Alexander Withers from Cap<sup>t</sup> Kin's who also gave himself up, I have mustered with the infantry — and the whole, on one muster Roll as a detachment.

Humphries will be left out of my quarter if I do not hear of him by next detachm<sup>t</sup> — Wainor and White are smart feifes & a proper since and ago, to learn & do this duty of musick; the first has a father in service — the latter is without any, they are both inlisted for 5 years upon contract to wait for bounties and receive but private pay until they can do the duty of musick, — proficient now but, and play (conselly) several times on the fife — they learn both.

Hunt and Seton do Duty — are Duly well looking soldiers, both inlisted for 5 years and intitle to full bounty. Most of the mens times expire in the course of next year, begining with my best drummer (Jack Carson) on the 10 February — If it is contemplated to reinlist them, many and inducements ought to be forwarded in time. If not, a number of blank discharges — However, I shall want some, and blank Muster and Pay Rolls —

It is mortifying to me that any of this detachm<sup>t</sup> desert — it is not (flatter myself) owing to

a want of proper precautions, or a lax discipline; but a desire of change, or the allurements held out on the other side the water, when every emigrant is intitled to 200 acres of land on taking the oath to that government, — a large bounty if he inlists, or high wages if he prefers working — Indeed, most of their stories (harangues) are inducements to work out on wages the principal part of their time: this is found necessary to keep them.

Heaton and Pam are employed on taking up Major Rivardi's baggage to the landing on the Canadian side when they deserted. Hart being at the same place after plank, to make a raft up to salt but in; also deserted, but has since thought better of it, and returned to his duty. I wish the pay or encouragement such as to induce our others to remain in service the full term of their engatment; a bounty at the end of their service [for the time that even with of the time] wou'd have more advantages, than the one at the commencement — I am apprehensive that many after reinlisting for 5 years, with the first opportunity, go off; this has been the case with most of the deserters from Detroit. — But to prevent I will make it as difficult to them as possible.

We have no news — but most of the military in upper Canada have orders to hold themselves in readiness to march to Quebec at a short notice; — supposed to meet the same soldiers who have landed at St Johns. If they invade Canada, Phaps the rage to get situations on that side the water, may not be quite so great as at present —

The Adjutant Gen<sup>l</sup> has called for my Returns, Muster & Pay Rolls — I have sent them for September and have duplicates of yours prepared for October — but I don't chuse having any more intercourse until May or June — I shall, therefore, agreeable to my original design continue to forward them to you —

I am waiting every moment expecting to see the vessel I have engaged to go after Cap<sup>t</sup> Littlefield — she is now just rigged and calculated for the Oswego harbour — no other vessel on the Lake dare venture to go in; so uncertain of the weather is not favourable — besides, I freight her for 200 dollars less than I cou'd get any other of size to bring the troops and stores — all the inconveniences in the business is, that I have to wait 8 or 10 days for her going in — I have by sound — that a detachm<sup>t</sup> is at Oswego — but Cap<sup>t</sup> Littlefield has not yet announced it to me —

I will thank you to inclose a news paper or two with your dispatches for this post — it is seldom we get one — We all wish to see the return of member for next Congress. the Alternat in a [undecipherable] see

I have the honor to be
your Obedient Servant

Sir,

The annexed instructions have been given to the Storekeeper in this City, M<sup>r</sup> Harris for his Government to which you will be pleased to attend.

1. You will as soon as the Returns directed therein shall be made to you charge M<sup>r</sup> Harris with all the articles which he has in store, and turn over to him any which you may have under your particular care, taking his Receipt for the same. You will also debit him with all those which he shall in future receive. To enable you to do the latter the Purveyor of public Supplies will be directed to furnish you with invoices of all articles delivered to the said Storekeeper and his acknowledgment of their reception.

2<sup>d</sup> As Superintendant you will inspect, at least, monthly, into the state and condition of the Stores and make report thereof every two months to the Secretary of War in writing.

3. As often in your opinion as any military stores shall be wanted or any repairs of Ordnance, Arms or military articles are necessary to be made, you will state the same to the Secretary of War in writing that such order may be taken as the case may require.

4. You will visit once every year the principal arsenals, Stores and Armouries, inspect the articles deposited or made therein, and compare them with the Returns and report upon each respectively your observations and remarks in writing to the Secretary of War.

5. You will require from all persons intrusted with the safe keeping or manufacture of any military Stores to render you a quarterly Return, exhibiting the articles on hand and what they have received, manufactured, or delivered during the preceding quarter.

Sir,

In a letter of the 29<sup>th</sup> of September from the Comptroller of the Treasury to me, was enclosed your remarks on the allowance to be made to the late Ensign Ezekiel Polk, with a statement of the ballance made to be coming to him. It does not appear that in making up the ballance any allowance has been made M<sup>r</sup> Polk for undrawn or back Rations, for Rations furnished to the recruits by him enlisting, bounty to them advanced or compensation for enlistment.

It is understood that M<sup>r</sup> Polk received his appointment in August, that he joined his Captain at Halifax in September or October; that he was ordered on a recruiting party; that he enlisted Seven Men, viz. James Johnson, Adam Hayes, John Boyd, Thomas LePiere, Robert Wilkins, Joseph Pope, & Benjamin Pope; that he marched to join his Corps in December and got as far as Fayetteville, about half way to Halifax, with his Soldiers, when he was taken so ill as to prevent him from going any further; that he was removed back to Charlotte, where he continued to sometime in February, that he then set out and joined his Captain at Halifax; that his health was then so far impaired, that he returned to Charlotte & sometime afterwards set out for the West Indies.

Accompanying this you will find the deposition of Thomas LePiere one of the Soldiers who was enlisted by M<sup>r</sup> Polk; by it you will perceive, that he furnished the men by him enlisted with Provision for more than thirty days, and that he advanced to each Soldier two Dollars in part of their Bounty, & that he advanced to them money at Fayetteville to bear their expenses to Halifax when he was taken sick; from whence it is fairly to be understood that part of the 70 Dollars received by Captain Montfort by M<sup>r</sup> Polk has been appropriated to the use of the United States.

I have herewith sent you an account against the United States of what appears to me to be the dues of Ensign Polk. Such of the charges as are not founded on Law or the Instructions of the Department of War, will of course be rejected; but I flatter myself the most of them will merit your attention and a revision of the allowance.

I am Sir with respect your

55589:
[folios 40-41]

Maugulien S<sup>t</sup> Georges River Oct 18<sup>th</sup> 1796

Sir

I had the honor to receive your letter of the 22<sup>d</sup> of July a long period after its date, owing to an absence from home. Since my return, I have been endeavoring to ascertain the several objects of your inquiries, and have to regret that the information I may convey is not so authentic as may be required, but imperfect as it is, I submit it with sincerity to your view.

First. The number of people at S<sup>t</sup> Andrews which is a town at the mouth of the River claimed by the British as the S<sup>t</sup> Croix, may be about six or seven hundred; Settlements extend up the River about nine miles to the head of navigation, & for seven or eight miles above the head of navigation. The whole number of Settlers under the British government, on the Territory claimed by the United States, to be estimated at 2000, it would not be far from the true number.

2<sup>d</sup>. The Americans are thinly settled on the Western side of the River called by the British the S<sup>t</sup> Croix, except far down the bay of Passamaquody, at Fradley's Island, where there is a handsome settlement of about 30 good houses & a flourishing fishery, the whole number of inhabitants from the bay of Passamaquody to the head of the River, may be estimated at about 300. But as the climate is temperate & favorable to health & longevity, the soil excellent of producing Wheat & all other valuable grains, many fine & grass in abundance, the lumber in high estimation & great in quantity, the fisheries contiguous & inexhaustible, & the situation good for commerce foreign & domestic, the country must under such circumstances soon fill with people; I require no 20 years to predicate that end. The great number of fine bays & harbours in the District & [undecipherable] an extent of near three hundred miles, & the immense number of fish of all sorts in the vicinity from the whole to the muscle render this District a source of hardy yeomen who in all emergencies will afford security to the American commerce, & be a mean of solid dignity to the national character.

3<sup>d</sup>. The commerce between the British & Americans is not great, vessels however on both sides visit in the Stream & receive Articles from Boats of the opposite side; the Americans carry Plaster of Paris & carry it to New York & Philadelphia. The British have received boards, lumber & fish to a considerable extent. But the French Privateers have in a great degree prevented this for the last two years by capturing most of the vessels belonging to New Brunswick. It is very probable that before these Articles [undecipherable] & some last Indian goods are directly obtained by the British from the American side. Playing cards & any other articles on which a high duty is imposed by the United States may be easily procured from the British.

4<sup>th</sup>. Dudley's Island or the Island on which M<sup>r</sup> L. Pernier the Custom house Officer resides appears to be the proper place to receive their Commerce with coasting trade to ply incessantly up & down the Bay & River.

5<sup>th</sup> I have not been able to obtain any information on this head

6<sup>th</sup> The intercourse with the contiguous parts of the United States & the Province of New Brunswick is prohibited and the prohibition is rigidly enforced, it seems to be the sentiment of the commercial inhabitants that it should be so as they are apprehensive that the Citizens of the United States would encroach in case of a free intercourse & their carriers in all things.

7<sup>th</sup> The Country near the Highlands which form the boundaries between the District of Maine & Canada north of Penobscot River is susceptible of high cultivation. This is proved fully by a French settlement high up the River S<sup>t</sup> John's 190 miles from its mouth, where the River runs almost east. In the time of the American War a number of French families removed from the Bay of Fundy to this place, where they raise cattle & sheep, wheat & other grains in considerable quantities. There is no road from the District of Maine to the said Highlands, although there is a post road from the City of S<sup>t</sup> Johns on the River of that name, the Capital of New Brunswick, to the City of Quebec; the post goes twice a month. But canoes may pass out of the waters of the Penobscot into those of the S<sup>t</sup> John's & into the Waters of the Rivers S<sup>t</sup> Lawrence to Quebec with only about 4 miles of carrying place [which] is to be understood when the Waters are High. It is known that no roads are in immediate connection from this district to said Highlands.

I am Sir with entire respect

Your most obedient
humble servant

[signature]

[To the honourable
The Secretary of the Treasury.]

55599:
Philad. 19 Nov<sup>t</sup>. 1796.

My dear Murray.

The plot thickens. I inclose you a sketch by Bashe of the design. It is not well done; but to prevent misconceptions the whole by M<sup>r</sup>. Cobet, a piece of 63 pages, will appear on Monday in Brown. It is a declaratory appeal to the people against the government; requiring laws to be repealed; decisions of the courts of justice to be annulled; refusals to be restored, and in short a change from pacific to hostile proceedings against Great Britain. I rather think it will not aid M<sup>r</sup> Jefferson's election altho evidently timed and intended to produce that result. I hope our people will not forget themselves on the occasion but cling to their independence and government.

I long to see you. If you should be here a few days before the appointed day it will be a complement to your friends and what they wish for     Till then adieu affety.

James McHenry

Is it not a little strange that we have not yet learned whether Wright or wrong has prevailed in Dundoman's district.

55608:
[Opinion Attorney
Charles Lee
General — on
Charges Whether
a court martial
or inquiry could be
instituted against
Gen. Wayne —]

Philadelphia 20<sup>th</sup> november 1796

Sir

As the charges exhibited against General Wayne by General Wilkinson have not been communicated to me, I have supposed they were not necessary to be known to enable me to form an opinion relative to the measures necessary to be pursued to do justice to the public, the accused and accuser. I have taken a general view of this subject and the following is the opinion which I have formed.

The President being by the constitution the commander in chief of the army of the United States possesses all the powers belonging to that office; one of which is to order a court martial upon any inferior officer whenever it shall appear to him proper and requisite. General Wayne is considered in the light of an inferior officer though commander in chief of the american forces in the western country and may be subjected to a trial before a court martial to be ordered by the President and it is within his discretion to determine whether a court of enquiry shall be instituted previous to the court martial or not.

If a previous court of enquiry is deemed expedient it may be ordered in my opinion without the consent of the accused, as the restriction in the 26<sup>th</sup> article of war passed 31<sup>st</sup> May 1786 is not applicable in its reason to the President of the United States who may lawfully whenever he sees cause, take the command of the army from Gen<sup>t</sup> Wayne and commit it to another; and that he may be the better enabled to exercise this discretionary power, [strikethrough: he must to have in his power] [underline: he must have authority] to order a court of enquiry even [underline: without the consent] of the officer, whose conduct is intended to be investigated.

But if this opinion is doubted, it will certainly be out of the reach of exception, for the accused to demand a court of enquiry for which purpose immediate notice should be given to him of the charges already produced, that it may be in his power to solicit a court of enquiry; and if this is not requested by him, a court martial should be ordered without any further intermediate enquiry.

If a court of enquiry shall be ordered, whether with or without the consent of the accused, the proceedings should be according to the usual forms and in pursuance of the 25<sup>th</sup> 26<sup>th</sup> & 27<sup>th</sup> articles of war passed in 1786 and when finished are to be transmitted to the President of the United States who will then determine whether or not a court martial shall be ordered.

I am very respectfully Sir your most obedient humble Servant
Charles Lee
Attorney Gen<sup>l</sup>

To the Secretary at War

55671:
Philadelphia, November 24. 1796.

The Talk of Opsiamingo, Chief of the Chickasaw Nation, to the Honorable James McHenry Secretary of War to the United States —

Friend and Brother,

Our Father the President of the United States in a Talk he sent us, which we received last Winter, expressed a desire to see some of our principal Chiefs — in consequence of which, you now see us here to receive any further Talk he may have to give us.

On our way here, we found the road crowded with people going to Cumberland. That country borders on our land, and notwithstanding the repeated assurance of protection in the possession of our Country, which we have received from the United States, we cannot help feeling some anxious forebodings from such an unexampled migration to Cumberland.

Our Boundaries are not yet marked, and frontier Settlers when they make Encroachments on our hunting Ground will readily find an excuse in their ignorance of our limits. We wish therefore that the President will order the line to be run immediately, and so marked, as to put it out of the power of any person to excuse Encroachment on that Ground. After this is done, we appeal to the justice of the United States to protect us in the full and undisturbed enjoyment of our bounty, already guarantied to us by our Father the President.

We are all now at peace with the United States and I am thus particular that no cause may hereafter arise to cause our Children to differ.

West point Nov 25<sup>th</sup> 1796

Sir,

I have received your letter of the 19<sup>th</sup> Inst respecting the Sergeant Majors & Quarter M<sup>r</sup> Sergeants mentioned in the Pay & Muster Roll for the month of October last. it is perfectly true that none were contemplated in the formation of the three Battalions added to the 1<sup>st</sup> already existing, but it is known that it was an Error in the framing of the Law for it is impossible to Execute the Details of the Regimental Daily Duty without a Sergeant acting in every Battalion under the Adjutant; and that one of the offices of the Non com<sup>d</sup> & Privates Detail or Roster, is filled. The Secretary of War (Col Pickering) promised the necessary addition to the Law of Organisation of the Corps of Art<sup>y</sup> previous to the last Session, and I am not informed whether or not his proposal has been adopted.

When I joined the corps, six or seven months after the Regiment had been collected here, I found three Sergt Majors & 2 Q<sup>r</sup> M<sup>r</sup> Sergeants appointed by the officer commanding in my absence, and when refering to the former Pay Rolls, I remarked that the extrapay of one Doll: per month had been constantly allowed these non commissioned officers by you, in conformity to the General regulation of the army, I concluded that it must have been obvious to you that they were necessary, and that you consented, tacitly at least, to the Pay allowed by law to non com<sup>d</sup> officers performing that duty in this army. I was induced thereby & therefore hesitated not to continue to do them that Justice which the officers of Government had done them, and they continued to be mentioned in the following Pay Rolls with

with the Monthly pay of 8 Dollars. if I have been mistaken, I wish you would Inform me of it, and they will in future be allowed but the common pay to Company Sergeants. I wish however you would not Stop the pay of October on account of that Error of mine.

I am with Esteem, Sir, Respectfully

your ob<sup>et</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup>

My dear Sir Cambridge 27. Nov. 95.

Your letter of the 19. I received yesterday and thank you for Tho. — one of which you sent to me before — I shall send both to Andapolis where they may work upon the public mind and do good.

Before you read the inclosed, should you ever read it, delicacy requires of me that you should know its history — after I read the [underline: Sketch] in the Aurora of Adets long list of grievances (w<sup>h</sup> I wish you could commit to Tracy & me in the committee of claims —) I was so struck with the intended tendencies of the piece that I thought a notice of it might be proper for this part of the country in our little weekly paper — I accordingly scribbled away "a correspondents remarks" — intending to write a number of long [underline: paragraphs] — on the several heads — & send them to Cowen — When I had embarked in the subject in the 2<sup>d</sup> page of the 2<sup>d</sup> sheet — a thought struck me that a proper respect for our cabinet precluded any remarks in the news papers till the Tone had been given by them —

and you will perceive the breaking forth of this thought when I refer to Byske<sup>r</sup> [undecipherable] — for then I thought I would continue scribbling on as a letter to you — just in the confidential, friendly way in which we have been accustomed to debate our public grievances — and so I continued all this day scribbling, as you may judge from the [underline: size] of the [underline: letter] — but I do not enjoin you to read it.

The notes from Valin's Commentary are in my common place a D<sup>o</sup>. I send them — I took them from M<sup>r</sup> King's — probably Smith has them. I never saw Valin — & have no rated him — or I would have been your extractor —

55745:
Blue Jacket a War Chief, in the Shawnoe Nation to his
Brother of the Fifteen Fires.

Brother  Upon your esto a mission to wixe some Essay.

Father  I speak to you in the language of truth, and request your patient attention. Jones not tell you how long I was attached to my late British father over the Waters of the Ocean nor how often I fought his battles on the waters of our great Lakes. for my name has been well known to your Nation.

Father.  My eyes are now opened. and my heart has been glad since I have been in friendship with my American Brethren.

Father.  I have been long deceived by the falsehoods of McKee and other British agents, who have ever urged myself and my two Brethren to keep up war against the fifteen fires. they have often told me not to trust to the Americans, that they only wished to get our lands and then drive us to the remote Waters of the West. that if I would cross the lake with them and go to Quebec I should be one of the first Men of their Nation. but I refused these treaties.

Father.  Long have I been blinded to my own interest and that of my Nation. I thank the great Spirit who sent that Bird whose spreading wings embraced Nation and diffused peace throughout our Country.

Father. When I fought for the British. I fought with bravery and sincerity. since I now found them carrying on a deception among us for many years past. I am now determined to break asunder the chain by which we were [undecipherable] and dissolve the ties of friendship by which we were bound. I have my own in holding them so long last in the hand. and since now I great difference between our friendship and that of my American Brother.

Blue Jacket a War Chief of the Shawanoe Nation to his great Father of the Fifteen Fires —

Father, Open your ears, and listen to what I shall say.

Father, I speak to you in the language of truth, and request your particular attention — I need not tell you, how long I was attached to my late British Father over the Waters of the Ocean, nor how often I fought his battles on the Borders of our great Lake. for my name has been well known to your Nation.

Father  My eyes are now opened, and my heart has felt glad since I have been in friendship with my American Brethren.

Father, I have been long deceived by the falsehoods of McKee and other British agents who have ever urged myself and my two Brethren to keep up the War against the fifteen fires. they have often told me not to trust to the Americans, that they only wished to get our lands and then drive us to the immense Waters of the West. that if I would cross the lake with them and go to Quebec I should be one of the first Men of their Nation. but I refused their intreaties.

Father, Long have I been blinded to my own interest and that of my Nation but thank the great Spirit who sent that Bird whose spreading wings embraced our nation and diffused peace throughout our Country.

Father, When I fought for the British, I fought with bravery and sincerity but since I have found them carrying on a deception among us for many years past, I have been determined to break asunder the chain by which we were held, and dissolve the ties of friendship by which we were bound. I have seen my error in holding them so long fast by the hand and since have found a great difference between their friendship and that of my American Brethren.

Father

55757:
Conference with the Indian Chiefs.

All the Chiefs and Warriors of the different Indian Tribes met in Council the Second of December 1796, except the Soldier who was sick.

When the Secretary of War addressed them in the following Speech:

Brothers,

The President of the United States, your father who loves you as his Children, has heard the request which some of you have made to him and agreed that you should all meet in one Assembly to strengthen before me, as a solemn Witness, that Chain of friendship which ought to connect you together and which he wishes may continue like the Sun, always bright.

The great Spirit whom your father the President and the people of the United States adore, requires from Men of every colour and language that they should live in peace and love each other. Nations which engage in War and forsake this part are sure to be hurt, though they should kill a great many of those they fight against, for war is a fire that burns the large Trees as well as the small ones.

To avoid this terrible fire good Chiefs and wise Men, whenever a dispute or difference happens between the people of their respective Nations will meet and try to have it settled, in a peaceable manner, and rather than go to War, will give up something to which they think they have a right.

By observing this line of moderation and strictly performing all its promises, a Nation may avoid a War that might cost it more lives and more prosperity than the thing about which it quarrelled was worth.

Your father the President wishes if any of you have any differences

Sir—

55886:
Conference with the Chiefs of the Choctaw Nation December 16<sup>th</sup> 1796

Eatchtehoorpoa.

The first talk I ever delivered was to Colonel Hawkins at Hopewell, I then presented him with an Eagle's tail. I now deliver in like manner one to the Secretary of War.

I give this in remembrance, and as the renewal of the old friendship which I made with the United States. My first speech was delivered when I was a young man, I am now grown old and I think it right and proper to renew my talk before I die, I have not spoken to any of the Officers of the United States since the first treaty when I was a young Man. I am the same altho I am grown old and I hope what I now say will be kept in mind and remembered by the children that are yet unborn.

The Great Spirit, who has given us a Being has lengthened out my days that I may again speak. I hope what I say may be kept in remembrance and that the United States and my Nation may for ever remain in peace. I hope that the United States may raise on their frontiers their Women and Children in peace and that our Women and Children may also be raised in peace, for the Sun shines equally bright and clear on both people.

The United States cannot accuse us of breaking any Promises; for we never broke any. Search back all former treaties that we have made and you will find that they have been kept sacred and inviolate. ———

[continues]

Sir

Lieu<sup>t</sup> Taylor has delivered me your Excellency's letter dated Detroit October 19<sup>th</sup> 1796, and according to your intention I have acquainted him with the orders I have received from the Governor General of this Province respecting the treaty of friendship, navigation and limits between the United States of America, and the King my master. Talk of the Secretary of War to the Chiefs and Warriors of the Chickasaw Nation.

The President your father has considered the Talk delivered by Opciamingo, Chinataha, Minkamataha, Major George Colbert, Thomas Brown, John Brown and George Augusta, the 24<sup>th</sup> November last.

In that Talk it is said that your Chiefs on their way to see him, found the road crowded with People going to Cumberland, and that they wished the Boundary line between your Nation and the United States to be run. Your father knows that a great many people go back every year towards the Indian country, these cannot be kept at home; but he will as soon as possible have the Boundary line run and marked that so none of them shall have any excuse for trespassing on your land from ignorance. He will besides employ all the means in his power to protect your land from intrusion, which he hopes will prove effectual.

Since the departure of Opciamingo your father has had a Talk with those who remained after him. They have wished to know when the Spaniards would leave the Chickasaw Bluff. This your father could not tell them. 55931:
Answer.

To the Chiefs and Warriors of the Choctaw Nation.

Brothers

Your father has heard the talk which was delivered to the Secretary of War by Ealchushoopia, Parshenahla, Holtomeba, and Shappanahoma. He is glad that you are well, and shall hold the Chain fast which unites you to the United States and desires that you may not suffer it to be broken.

Ealchushoopia has described the boundaries of your Country. Your father does not know whether the lines he has mentioned correspond with those laid down in the treaty of Hopewell: but he will have them written in a Book that they may be known and considered hereafter.

You wish that your land may be protected from the whites. This is right. Your father will always use his endeavours to prevent settlements on it; and as soon as Spain shall leave the Natches and Walnut Hills, he intends to send some of his Warriors to those posts who will help to keep bad white people from doing you wrong.

Parshenahla says that you will be glad after the Spaniards leave the fort on Tumbeckbee River, that it should not be occupied. Your father does not know that it will be wanted for a trading post. By the treaty of Hopewell concluded in January 1786 you know that it is agreed that the United States may establish three trading posts and that six Miles square are reserved by that treaty to each post. Nothing however is going to be done at present about these trading posts or the fort on Tumbeckbee and care will be taken, whenever it shall be convenient to the United States to erect any, to consult the Nation before any thing is done.

That it may always in future be easy for you to hear from your father, the President, and for him to hear from you when any thing goes wrong with you

That he came here on the invitation of the President — that at the instance of Governor Blount and from a desire to see peace established between his Nation and the United States he exerted himself greatly and with much difficulty succeeded in bringing about a peace. That since it has been made it has been faithfully observed by his Nation — that in October 1795 he held a Conference with Governor Blount, when mutual promises to preserve and strengthen the peace were given and received, that soon after in the Winter, the white People notwithstanding killed three of the Indians, but altho this would have justified retaliation, none has taken place, and he is glad his exertions have been able to prevent it. That no horses have been stolen since that Conference in 1795 and that he has uniformly exerted himself to prevent such practices. That he thinks it very hard that the Whites should kill Indians, and that they should not be punished for so doing. That ever since he was a Boy he remembers to have heard it said, that whenever such a thing happened the Whites should be punished, but though the Story has been always renewed upon every fresh Murder, the Murderer has in no instance been punished. That this has greatly weakened his belief in such promises. I shall write to M<sup>r</sup> Dinsmoor on this subject, who will inform you whether he can be wholly or partially, given the Factory. If the former, he is to be about three hundred dollars per annum and his board, which is to be charged to the Store. At the same time, should any occasion occur to render his services useful to M<sup>r</sup> Dinsmoor, he is to understand that they are to be rendered as heretofore.

You have stated, in letters to the Purveyor, that you can buy upon the Spot, or delivered at the factory, Hominy at 8/6 per [undecipherable] Virginia currency, Lead at 8, and Salt at 14 dollars per bushels. Lowry is also mentioned as another article that may be procured cheaper with you than here.

Both our prices will make these articles come lower than they can be sent from this town, I shall instruct Col Henley to purchase such quantities of them, or either of them, upon your requisition, as you may stand in need of from time to time, to be paid out of the proceeds of your remittances.

The casualties attendant upon the trade in which the public have engaged, and frequent alterations in the prices of Indian Goods, render it expedient that it should be conducted in such a manner as that it shall produce a net annual profit, when with constitute an increasing fund to meet these casualties and contingencies. Besides, whenever it shall please Congress to suspend the experiment, there should be found effects that will bring at public Sale an amount equal to the original Capital employed, clear of all expences whatever; a circumstance which renders such a fund indispensably necessary. You will, therefore, be pleased to keep this object always in view; and so proportion your selling prices as to make sure of this annual profit. And, that the state of the trade may labour under no uncertainty, and the progress of the fund be fully known, you will take, and transmit once every year, an inventory of the effects of the factory, stating their value; and deduct right therefrom all expences of the year; so as to shew the surplus gained to the fund, to be laid before the President; and will annex thereto your Oath that it is just and true Statement of the goods on hand and the effects of the Factory.

I am Sir, &c
[Signed]   James McHenry

56071:
War Office January 2. 1797.

Sir

The Creek Chiefs will leave this City in a few days and return I hope satisfied with their reception and presents. It being probable however that some of the Chiefs who have staid at home may think those who visit the seat of Government are the best treated and be inclined from that circumstance to follow the same course oftener than would be proper or convenient, or get discontented on the sight of presents, which they have not shared in. I inclose you five hundred dollars to be disposed of in such manner as may obviate these effects, if on your arrival in the nation, you should find it necessary so to apply it or any part of it. You will keep an account of its expenditure and when practicable get Vouchers or receipts

I am Sir Yd
Your obed Servants
sign<sup>d</sup> James McHenry

Benjamin Hawkins Es<sup>q</sup>

Sir— We arrived here this morning after a passage of two days from Savanna have not time to collect any information of importance but as it is post day think proper to inform you of this circumstance. I am informed by Major Freeman there are considerable numbers of Indians at Colerain waiting for supplies hear nothing from Col<sup>t</sup> Gaither and fear much difficullty in satisfying the Indians as there appears to be no proper agent there for their business, Major Freeman goes the first opportunity for Savanna & Charleston our goods are much damaged which I fear will operate considerably against the Indian trade am told there are considerable felons at Colerain which we intend stopping by the Brig duty Capt<sup>n</sup> Mann for Philadelphia am with due respect your most obedient Ser<sup>t</sup>

E. D——?

56124:
Fort at Whetstone Point Jan<sup>y</sup> 6
1797

Sir

Enclosed I transmit to you the Receipt Rolls, for the payments made to a part of my Company for the months of October and November, as also the muster and pay Roll of the whole for the month of December. —

You will observe Alexander for whom pay was drawn is not included in the Receipt Rolls, owing as I have been informed to his having been detained in Philad<sup>a</sup> by the civil authority. — Should this be the case, I could wish the Recruiting officer at Philad. or some other person might interest himself to obtain his release and send him forward to me. — I have omitted likewise to pay Robert Dean confined for Desertion. —

Supposing the reward for apprehending him might be claimed, and that it would be proper it should be discharged from his pay, was my inducement for withholding it — Another consideration, that he is totally worthless as a soldier, and ought to be discharged, not having done more than one tour of duty since he Joined the Regiment. —

If I am in error in this, he can be paid up next payment.

I am Sir

Your Obed<sup>t</sup>. Servant

Staats Morris
Capt. A<sup>t</sup>. C<sup>y</sup>.

W<sup>m</sup> Simmons Esq<sup>r</sup>
A. W. D.

56126:
Pittsburg 6<sup>th</sup> January 497

Sir

Your letter of the 30<sup>th</sup> Ult. is this moment come to hand together with the Packet of News Papers.

The weather hitherto has continued uncommonly severe, this day there is an appearance of a change and its consequences in dreads by some thousands whose boats are annoyed by Ice. Hamiltton arrived yesterday with the Indian Baggage together with the Stationery &.

The Barrel of Sugar Popps has arrived very reasonably in deed.

You will find this accompanied by an abstract of Fines received at Allesbury from Ult & also to last of September 1796 continue together with voucher of fines during that Period. And you will find enclosed an Estimate of Objects of Expenditure at this post Worth Hereon advancing during the last three months of the Year 1796 Amount $643 100 dollars a part of that Share anticipated by drawing of Gen Neville. On the 8<sup>th</sup> Drawn you in favour of Simon Hyenty for 600 dollars this day have drawn on you in favour of Bezaleel Wills for 2000 Dollars but the last Draft Specimen will be presented to you by the Hon James Glass on whose account that sum has been deposited by Mr Wills with me. The Comg Gen. is assured here & earnestly seeing you in the course of next month, and of Iffect that Item he should from my post I shall accompany him. There still however to request you to urge my claim of compensation for former Services.

I am Sir

Samuel Hodgson &c &c &c
Philla.

N. Ens 66. B. H.

The Secretary of War's letter to the Committee of the House of Representatives, and Estimate, relatively to the Sea Board Fortifications.

War Office, January 10,<sup>th</sup> 1797.

Sir,

The Report from the department of War to Congress dated the twentieth day of January 1794, will enable the committee to form an opinion of the number and state of the forts and harbours, at the period to which it refers.

The alterations in those forts that have taken place since that period, consist chiefly in depredations made by time, on such of them as have not been garrisoned; and in such repairs and additions as could be made by the Garrisons where troops have been stationed, or that were wanting to their accommodation.

In the former description are comprehended the works at Portland in the district of Maine; Portsmouth, in New Hampshire; Gloucester, Cape Ann, Salem, Marblehead, Massachusetts, New Port, Rhode Island, New London, Connecticut, and Savannah, and Point Petre, Georgia.

In the latter description are comprised the defences at Governors Island, New York; Mud Island, Philadelphia; Whetstone Point, Baltimore; Norfolk, Virginia; Wilmington, North Carolina; and Fort Johnson, Charleston, South Carolina.

The forts which have been without Troops, must be presumed to have suffered considerable injury from time alone, & will require, if the circumstances of the military Establishment and frontiers should not admit of their being garrisoned, about three thousand five hundred dollars, annually to pay Persons

Sir,

The case of Colbert who has petitioned Congress to be paid for provisions who he furnished a party of Inhabitants from [undecipherable] who went into the Chickasaw Nation to help them to resist an invasion by the Creek, offers several matters for consideration.

Are the Chickasaws entitled to protection from the United States by any positive or specific stipulation in their treaty, and if entitled does the protection apply to the case in question.

The United States entered into a treaty with the Chickasaw Nation in the year [undecipherable] in which the United States stipulate, to give peace to the Nation, and to [undecipherable] into their former and protection in certain enumerated conditions, Among these are.

That all prisoners Citizens of the United States and all Negroes and property taken from the Citizens thereof during the war should be [undecipherable].

That the Chickasaws should be under the protection of the United States and no other Sovereign whatsoever.

That they should have and live within certain defined boundaries.

That they should deliver up to be punished by the Laws of the United States, any Indian or other person taking refuge among them who should commit a robbery, murder or other capital crime on any Citizen of the United States or a person under their protection &c.

Such are the conditions required to be observed by the Chickasaws to entitle them to the protection of the United States. Have they fulfilled these conditions. It would perhaps be found on examination, that they have not there delivered all property taken from the Citizens of the United States during the war, nor yet conducted themselves in all other respects agreeably to the Treaty. It is certain also that the nation or a part of it have permitted Spain to erect a fort and garrison it within their limits, under colour of protecting them. Having failed on these points on their part it might be said that they cannot claim of right as perfect compliance on ours.

I do not mean to intimate however that these departures from the conditions of the Treaty have absolved in any degree the United States from their engagements. They are such as might have been expected to have happened,

from the peculiarity of the Indian situation, their want of police or laws to compel their people to give up what they had taken, and their inability to defend themselves from foreign intrusion. But it is presumed therefore that the promise of protection is still obligatory on the United States.

Of what nature then is this protection. Is it to operate against aggressions by Citizens of the United States only; or is it a general protection, having relation to whatever might endanger their existence as a Nation or People?

When it is considered that encroachments upon their land is the danger to which the Indians within the United States are most exposed, and that which we find them most desirous to guard against by treaties, it is fair to presume, that the protection meant in this Treaty has reference chiefly if not wholly to that object, and that the surrender made by them in the treaty of a part of their lands on which they were accustomed to hunt, was to buy the price of the protection of the remainder.

This construction, as being the most natural one, because most conformable to Indian feelings, and desires, and comprehending what may be reasonably promised by the United States, may be received as the true one. Had military succours in cases of invasion in various been contemplated by the parties, there would have been words introduced into the treaty expressive of the intention.

Admitting however a different construction or that the protection here stipulated for, implies military succours whenever the Nation should find itself engaged in a war, still it would be a duty incumbent upon the United States to enquire which Indian nation was the aggressor, before they could lawfully furnish it; and to judge besides whether the nation demanding the succour was not competent to dissipate the invasion without it.

I should therefore premise the former interpretation as the truest; but which ever is adopted, the claim of the petitioner becomes equally negative, the succour being furnished without authority from the United States.

As a general rule perhaps it is the wisest and cheapest policy for the United States to take no part in the wars of the Indian Nations with each other,

further than as mediators or umpires between them, where they can effectually interpose to adjust their differences.

Were the United States to pay for the provisions it would be laying a foundation for the Nation to expect like of assistance on future occasions, and would besides furnish the military adventurers with a claim against the United States for that service.

It is however to be observed, that a thing which if thought grievous by a Citizen, would be justly regarded as improper, acquires when urged by an Indian a degree of respect, proportionate to the share of influence he may possess in his nation in conjunction with the power of the nation to injure or serve the United States. For this reason it is not always safe or expedient to reject their applications which have of course of right, nor safe or expedient to yield to them formally, when doing so would establish an inconvenient or expensive precedent. The conduct in such cases is obliged to steer a middle way where the respect is not wholly inadequate for it. Colbert therefore was a rising Character in his nation, and as one of the principal chiefs whose influence is considerable and increasing he has [undecipherable] presented what was calculated to have satisfied him.

I am of opinion therefore that it would be proper to reject in his case.

That however commendable the motive might be which induced the party of frontier Citizens to offer their services to an Indian Nation threatened with invasion, yet inasmuch as the proceeding was unauthorized by Government, and countenance might lead other Citizens to a like interference, and thereby involve the United States in hostilities with the offended Nation, and inasmuch as the United States are not expressly bound by treaty to afford succour to the Chickasaws in their wars, and as it would be inexpedient to establish a precedent which might countenance the principle, the Committee are of opinion that the prayer of the petition might not to be granted.

With great respect
I am Sir
Your most obedient servant
James McHenry

Pittsburg 20<sup>th</sup> January 1799

Sir,

Your letter of the 19<sup>th</sup> instant accompanied by the Pittsburgh News Papers is come to hand this moment, at the same time I am favored with a letter from the Secretary of War of the 15<sup>th</sup> instant which relates entirely to Business that must be transacted in Phil<sup>a</sup> — I have enclosed you a Copy of it and have to request your immediate attention to that Business, Viz to obtain a deed in the name of the President of the U. S. for Lots N<sup>o</sup> 37 &38 at Fort Le Bœuf from the Town of Pittsburgh County of Allegheny — You will please to observe that on making choice of ground on which to erect the Public Buildings, Council necessary to occupy a part of three lots and therefore at the Publick Sale in Pittsburg on the 15<sup>th</sup> of August last Purchased them for the United States before the Secretary of War of it. I expected that an Application to the Legislature of Pennsylvania, this ground together with an adjoining Publick Square would have been ceded to the U. S. but for reasons assigned by the Secretary of War this has not been done. It is therefore necessary that you be pleased to make application to Clement Biddle &<sup>y</sup> who is empowered to transact the business respecting the Sale of these lots and you will find by the account of Sales now in Col<sup>s</sup> Biddies Possession that Lots N<sup>o</sup> 37 was sold at 135 dollars & N<sup>o</sup> 38 at 150 dollars both in my name — As soon as you have obtained a deed you will be pleased to transmit it to me in order that it may be recorded in the Alleg: County — The fee is not yet broke up from any appearance of it.

You will find this accompanied by an abstract of issues of Pays at this post from the 1<sup>st</sup> of April to the last of September

Having lately arrived from the City of Cape Francois in Saint Domingo, I Beg Leave to Inform you Some Intelligence of a Private Nature which I heard during my Stay there Viz, that between the 6<sup>th</sup> and 12<sup>th</sup> day of December Last, being in Company with a M<sup>r</sup> [undecipherable: probable reading "Labreze"], a Merch<sup>t</sup> of the Cape, he Informed me that he had heard the Commissary [undecipherable: probable reading "Sthomas"] Declare that if M<sup>r</sup> Jefferson was Elected President of the United States he would Annul all those Decrees Lately Passed So Injurious to the American Commerce, but if M<sup>r</sup> Adams was Elected President they Should all be Continued in force, as Also on the 23 day of Dec<sup>r</sup> Last I was Informed by M<sup>r</sup> [undecipherable: probable reading "Geniere"] that he had heard one of the Officers of government say that the French Minister Adet had wrote out to them that they Could not Possibly Treat the Americans too Bad, this Intelligence I Believe was Received by a French Gentleman who Came Passenger with Captain Decosta from this Place, and brought Dispatches from the French Minister here to the Directory, Cap<sup>tn</sup> Decosta Left Philadelphia About the 20<sup>th</sup> November & Arrived in Cape Francois on the 8<sup>th</sup> of December. It was not Believed in Cape Francois Island that the Directory condemned our Vessels & Property by Orders Received from France, but had done it from [undecipherable] the Decree Issued by the National [strikethrough: Convention] Directory, Respecting the Treatment of Neutral Powers, and which Decree they Received by the Schooner General Green who Arrived from here About the 5<sup>th</sup> of November. Previous to this Vessels Arrival we had been Assured by the Directory that all our Vessels Should be Restored, Provided we had no Contraband Articles onboard, and a Decree had been Passed forbidding the Privateers of the Republic to Capture any More of our Vessels and their Conduct in Other Respects to the Americans was Friendly. The Correspondance between the Secretary of State and the French Minister here. Arriving Shortly After the Schooner Gen<sup>l</sup> Green by the Brig Abigail of New York, there was an Immediate Change Took Place in the Conduct of the Directory Towards the Captured Vessels and those daily Arriving from the Continent by the Cargoes of those Vessels Arrived, being Put in Requisition for the Use of the Republic, and if the Owners of them Refused Selling them to the Administration, the Cargos was Taken by force for the Use of the Republic. I Left Cape Francois on the 24 of December, at which Time their Business was Daily Pending in our Vessels, Either from, or Bound to English Ports, and there had been No Instance of any of the Vessels Under These Circumstances being Cleared. I Remain with Respect.

Isaac o W Kim

Sir

You will very much Oblig me, if you will please to enclose me by the next post Eight Hundred Dollars. out of my accounts rendered for 95 and 96 that sum will enable me to repay money borrowed and advanced in support of the recruiting service in 95, for which I have been paying interest.

The ballance due me may remain in your hands, untill I come forward and settle my Accounts

The letter incloseing the Eight Hundred Dollars, you will please direct (in my absence) to M<sup>r</sup> Peter Hershell in Staunton. and I hope Sir, you will not omit sending it by the first post; as my Credit may be materially effected by the neglect. money being extremely scarce at present in this part.

I am
Sir
Your ob<sup>t</sup> Humd Servant

Alex. Gibson Cap<sup>t</sup>.
4<sup>th</sup> Reg.<sup>t</sup> U.S. army

56409:
To Benjamin Hawkins, Andrew Pickens and James
Winchester, Esquires.

Gentlemen,

The President with the advice and consent of the Senate having appointed you Commissioners to ascertain and mark the boundary line [strikethrough: agreeable to treaties between the Indian Nations] and the United States, you are hereby vested with all authority appertaining to the said appointment and directed to proceed to ascertain and mark the boundary lines between the United States and the Creek, Cherokee and Chickasaw Nations viz —

The Creek boundary as defined in the Treaty of 1790 and supplementary treaty of Coleraine of 1796 in the words following vizt —

Treaty of 1790. Article 4.

" The boundary between the Citizens of the United States and the Creek Nations is and shall be from where the old line strikes the River Savannah, thence up the said River to a place on the most northern Branch of the same commonly called the Keowee, where a northeast line to be drawn from the top of the Occunna Mountain shall intersect; thence along the said line in a southwest direction to Tugelo River, thence to the top of the Currahee Mountain, thence to the head or source of the main South Branch of the Oconee River called the Appalachee, thence down the middle of the said main South Branch and River Oconee to its confluence with the Oakmulgee which forms the River Altamaha and thence down the middle of the said Altamaha to the old line on the said River and thence along the said old line to the River St. Marys"

Treaty of Coleraine Article 2<sup>d</sup>

" The boundary line from the Currahee Mountain to the head or source of the main South branch of the Oconee River called by the white People Appalachee, and by the Indians Tulapocka, and down the middle of the same shall be clearly ascertained and marked, at such time and in such manner as the President shall direct. And the Indians will on being informed of the determination

Sir,

In the Contract between the United States and the Proprietors of the Hope Furnace in Rhode Island for Cannon — it is provided "that an allowance for the extra expence of boring the Cannon from the solid shall be made by the United States, if on a consideration of the said expence and all advantages & disadvantages attending the operation, it shall appear that anything ought to be paid on that score to the Contractors"

Sir

When Virginia in March 1784 ceded to the United States the lands north west of the Ohio within the limits of her charter, no reservation was made for satisfying the claims for bounty lands of the State Officers not on continental establishment of which description John Nelson ice his petition is stated to be. Consequently the United States are not bound by the terms of cession to satisfy the claim of John Nelson or any other of the like kind.

The Indian right to the land between Cumberland and Tenessee rivers, whereon locations were made for the use of John Nelson and others in the State line of Virginia was not extinct at the time of those locations and therefore they must be viewed as made subject to that right and liable to the possibility of being [strikethrough: left without] upon the boundary line of the lands allotted to the Indians when a peace should be made with them or a contract concluded with them. In making the treaty of 10<sup>th</sup> Jan<sup>ry</sup> 1786 with the Chickasaws congress exercised a lawful right and did not do an act by which John Nelson was deprived of land to which he or Virginia under whom he claims had a complete title. The Indians had never consented to cede those to Virginia, and the utmost right of Virginia was a pre-emption right — This pre-emption right is not violated or taken away by any act of Congress but is deemed to exist in full force. Whenever the Indians will surrender their right to those lands by treaty, the State of Virginia ought to exercise her right of pre-emption and when obtained the location title of John Nelson to the lands in his surveys should be preferred to all others under Virginia protection to it. Till the Indian right shall be extinguished in a valid and regular manner to the tract of country, or Virginia shall [strikethrough: have] [strikethrough: the lands] for satisfying claims of this kind they must remain as they are. 56421:
Dear Sir, Philadelphia Feb.<sup>y</sup> 2. 1797.

I send you M<sup>r</sup> Swan's letter to Gen<sup>l</sup> Smith, in which the former would have it understood that the conduct of Santhonax & the other agents of the French Gov ernments have not determined on their late depredations on American commerce, in consequence of any orders or letters from M<sup>r</sup> Adet; and that he has no commu nications from France that authorize the conduct now followed there; and that he (M<sup>r</sup> Adet) believes that it can never have entered into the "Head of power" (by which it must be presumed he means, the Directory in France) to make such a regulation.

Without enquiring whether M<sup>r</sup> Swan's statement is or is not correct, I will just remark, that the first captures made of American Vessels by order of Victor Hugues, for having Horses &other contraband articles on board, are expressly grounded, by that "special agent of the French Directory," on the advices he had received from M<sup>r</sup> Adet, under the date of the 15<sup>th</sup> or [undecipherable: probable reading 22<sup>d</sup>] of July last; and that twelve days after July 14<sup>th</sup> M<sup>r</sup> Adet, in answer to a number of questions I had proposed to him relative to [strikethrough: any] orders which might have been issued by the French Government or any branch of it, for capturing American Vessels, professed entire ignorance on the subject.

I will further inform you, that the capturing of American vessels going to or from British ports is not confined (as M<sup>r</sup> Adet seems inclined to have us believe) to the West Indies: the same game is playing in Europe: and not against Americans only: for the French privateers, be side two of these, had captured three Swedes & two Danes, and carried them into Spain, or the Spanish port of Ceuta on the Barbary Coast: and the French Consul at Cadiz avowed his determination to con demn all neutral vessels going to or coming from the ports of the enemies of France, adding, that he had authority so to do. Such was the State of things agreeable to my latest information from Spain.

Thus much I thought it would be agreeable to you to know, after perusing Swans letter to General Smith.

I remain respectfully yours
T. Pickering

James McHenry Esq<sup>r</sup>

56502:
War Office, February 19<sup>th</sup> 1797.

Sir,

I have received your two letters of the 2<sup>d</sup> & 3<sup>d</sup> of January last.—

A correct knowledge of the number, and views of the settlers, on the Indian land, being necessary to enable the Executive to determine upon the measures proper for the occasion, you will be pleased to take immediate steps to send one of [strikethrough: those] [strikethrough: two] persons among them, qualified for such a mission, and in whom you can confide, instructed to ascertain, with perfect exactness, their number, situation, views, and means for resistance; all which you will transmit, as soon as possible. I shall count upon your sagacity, in selecting fit characters; in keeping from them any intimations which might lead them should they meet, to suspect that they were sent on the same errand, and upon the knowledge of the mission being kept from every other person.

It is likely that more troops may be ordered to Tennessee; but the number cannot at present be ascertained.

I think the Doctors bill high; but if it cannot be lessened, with propriety, it must be paid.

Should the misbehaviour of M<sup>r</sup> Lillis render his removal indispensible, you will consider whether Lieutenant Wright might not supply his place. This gentleman is well recommended to me, and from appearances, I should presume upon his attention and capacity.

As it is inconvenient and attended with risk, to transport money from hence, to pay the troops in Tennessee, you may draw upon me for the pay of Sparks's company, from the day they were [strikethrough: kept] [strikethrough: in] [strikethrough: hope] mustered, the paymaster, to the first of January, and for the pay of Rickord's, and Waddy for November and December all.

With great respect
I am Sir
Your ob<sup>t</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup>

James McHenry

Colonel Henley.

Sir,

I have received your letter of the 5<sup>th</sup> of January Ultimo, by Lieutenant Wright.

My letter of the 27<sup>th</sup> Ultimo (of which I enclose you a duplicate) explains the objects that you are at present to attend to, and suggests the principle that is to govern in giving a final disposition to the Troops on the frontier.—

Perhaps the Commissioners may agree with the Indians, that the posts may be established within their Country, should it offer sites better calculated for their, and the protection of the Tennessee Inhabitants.
