Dear Sir

In one of the last letters which I received from the Late Majr. Gen. Wayne he informed me that the British had erected and garrisoned a work on the Isle de Bois Blanc, and requested instructions how to act, suggesting, that our submitting to its being so occupied without remonstrance might in time be construed into a relinquishment of our right to it. The same intrusion has also been stated to me by Brig. Gen. Wilkerson, with the addition that he has understood that the post has been taken by the special order of the British government.

Being in company with M<sup>r</sup> Liston yesterday evening, I took occasion to mention to him the situation of the Island, [strikethrough: occupied by a British garrison, subjoining] that as I [strikethrough: had] intended as soon as I had Leisure to employ him and the Secy of State on the Subject. To this he replied that he hoped the matter could be [strikethrough: settled] without its taking a diplomatic course that he would rather the vacation should appear a voluntary thing, and that if I would be so obliging as to give him a memorandum of the fact he would immediately write to Candada respecting it.

Col<sup>t</sup> Rochefontaine to drive the Team, for which he allows him a part of the earnings for his labour — that the materials as well as the making the Waggon was paid for at the expence of the United States and from other information no doubt remains with me but that the Horses are also Public Property — Mr Fleming also informs me that although the Receipt is signed by M<sup>r</sup> Connice — he pays the nit amount after making a deduction for the drivers to Col<sup>t</sup> Rochefontaine —

Thus Sir it appears that Col<sup>t</sup> Rochefontaine is receiving Pay for the Hire of a waggon and Horses employed in the Public Service and which is Public Property —

I shall accordingly deduct all charges of this nature from the Accounts of M<sup>r</sup> Fleming, as illegal in two Points of view — first it being contrary to Law, agreeably to the Resolve of Congress of the 15<sup>th</sup> July 1780 for an Officer to be concerned in any Team Boat &c, while in the service of the United States — & Secondly — because the Property hired appears to be Public Property —

I am aware Sir of the delicacy of my situation in bringing forward a charge of so serious a nature — But I should conceive myself wanting in my duty as a Public Officer did I not on any appearance of fraud to the Public make it known that it might be guarded against in future — I have therefore conceived it necessary to inform you that you may direct the necessary [strikethrough: step] steps to be taken that the Officer may be brought to account —

Sir

Agreeable to your desire, I have now the honor of transmitting you a list of Such Officers & men as I consider necessary to keep employed, for the care and preservation of the frigate Now building [undecipherable] this City: that is to say after she is launched Completed and the master Carpenter and other artificers are discharged, and the Ship laid up —

If the Chinese System is not to be adopted, and the United States and the people [undecipherable] continue their Commercial habits, of trading beyond the Sea, it is evident, that whenever two European powers are at War we Shall always be Subject to insult and depredation from their Public, and private Ships of war, unless we have a Navy to defend our rights, and Support the honor and dignity of our flag. But without Officers what can be expected from a Navy; the Ships cannot man themselves, Nor will the best of Soldiers answer as Substitutes for Seamen. This every man must be convinced of, that reads the Numerous accounts of British & French engagements at Sea, in which we find the former always victorious, not because they are a braver people, but on account of their knowing their duty as Seamen and Tacticians, Whereas the latter Nation is but little acquainted with either of them.

Thus Sir it is evident that, if we are to have a Navy, we must make Officers to Manage the Navy and this can only be done by employing a few Ships of war, in cruising about in times of peace & by manning the [undecipherable], for in a very few years more there will scarcely be an officer fit for Service to be found who required any practical knowledge, during our Revolution, and to introduce foreigners into our Navy would appear to me a very dangerous policy.

For the above reasons, I Should be glad to see active and respectable men appointed as Lieutenants and Midshipmen, in order that they might be brought on to learn the art of Marine Science and to Supply the place of those, who in a few years will be incapable of this art of Service. But knowing the pusillanimity of Congress, and Supposing the Executive will let the Business in question remain in Status quo, until the next Session, I have only made out a list of Such Officers as are Necessary to take Care of the Ship, Stores and Other public property within the Yard—

It is always considered that even Small Merchant Ships, Suffer more from being laid up in port the under the eye of the Owner, then when in actual Service, and I am convinced, the fact is so, Since the necessity of having proper people to take Care of these Ships when afloat is very Obvious.

This frigate while laying in Ordinary, will be moored at the end of the Wharf Where She is now building (with two anchors out) Near to which are all the Magazines of Stores, Containing the articles of equipment, Which are under Care of the Clerk, and Should in My Opinion Continue So, as he appears to me a faithfull, honest, diligent [undecipherable] and Careful Young Man

[If] the Arrangement [undecipherable] offer, meets with your approbation. I wish as Soon as the frigate is launched Order the Clerk and Petty Officers [undecipherable] and prior to [undecipherable] employed, to take [undecipherable] their abode [undecipherable] — keep watch on board, and by that means they can [undecipherable] the Store houses and all the Other public property within the Yard as well as the Ship: But while every thing that respects the frigates is now in Motion, [undecipherable] certainly be most economical to Completely finish them, and provide every necessary article required for their equipment, except provisions, in order that they may be ready for any emergency.

When the Contract was Made with Stoddert for his grounds, that now enclosed as a public Yard, and on which are Several buildings for the accommodation of the Materials, it was agreed to pay him for the Said lot now enclosed, a Rent of four hundred dollars per annum, during the pleasure of the Government. I have therefore made a Calculation of the probable expense, that will attend this Ship, while laying in Ordinary, including the Said rent.

Rent of Navy Yard per annum . . . . . . $400
One Captain 75 [pr] M<sup>o</sup> & his rations per day . . 1338
One Clerk to attend the Yard and Ship . . . . 600
One Boatswain per Month to find himself $30 }
One Carpenter ditto . . . ditto . . . 30 } is per annum 1680
One Cook . . . . ditto . . . ditto . . 20 }

Paints, oil, brushes, brooms, buckets, wind Sails } per annum 982

[undecipherable] Dollars 5000

also I have Contemplated that the persons employed to attend, watch and take Care of the Ship while in Ordinary Should find themselves provisions &c, as a Cook will be Necessary to draw their victuals on board and Such a person may also be useful, in aiding the others in doing the various duties of the Ship: Otherwise four Seamen would be necessary instead of three, which amounts to the Same thing.

The expense [I've] Stated will perhaps appear high to you, but unless proper people are employed, their will always be a waste and plunder of the public property, and I know of no way of Sparing this expense, but by Constructing the Ships after they are built at one place, and then it might be curtailed very Considerably from the foregoing Calculation, & many Other Savings Made to the United States.

In My report to you in December last, I Stated that if the winter was not unfavorable to us, that this frigate would be launched in May ensuing; but as two months has been lost, owing to the Severity of the weather, She cannot well be put afloat before July, unless Some extraordinary efforts are made, and the workmen Augmented: Therefore [undecipherable] will be pleased to refer to my Said report and add, that the bottom is now all planked except two Streaks; the upper works the Same all but two Streaks: The orlop and lower deck beams all in and Mostly knee'd the other decks beams ready. Westpoint March 12<sup>th</sup> 1797

Sir

I received your letter of the 4<sup>th</sup> Inst<sup>s</sup>. Head has been paid this part of bounty due him; as to Spafford, upon investigation I found that a reward of 10 Dollars had been paid Serg<sup>t</sup> Seamen for apprehending him; likewise Sundry other charges which were brought against the US. by the pursuing party, I therefore concluded that the balance of bounty Due him was wholly exhausted by the expences of the Public on account of his desertion.

The Muster Roll for february as well as all the Subsequent ones will be made to contain the Trade or occupation of every artificer in the corp, it will be also accompanied with a Certificate of the time that every one has been employed in each month, you will from it deduct if you think proper the additional pay that they are entitled to by law and by their engagement; but I dont conceive myself authorised to do it, and I will take this liberty to Submit to your examination my reasons for it.  an artificer is Enlisted to be made use of for the Publick Service as a tradesman and as a Soldier, as circumstances may require, and the Public has agreed to pay him nine [undecipherable] Dollars per Month.  if he is found to be unequal to the duty of an artificer of cours

he is, after a legal investigation, to be placed upon the Pay Roll at the rate of four Dollars only as a private Soldier.  if he is employed as an artificer and if [undecipherable] he is wasting away his time; he is to be punished at the Discretion of a court Martial, which may Direct Stoppages to be made out of his monthly pay.  if he falls Sick, he is to be paid as if he was Constantly employed:  upon that I will however add some observation.

when a non comd officer and Private are Sick in the hospital, the whole of their pay or a part of it at least, might be Stoped with propriety;
1<sup>st</sup> because the Public is at great expence to have the Hospital attended to and furnished with Medicines and other necessaries.
2<sup>d</sup> because nine tenth of the Sick are brought to that Situation by Intemperance, by the wish of Screening themselves from duty, and too often from deceiving the recruiting officer upon the State of their Constitution when they were Enlisted.
3<sup>d</sup> because when a Man is in the Hospital, he has no occasion for his pay, being provided with every necessary and it is, [undecipherable: probable reading "his pay"] but an inducement to intoxication which to my knowledge has been the cause of the death of many.

a circumstance in which it would be highly proper to Stop the whole or part of a non comd officer or Privates pay, is when they are going upon furlough.  it would have at least that good effect of removing from their mind

the wish of applying so often for Leave of absence.

Do not mention the comd officers, because I know some upon whom it would fall, I learn that they would not be able to Support the Dignity of their Station.

The artificers as soon as they are Enlisted should be ordered to West point when [undecipherable] are employed and for those on repairing Barracks Public Store and Building I have no [undecipherable].  I am in returns from New York and North Carolina; artificers who cannot be employed there for the Public good.

a return from Charleston S<sup>o</sup> Ca has discovered to me an Evil which arises from the Ignorance Some officers are kept in with respect of Military laws.  I have remarked that Captain Kalteisen had continued Enlisting men for 3 years when a law had ordered the Enlistments to be made for five years.

I am Respectfully,

Sir

your obed<sup>t</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup>

Sir,

[14 March 1797
John Adams]

The President of the United States, requests the Secretary at War, to take into his consideration the following Questions and make report of his opinion in Writing.

1. Whether the Refusal to receive M<sup>r</sup> Pinckney and the rude orders to quit Paris, and the Territory of the Republick, with Such Circumstances of Indignity, Insults and Hostility, as We have been inform'd of, are bars to all further measures of Negotiation? or in other Words a fresh mission to Paris be too great an humiliation of the American People in their own Sense and that of the World.

2. If another mission be admissible, can any part, and what parts or Articles of the Treaty of Amity and Commerce with Great Britain, be offered to France or ultimately conceded to that Power, in case of necessity, if demanded by her.

3. What Articles of the Treaty of Alliance and of the Treaty of Commerce with France Should be proposed to be abolished?

4. Whether it will be prudent to Say any Thing, concerning the consular convention with that Power, and if it will what Alterations in it Should be proposed?

5. Whether any new Articles Such as are not contained in either of our Treaties with France or England Shall be proposed, or can be agreed to, if proposed by the French Government?

6. What Documents Shall be prepared to Send to France as evidence of Insults and Injuries committed against the Commerce of the United States by French Ships of War, or Privateers, or by French [undecipherable: probable reading "Commissious"] Agents, Officers, or Citizens?

7. In what terms Shall Remonstrances against Spoliations of Property, Capture of Vessels, Imprisonment of Masters and Mariners, Cruelties, Insults and Abuses of every kind, to our Citizens be made?

8. In what terms Shall restitution Reparation Compensation and Satisfaction be demanded for Such Insults and Injuries?

9. Shall demand be made of Payment to our Citizens, for Property purchased by the French Government in Europe, or in the East and West Indies.

10. Shall demand be made of the French Government of Payment for Vessels and Cargoes, captured and Seized, whether by Ships of War or private Ships?

11. Shall any Commission of Inquiry and Examination like that with England be agreed to?

12. What Articles in the British Treaty can be offered to France, without Compensation and with Compensation, and what Compensation Shall be demanded?

13. Shall a Projet of a new Treaty abolishing the old Treaties and Consular Convention be proposed to France?

14. Shall Such a Projet, with a Projet of Instructions to the Minister, be prepared and laid before the Senate for their Advice and consent, before they be Sent to Europe?

John Adams

Philadelphia 14. March 1797.

another Letter mentioned the impropriety of paying an Adjutant to the 4<sup>th</sup> Bat<sup>n</sup> as long as there are no men of that Battalion in this Garrison the Same reasoning might apply to the two other Adjutants, who are filling the offices of pay M<sup>r</sup> & D<sup>r</sup> M<sup>r</sup>. for they are not confined to the Duties of Adj<sup>t</sup>. to the 2<sup>d</sup> Bat<sup>n</sup>. and to the 3<sup>d</sup> Bat<sup>n</sup>. but they both preform Duties in the Staff, which you are convinced in your [undecipherable] of [undecipherable],

is deserving an extra pay. when you are acquainted with the Duti. of the Ad<sup>t</sup>. of the 4<sup>th</sup> Battalion and with the Usefull Extra duty which he is performing with the corps, you will own the same principle which animates you, declare that he is as deserving of the pay of adj<sup>t</sup>. to which I appointed him, as the two others.

by the organization of the corps of Art<sup>s</sup>. & Eng<sup>s</sup>. the artificers are distributed in the comp<sup>s</sup>. and they are Subject to the Internal police & discipline of their comp<sup>s</sup>. under the immediate authority of their Capt. and other officers of the comp<sup>y</sup>. the Law as therefore provided for the organization of the artificers, [underline: while they act in the capacity of Military men.] but when they act as tradesmen, they are all upon a level, and none has a right to command to the other. when I joined the corps, the artificers were under the direction of M<sup>r</sup>. Hennings foreman (Capt. wright); under that arrangement, the artificers did little or no good, discontentment, Military men would not be under the command and Direction of a man in civil life, the want of Subordination caused disorder, Tools were Missing or Stolen, the Military artificers accused the Civil ones to be the authors, and vice versa. I appointed a Noncommissioned officer to command them and to take charge of the Tools, leaving the Direction of the Works to M<sup>r</sup>. wright; that alteration removed Some Evils, but did not Establish

that Spirit of Emulation So necessary to a Body of artificers, to turn it to the Public Advantage. — I proposed the Direction of the artificers to the officers. but Many refused it for fear of Deviating from the Duty of a Gentleman in applying themselves to the Direction of Trademen, others considered that Duty as foreign to that of an officer of Art<sup>s</sup>. & would not Chuse to do it out of their Tour, unless they were paid for it. the artificers were then placed under the immediate Command of officers, who by turn and Monthly were to attend them daily; it was considered both as an encouragement to Learning, and an advantage for the Service. my Endeavours were totally defeated and experience taught me that the only mode of turning the artificers to Public use, was to lay them under the command of an officer Capable of Directing them in all the Branches of Mechanics, and who would Devote his whole attention to it for the consideration of Some extra pay. Lieu<sup>t</sup>. Drausy united in him all the Talents which I could wish and would consent to take upon himself the charge of that essential Duty for the extra pay of an adj<sup>t</sup>. I had the adjutancy of the 4<sup>th</sup> Bat<sup>n</sup>. Vacant, I proposed the Case to the Consideration of the Sec<sup>t</sup>. of War in September last, & I appointed M<sup>r</sup>. Drausy Adjutant to the 4<sup>th</sup> Bat<sup>n</sup>. under the Circumstances aforesaid, and under the immediate Control of the Sec<sup>t</sup>. of War. — M<sup>r</sup>. Drausy has ever Since done the company duty, the Adjutant Duty, and the direction of the artificers, has been attended to by him with much

credit to his Mechanical genius, to the advantage of good order and discipline, and to the very great profit of the U<sup>s</sup>. for Since he has had the Direction of the artificers, they have repaired the Barracks for the Troops of this garrison, they have covered the Powder Magazine 2<sup>d</sup> over. they have Constructed 2 Mortar Carriages, & 2 travelling field 4 pounder Carriages, with their implements, and have Elected a great deal of Timber Seasoning for further wants. but to resume myself;

The Pay of Adjutant may be refused to Lieu<sup>t</sup>. Drausy for his extra Services for the Months of Jan<sup>y</sup>. & Feb<sup>y</sup>. last; but it will not be consistent with that Justice which regulates the Usages of your Department, for he was appointed [underline: agreeably to the rules of the army], and he has performed [underline: the Services attached to his appointment.] if he is deprived by authority of the appointment and pay of an adjutant, it will be an Injury to the Public, but I will have done my duty in representing that the artificers will become mostly useless in losing an able officer to direct them, and the officers of the corps, will be deprived of a kind of Instruction which can be obtained but in the Shops where artificers are employed in building implements of artillery.

I am very Respectfully, Sir,

Your obed<sup>t</sup>. Serv<sup>t</sup>.

To Brigadier General James Wilkinson.

Sir,

Such of the Posts on the line from Fort Washington to Fort Massac, as shall appear to you unnecessary to the security of the communication between those two, you are hereby authorized and directed to vacuate, and to apply their Garrisons, or an equal number of troops from any other, to complete the detachment ordered to the State of Tennessee.

As to the new cordon of Posts suggested in your letter of the 4<sup>th</sup> of February ultimo and reiterated in that of the 10<sup>th</sup> instant, it cannot now take place, without imposing the necessity of a recal of the Order of the 21<sup>st</sup> of February ultimo and nothing thereby, interests more valuable to the Union, than any apparent advantages attached to the immediate execution of the Scheme. It shall however receive further consideration as soon as it is perceived, that the peace of the southern frontier can be preserved by a less force than that which seems to be at present indispensable.

On the 10<sup>th</sup> of September last the late Major General was directed to take measures to receive the Posts within our Territory, stipulated by our treaty with Spain to be delivered up to the United States. Unless you have a Copy of his instructions to the Officer detached for that purpose, you will be pleased to enquire into the force ordered on that occasion and often small, to render it by an addition competent to garrisoning the Posts at the Natchez and Walnut Hills; it not being contemplated at this moment to occupy any other.

Philad. 24 March 1799.

Dear Sir.

Once more at home, and I flatter myself recovered from the fatigues of your journey. Treasury Department
March 29<sup>th</sup> 1797

Sir,

Your letter of the 17<sup>th</sup> Ultimo informing me of the measures taken to supply the Troops in Tennessee has been duly received —

In consequence of your statement of the difficulty of procuring supplies — and which difficulty will be encreased by an additional number of Five hundred Men now on their march to Tennessee — it has been deemed most adviseable to provide for the supply of that part of the Army intended to be stationed in your District, in the general Contract entered into with Colonel James O'Hara, a copy whereof is transmitted herewith for your government. I have therefore to request that you will enter into no Contracts whatever after the receipt of this letter — but that you will continue to furnish the Troops with Rations &c. by means of temporary arrangements until M<sup>r</sup> O'Hara is prepared to enter on the buisness — If before the receipt of this letter however, you should have made any agreement or Contract for any specific time, it is to be understood that in

in such case M<sup>r</sup> O'Hara is not to commence issuing until the expiration of the term for which the said agreement or Contract was made. As it is highly necessary that the Contractor should be made acquainted with what has been done by you in this business for the purpose of enabling him to make his arrangements, it is my wish that you give me the earliest information possible on the subject.

I am with Consideration
Sir
Your most Obed Servant
[signature: Wm Wolcott]

David Henley Esq<sup>r</sup>
Agent for the Department of War

He may on extraordinary occasions, Convene both Houses or either of them &c<sup>a</sup>

As no extraordinary occasion has as yet occurred since the Establishment of this Government, there can be no precedents to Guide us, and as it is not impossible or improbable, that such an extraordinary occasion as is intimated in the Constitution may some occur, the President wishes that a Precedent may be formed, which thereafter require no alteration.

I am, with consideration,
SIR,
Your most humble and obedient servant,
MANUEL GAYOSO DE LEMOS.

It is conceived that the Contract with Crozier & McCarry is very objectionable, not only on account of the price of the Ration, which is far beyond any thing heretofore demanded [strikethrough: for supplies] in Tennessee — but because it extends to other parts of the State not authorised by my letter of the 23<sup>d</sup> of November 1796 — in which you were pointedly confined to the making a Contract for Supplying the Troops intended to be Stationed at Telico Block House — You will therefore inform Crozier & McCarry, that the subject was not properly understood at the time of making the Contract, and consequently that no Supplies will be required from them excepting for the Post of Telico — The fact is, that the Troops now under marching orders for Tennessee were provided for under the Contract with Col<sup>o</sup> James O'Hara for the year 1796 — and are also included in the Contract entered into with that Gentleman for the present year — I shall conclude with requesting that you will take immediate measures for putting this business on a proper footing and that you will consider all the Troops now Stationed [strikethrough: or to be stationed] in Tennessee (those at Telico only excepted) as provided for under the Contract with Col<sup>o</sup> O'Hara. —

I am with consideration
Sir .

Your obedient Servant

I am

Sir

Your Humble

Servant

Sir   }

James Hamiltons Waggens leave this City this Day for Pittsburgh laden with supplies on account of the Wyandot Delaware & Shawnee Indians Annuities for the current Year. And Sunday other articles to you address as per Invoice which he has with him. I know not wether you may have received any particular Instructions from the Secretary of War or General Wilkins relative to the ultimate Delivery or further transports of these goods, but I have a right to Expect you have been informed on the subject. I will however, make the matter certain & Inform you. I should conclude that the Delaware & Shawnees supplies would be sent up the Algany and the Wyandots down the Ohio to Washington or some other Posts on that river but circumstances may make some other route more Eligible and of this I will endeavour to be Informed Wheresoever and to Whomsoever you send or Deliver the goods you will send the enclosed Invoice. When the supplies in full are forwarded for the other nations similar Invoices will accompany them.

Sam
Sir,
Your Most Obedient Servant

Samuel Hodgdon

S I R,
YESTERDAY, by Lieutenant John M'Clairy, I received your answer to my communication of the day before. I am sorry to find the construction you give to such an official information, which leaves no room of doubt.

The project of an attack from the British in Canada, is positive, and in consequence thereof, it is the duty of the Commander General of this Province to oppose it by every means in his power, tho' the probability is, that they will not be able to carry their plan into execution, as we rely on the friendship of the United States, who certainly will not voluntarily permit such an armed force to pass through their territory, to attack the dominions of his Majesty; but, as when such an expedition was proposed, the British knew very well that to accomplish they must necessarily pass through the territory of the United States, they certainly have had it in view either to pass the Posts by surprize, or some other combination secured to them the means of reaching Illinois: it to prevent the effects of such an event that the said Commander General takes every measure to obstruct their effects at their first approach, or a continuation of it, if fortune should favour them in Upper Louisiana.

We are far from acting in a manner so as to alter the good understanding that happily subsists between our nations. Political reasons have caused a suspension of the evacuation of these Posts; reasons that are to be settled ministerially, and that are out of my line to controul; my duty is to comply with the superior orders of my General in Chief, which are positively to keep the best harmony with you, and attend to every other object concerning the safety of this Province.

There is no reason to apprehend that the Treaty between the United States of America and his Majesty will not take place in every point; the delay experienced in regard to one part of it, is not a violation of the Treaty, and is only referred to the regular ministerial procedure, which, when settled, will be exactly complied with; in the mean while, no alteration can take place, nor can any part of his Majesty's dominions be considered as abandoned or delivered in a solemn and regular manner, and until that period the dominion of his Majesty does not cease.

The communication that the Commander General of this Province has ordered me to impart to you, is a living proof of the good understanding that he is do[ing...]

Sir.

I received your letter dated the 5<sup>th</sup> instant, delivered me by Lieutenant John McClary, in reply to mine of the 3<sup>d</sup>, by which, and by our conferences, I am persuaded of your disposition to cultivate that good harmony that is justly due to our Nations — on my part I pledge my honour to you that I shall invariably continue considering you not only as I do every Individual of your Nation, but yet more particularly under the sacred views of the Representative; as likewise every person under your command, and under the direction of the Honourable Andrew Elliott.

I do assure you likewise, that my conduct shall be such, as not to merit the reflection of your Nation, nor expose mine to any contest on account thereof, being answerable by my duty, and by my honour, to act with such propriety as will justify me in my public capacity.

Sir

I received your letter of the 28<sup>th</sup> Ult<sup>o</sup> enclosing a Copy of certain Resolutions of the House of Representatives passed on the 3<sup>d</sup> March 1797, requiring statements & Estimates relation to the military and naval Establishments, with request that so far as depends on this Office, measures might be taken to enable the Secretary of Treasury to comply with the said Resolutions.

In conformity thereto I have proceeded in establishing the forms by which the Secretary of the Treas<sup>y</sup> is of opinion I am to be governed in rendering the said acco<sup>ts</sup> and as it will be a duty of great labour, and will require the strict attendance of at least two Clerks to compleat them within the time limited, I conceive it proper to inform you, that if that number should be taken from those now employed in the Office, the current business can not be pursued with that accuracy and diligence which is necessary. I therefore beg leave to submit to you Sir whether it would not be proper that I should appoint two additional Clerks, although there are no appropriations at present and depend on bong[?] appropriating hereafter. If you are of this opinion you will be aware that the Salary of men of sufficient abilities [taking] into view the temporary appointment) will be greater than the ordinary allowance to Clerks I am of opinion that it will require about Eight Hundred Dollars each p annum— your decision for my government I request as early as convenient that I may pursue the business with all possible dispatch.

W<sup>m</sup> Simmons Act<sup>t</sup>

This is to certify, that it appears by the Muster-bills filed in the Office of the Accountant of the War Department, that Thomas Frearm a Serjeant in Captain Sparks's Company of the Third Sub. Legion of the United States was discharged on the ninth day of April, one thousand seven hundred and ninety five.

C. Brown, John M. Scott, and R. Allison, Army Surgeons, certify that the said Thomas Frearm produced to them a certificate, by which it appears that he was wounded by the Enemy, while in the execution of his duty in public Service. They further certify that they have examined said wounds, viz. a ball passing through the right Lobe of his lungs, by which his respiration is much impeded in bodily exertions — thereby depriving him of the means of acquiring a Subsistence by labour — they therefore think him entitled to a compensation equal to [underline: three fifths] of that allowed for the highest disability.

Wherefore he is entitled to receive an annual allowance at the rate of three dollars per month, during the continuance of his disability aforesaid; of which he is to produce every six months a certificate of two respectable Physicians on oath: said pension to commence from the time of his discharge.

Given at the War Office of the United States, this fifteenth day of May, one thousand, seven hundred, and ninety seven.

James M<sup>c</sup>Henry
Sec<sup>y</sup> of War

57659:
HEAD QUARTERS,
*Fort Washington, 22d, May 1797.*

# GENERAL ORDERS.

TO prevent the necessity of repetition—to establish principle, without which there can be no permanent order—to define the rights of individuals—to exclude caprice—to promote economy and precision—to disseminate an uniformity of duty, and of service throughout the army—and to impress the necessary ideas of subordination and discipline, the following regulations have been digested, and must be duly respected by all ranks.—

1st. Precedence in command is attached to seniority of corps, and the oldest commission, subject to such deviations as the commander in chief may deem essential to the national weal, and the point of honor is determined by the following gradation:

1. Guard of the President.
2. The attack.
3. Reconnoitering parties and Corps of Observation.
4. Foraging before the enemy.
5. Posts in the enemy's country.
6. National barriers.
7. Detachments and Out Posts.
8. Guard of the trenches.
9. Van guards to the front.
10. Rear guards in retreat.
11. General courts martial.
12. Guard of the commander in chief.
13. Guards of camp or garrison taken from the line.
14. All other guards mounted from the grand parade.
15. Guards of general officers and the staff, according to rank.
16. Pickets.
17. General fatigues.
18. Regimental police.

Should a tour of service occur while an officer is on any subordinate duty, he shall be relieved, but the tour on which he was engaged, shall pass to his credit. If an officer's tour for general court martial, picquet, or fatigue occurs while he is on any other duty from the grand parade, he shall not be relieved, but is to stand for the next tour.

2d. In all services by detachment, the corps are to furnish according to their strength; the longest off, the first on. But in all cases of duty and of service, where it may be found practicable, the troops are to operate by companies, battalions, or regiments.

Sir,

By this days post I am not favored with either letter or news papers from your Office. Therefore I thought can clude you must have been absent on post day or to much engaged.

James Hamilton has arrived with the Indian Goods, Wampum Shawanes & Delaware and as usual in need of money of which I have supplied him with 60 dollars for which his receipt is enclosed. That sum you will be pleased to stop at settlement of his account & place it to my credit.

James Hamilton's receipt for a Trunk holding the property of Doctor Ransolen to be left at your store, is also enclosed.

Also yesterday drew on you in favor of John Weenshall for 500 dollars at 5 days sight which be pleased to pay and charge as usual.

All the Powder on hand at this post fit for use, except one forty pounder, is now on board a boat destined for Fort Washington.

War office, May 29<sup>th</sup> 1797.

Sir,

I have now before me, your letter of the 21<sup>st</sup> of April last, on the subject of extra compensation paid by you, to a holder of the Panneau for conveying the public letters and Dispatches to and from the Post office at Peekskill. I should have given you my opinion on the propriety of the charge before this time, but detained it, until I could riper any, in writing from the Post master, on what rate he would undertake to perform the same service. His answer has been received the result is, that he cannot get it done under once a week $2 — twice a week $1 — three times $1 and free foirage. — This being the case, it is evident that your arrangement of half a dollar a trip, is the more oeconomical; and consequently ought to be adopted. I have therefore admitted the account as stated: — and in order that this necessary duty may be brought into a regular train of execution, you will be pleased to consider this letter as an

57820:
State of Tennessee, Knoxville 6th June 179[7].

Sir:

A few days past I was favoured with your duplicate of the 20th of April, tho as yet the original is not come to hand.

The conduct of the executive of this state has uniformly manifested his intention to preserve the peace of the frontiers by all the means in his station, and the laws had put in his power. The very great and essential advantages and benefits accruing from such a situation of affairs, requires no great share of sagacity to discover the propriety of such an arrangement and measure; and should every other executive department he as pacifcly disposed, I should not entertain a doubt but peace and tranquility would abound throughout the United States. I acknowledge that the chiefs of the Cherokee nation have discovered an entire disposition for peace for some time, not from any good-will for the people of the United States, for it is well known they never entertain any towards them, therefore from such a principle their pacific conduct have not arisen. When I say they have not any good will for the people, I speak from experimental knowledge of forty years. When the French attacked America, when under the Brittish government, the Indian tribes generally joined the former, and America felt the weight of their savage ferocity; again when America was invaded by the Brittish, they uniformly turned round in opposition to the Americans and French. From such a line of conduct, the information obtained from history, I am not induced to believe they ever had, or will have any good will towards us; and I have good reasons to believe their pacific disposition proceeds from another source.

You are pleased to mention that accounts arrived that two of the Cherokees had been cruelly murdered, and whether the intention of the act was to disturb the peace, to create difficulties to the removal of the settlers, or to obstruct the operation of the Government on the frontiers, was not then necessary to be examined.

If the same person who give you the information of the murder being committed had given himself the trouble to have stated to you that one of those Indians had actually been at the murdering of a brother of one of the two men, who it is supposed killed the Indians referred to, and also some of the same party at the murder of the mother, two sisters and sister-in-law of the other, you might probably have accounted for it and suggested the reason. I say murdering of those white persons, because it was perpetrated in the time of profound peace. This outrage committed on the two Indians was by two hunters who were in company with them, hunting in a remote part of the state of Kentucky. And when an account of its having been done was communicated to me by the executive of that state that there was just reasons to believe it was done by persons living in this; my orders was immediately issued for apprehending and securing the persons suspected, with directions to be safely conveyed to the state of Kentucky to be tried by the laws they had offended and transgressed against. The transgressors immediately fled and left the state, well knowing they could find no shelter in it; and I am determined they shall be dealt with as the laws direct, if they can be taken. If not, I am resolved they shall not be suffered to reside in any part of the state of Tennessee.

I am not fond of forwarding complaints against the Cherokee nation, on account of some murders and thefts committed by some lawless fellows of that tribe, conceiving it would be as difficult for the chiefs to prevent those disorders in every instance, as it would be for the rulers in Philadelphia to restrain murders and roberies often committed within that and other neighboring cities. Having good reasons to believe few representations go forward of the brutal and savage conduct of the Indians, I beg leave to inform you, that several very cruel and barbarous murders have been committed on several of the peaceable citizens of this state by the Cherokees and Creeks, also a great number of horses stolen by those nations in the course of autumn and winter last, retaining in captivity a number of white persons, negros and other property, in violation of the treaties and solem promises made to the contrary. It is an unpleasant reflection to behold as it were our dearest and nearest relatives in the hands of savages, sold and bartered from Indian to Indian, and from nation to nation, in order to glut and satisfy the ambition of savage cruelty; for to remedy these enumerated and aggravated grievances, I trust and confidently rely that decisive steps will be taken. Justice and policy require it, and if neglected will be a reproach to the government of the United States.

I am, etc.,          (Signed) John Sevier.

Honorable James McHenry, Secretary of War.

Extract of a Letter from the Secretary of War to Brigadier General James Wilkinson — dated War Office 9 June 1797.

"Yesterday the Secretary of State received letters from M<sup>r</sup> Elliott, by which it would appear that scruples on the part of Governor Gayoso had retarded the evacuation of the posts.

These scruples or objections are 1<sup>st</sup>. That in his opinion the forts ought to be demolished. 2<sup>d</sup>. That he thought it necessary to continue his force in that quarter till the claims of Spanish subjects to lands should be adjusted by negociation.

As to the first our Officer may be instructed to agree to the demolition of the works if insisted on. As to the second he will inform the Governor that he is authorized to say that no person shall be disturbed in his possession or property till an opportunity has been afforded to apply to Congress and that they may rely upon their claims being adjusted upon the most equitable principles.

It is to be presumed that on receiving these explanations the Spanish Garrisons will be withdrawn. If however contrary to expectation this should not happen, our Officer is to take a secure position but not so near them as to give any cause to the Spanish Garrisons to apprehend insult or injury. —

"Yesterday the Secretary of State received letters from M<sup>r</sup> Elliott, by which it would appear that scruples on the part of Governor Gayso had retarded the evacuation of the posts.

It is to be presumed that on receiving these explanations the Spanish Garrisons will be withdrawn. If however contrary to expectation this should not happen, our Officer is to take a secure position but not so near them as to give any cause to the Spanish Garrisons to apprehend insult or injury. —

Department of State
June 10 1797

Sir,

The Chevalier de Yrujo has just parted from me. He brought two letters in the Spanish language from the Baron de Carondelet which he said he would literally translate to me. These letters mentioned his dissatisfaction with M<sup>r</sup> Ellicott the Commissioner for running the boundary line between the United States and Florida, on account of his conduct at the Natchez as communicated to the Baron by Governor Gayoso. The Chevalier has promised me Copies of the Barons letters. After some conversation on the subject the Chevalier expressed his wishes; and I take it the wishes of the Baron Carondelet, that M<sup>r</sup> Ellicott as a skillful man in his profession, might be confined to his appointment of running the boundary line and that a discreet cool and prudent officer might be appointed [underline: to command the American troops who shou<sup>ld</sup> take post at the Natchez and whose arrival there was expected.] The Barons two letters were dated, one about the 25 of March the other the 20 of April. I asked the Chevalier where he supposed the American Troops would take post, if the Spanish Troops did not withdraw from the Fort. He answered that the settlement was large and there were plenty of houses in which they could find Quarters. One conclusion results that the Spaniards have yet entertained no idea of using force to prevent our troops making an establishment at the Natchez. The Baron de Carondelet has written to the Prince of Peace for instructions about the manner of evacuating the posts whether to leave the Works standing or to demolish them.

I am Sir &
Tim<sup>y</sup> Pickering

The Secretary of War.     Copy.

War Office 15 June 1797.

Sir,

Should this dispatch find you where I expect it will, at the Natchez, [undecipherable: garrison] still in possession of the works at that place, you will [undecipherable] communicating to the commanding Officer there the enclosed copy of a message from the President of the United States to Congress, and to the Inhabitants of the Natchez its contents, that both may be fully possessed of the intentions of Government. You will also inform the Spanish Commandant that you are instructed to pay the strictest attention to the engagements the United States have entered into by the treaty with his Catholic Majesty, to permit the demolition of the works, to use your utmost endeavours to preserve a continuance of the pacific dispositions of the Indians within our limits towards the subjects of his Catholic Majesty or his Indians, and to prevent their commencing hostilities of which there is no appearance, against either conformably to the fifth article of the said treaty. That you flatter yourself after these candid assurances, that you will have the immediate pleasure to announce to the President a full compliance with the treaty on the part of the Commander of his Catholic Majestys forces within the United States.

With respect to the Government of your posts. You will keep the Works always in a condition to resist attacks; practise the same precautions against surprize as if the United States were actually in war; fix upon regular and stated hours for exercise; pay the strictest attention to the arms, accoutrements and cloathing of the men; direct four toll rolls every day; viz the first at Sun rise, the second at the hour of dinner, the third at that of supper, and the fourth an hour after retreat by a visit made to their huts or quarters by a Subaltern Officer; have the sick and the Soldiers quarters visited every day by a Subaltern Officer who shall examine into their situation, see there is nothing out of orders; that their provisions are wholesome and well cooked, that no quarrels exist among them, that they do not game, get drunk or commit debaucheries. You will also examine, in conjunction with the next Officer in command, once every Month, the state of the Works, Barracks, Huts, Magazines, public buildings, Stores of every description and all articles the property of the United States, and make a written Report thereof to the Secretary of War to be sent as often as occasions or opportunities may offer.

With respect to your general conduct. You will endeavour to gain the good will of the civil Officers and inhabitants of the district, without losing sight of those measures necessary to be inforced for the preservation of the peace of the frontier, and will as far as in your power be kind and attentive to such of the Indians as may visit you. —

As the times of service of some of the Soldiers of your detachment may [strikethrough: expire] who may be inclined to reinlist, I inclose you inlisting instructions and authorize you to draw on me for such sums as may be necessary to keep up the complement of your command by fresh inlistments either of old soldiers or others

I am Sir

with respect

Your obed Servant
James McHenry

Captain Isaac Guion

"Should this dispatch find you where I expect it will, at the Natchez, and the Spanish Garrison still in possession of the works at that place, you will be pleased to lose no time in communicating to the commanding Officer there, the enclosed copy of a message from the President of the United States to Congress, and to the Inhabitants of Natchez, its contents, that both may be fully possessed of the intentions of Government. You will also inform the Spanish Commandant, that you are instructed, to pay the strictest attention to the engagements the United States have written into by the Treaty with his Catholic Majesty, to permit the demolition of the works, to use your utmost endeavours to preserve a continuance of the pacific dispositions of the Indians within our limits towards the subjects of his Catholic Majesty or his Indians, and to prevent their commencing hostilities, of which there is no appearance against either, conformably to the fifth article of the said Treaty. That you flatter yourself after these candid assurances, that you will have the immediate pleasure to announce to the President, a full compliance with the treaty, on the part of the Commandaries of his Catholic Majesty's forces within the United States."

M<sup>r</sup>. Putman & his command are 13 miles above this — at Port Schlosfer — he reports to me once a week.

58050:
An ACT

*To provide for the further defence of the ports and harbours of the United States.*

**B**E IT ENACTED *by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America, in Congress assembled,* That for fortifying certain ports and harbours of the United States, there be appropriated a sum not exceeding one hundred and fifteen thousand dollars.

Sect. 2. *And be it further enacted,* That the said appropriation shall be paid and discharged out of the surplus of the revenue and income beyond the appropriations heretofore charged thereon.

Sect. 3. *And be it further enacted,* That the President of the United States be, and he is hereby empowered to authorize any of the states which were found indebted to the United States in a settlement of the accounts between them and the respective states, to expend under his direction, the sums respectively due from them, in fortifying their ports and harbours; and the sums which may be so expended, shall be passed to the credit of the said states, on account of the balances found and reported by the commissioners for settling the accounts between the United States and the individual states, to be due from the said states to the United States. *Provided* the said states shall and do cede to the United States, the lands or places on which such fortifications shall be so erected, in cases where the lands are the property of such state.

JONATHAN DAYTON,
*Speaker of the House of Representatives.*
THOMAS JEFFERSON,
*Vice-President of the United States,*
*and President of the Senate.*

United States, *June* 23*d*, 1797.
APPROVED:

JOHN ADAMS,
*President of the United States.*

*Deposited among the Rolls in the Office of the Department of State.*

Timothy Pickering
*Secretary of State.*

58062:
AN ACT

*Authorizing a detachment from the Militia of the United States.*

Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America, in Congress assembled, That the President of the United States be, and is hereby authorized to require of the executives of the several states, to take effectual measures, at such time as he shall deem necessary, to organize, arm and equip, according to law, and hold in readiness to march at a momentive militia, the following proportions, respectively, of eighty thousand ered and six: from the state of Tennessee, eight hundred and thirty-four: from the state of Georgia, one thousand three hundred and thirty-five: from the state of South Carolina, three thousand five hundred and thirty-eight: from the state of North Carolina, seven thousand two hundred and sixty-two: from the state of Kentucky, one thousand five hundred and forty-two: from the state of Virginia, eleven thousand one hundred and fifty: from the state of Maryland, five thousand two hundred and sixty-seven: from the state of Delaware, one thousand one hundred and sixty-eight: from the state of Pennsylvania, ten thousand six hundred and ninety-six: from the state of New Jersey, four thousand two hundred and eighty six: from the state of New York, seven thousand nine hundred and twenty-three: from the state of Vermont, two thousand one hundred and fifty: from the state of Connecticut, five thousand eight hundred and forty: from the state of Rhode-Island, one thousand six hundred and twenty-six: from the state of Massachussets, eleven thousand eight hundred and thirty-six: from the state of New Hampshire, three thousand five hundred and fifty-eight.

Sec. 2. And be it further enacted, That the President may, if he judges expedient, authorize the executives of the several states, to accept any independent corps of cavalry, artillery or infantry, as part of the detachments aforesaid, provided they shall voluntarily engage as corps in the service.

Sec. 3. And be it further enacted, That the said militia shall not be compelled to serve a longer term, in any one tour, than three months, after their arrival at the place of rendezvous: and that, during the term of their service, the commissioned officers shall be entitled to the same pay and rations that are allowed by law, to officers of the same rank, on the military establishment of the United States: and the non-commissioned officers, musicians, and privates, shall receive the pay and allowance for clothing, prescribed by an act, entitled, "An act to regulate the pay of the non-commissioned officers, musicians, and privates of the militia of the United States, when called into actual service, and for other purposes."

Sec. 4. And be it further enacted, That this act shall continue, and be in force, for the space of one year from the passing thereof, and from thence to the end of the next session of Congress, and no longer.

JONATHAN DAYTON, *Speaker of the House of Representatives.*
TH: JEFFERSON, *Vice-President of the United States, and President of the Senate.*

Approved, June 24th, 1797.
JOHN ADAMS, *President of the United States.*

58088:
[Extract of a letter dated, July 28. 1797. from Major [undecipherable] to [undecipherable]]

"The British merchants of this place seem exceedingly opposed to every measure taken by the General in order to remedy the evils which actually threatened our garrison, the greatest part of which was always in a State of intoxication on account of the small liquor Shops held under the fanction of licenses issued by the Magistrates within the lines of our guards and Sentries. The proclamation which forbid such intolerable abuse has occasioned many murmers and remonstrances from a set of people who have long before that declined being considered as American citizens, bought Settlements on the British Shore, and expressed on every occasion their contempt for our government; although our money has enriched them since our taking possession of the Posts. The French here are very little better, and in my opinion not in the least to be trusted. happily they are indolent, cowardly and (with prudence) little to be dreaded. The emigrans from their Mother Country alone are dangerous. Yesterday we drumted out an Impostor born in Canada, who made several false depositions respecting the intentions of the Spaniards and French to attack Machinae and Fort Wayne. He pretended to have been a prisoner at the Illinois and gave a spurious account of the regular forces landed there, aiming I suppose to Spread the alarm among the Canadians and to lead the General into some unnecessary and perhaps improper measures — fortunately we found that he never was fince two years nearer of the Illinois than three hundred leagues.

Another man (a British Subject) was detected attempting to Seduce some of our Soldiers from their duty and was punished accordingly. It is so long fince we received an Express that we know nothing of what passed in Congress these Seven weeks past. The Indians are still very numerous here owing to their receiving plenty of provisions on both shores; but I find that they all expect to see their [underline: Fathers the French]. The little Turtle, although peaceably inclined cannot be persuaded that he received false information."

I also enclose a copy of a letter from Lieu<sup>t</sup> Pike at Natsby, it came to this place from new Madrid with M<sup>r</sup> Scott on the 28<sup>th</sup> by a man who went with M<sup>r</sup> Price as Drummer and whose term of service had expired. It appears by this letter as also from the enclosed extract of communications made to me by a M<sup>r</sup> Stacker, that the information given by the letter at Sea is accurate, at least they agree to corroborate in point of the general Boundaries — Captain Heth has joined me on the 15<sup>th</sup> Ultimo, and Captain Dunbar will [undecipherable] Campbell and his Company of Artillery Yesterday — If I may be

permitted to adventure an opinion, it is very evident the revenue offered by the Chevalier from the new Secretary of State are no more than so many good occasions, calculated to amuse untill some chain of circumstances may render it propitious to delay fully; the vigorous warlike preparation making at St. Louis of Upper Louisiana seem with other things to warrant this conclusion — I am preparing my self to encounter the rapidity of every crisis beside of Mississippi, and shall leave this place on or before the 10<sup>th</sup> instant, nor shall I stop at new Madrid unless compelled by superior force, commencement or shew of hostility, on the part of the troops of the United States when I have the honor to Command, and shall be studiously and scrupulously avoided — but all upon overt direct attack upon them shall be repelled, with the utmost energy of our small number, and such manner as I hope will not sully the reputation, or tarnish the lustre of the flag, of the nation.

A Conveyance offering by the Cumberland river, I should have been wanting in my duty not to have seized the occasion to make this communication which shall be followed by another through the medium of Cap<sup>t</sup>. Pike at this place, so soon as I shall have passed new Madrid — A Sergeant and three men are with the Chickasaw Villagers & at different times to apprise them of my coming.

With the highest respect.
Sir, I have the honor to be

The Honorable
James McHenry
Sec<sup>y</sup> to the Dep<sup>t</sup> of War

Mount Vernon 7. July 1797

Dear Sir,

By the last Post I was favoured with your letter of the 3. instant and thank you for its enclosure, although, on the same day, I had myself transmitted a copy thereof to the Secretary of State. —

I had doubted a while, whether to forward it to your Office or that of State, but finally resolved to send it to the latter, as it seemed more properly I thought, to belong to that Department. If the letter intercepted by Blount is a genuine one, and the Gentleman's hand writing is not easily mistaken or counterfeited, what excuse can a late Governor & present Senator of the U.S., or his friends for him, offer for such Nefarious conduct? — The defence must be curious, and will, I have no doubt, be connected with as much effrontery as art. — I hope, notwithstanding, if the fact is proved, that the author will receive all the Punishment which the Constitution and Laws of this Country can inflict; and thereafter be held in detestation by all good men. — To seek private emolument at the expence of Public Peace — perhaps at the expence of many innocent lives: — and to aim a stroke at the reputation of a virtuous character, hazarding his health, probably, his life, to promote tranquility between the Indians and our frontier Inhabitants, and by destroying his influence & well earned good name, as one the former, to render him incapable of serving his country, because he may be a stumbling block in the way of a plan which he has in contemplation, is a crime of so deep a dye as no epithet can convey an adequate idea of. — A poor wretch stealing the worth of a shilling, possibly to buy bread, would be hung, or confined to hard labour; and here, a plan (at which I can only guess) as one for to defraud the public of its money, — deprive citizens perhaps (in its consequences) of their lives, — to [strikethrough: undecipherable] native characters; — and ultimately, [strikethrough: undecipherable] involve its concomitants, will, more than probable, meet with advocaters. —

But as you inform me that the matter would be laid before Congress on monday last, I shall wait (with some degree of impatience I confess) to learn the result. —

Always, I remain
Your affectionate fr.
G. Washington

James McHenry Esq<sup>r</sup>.

On the other hand I hope the measures which are in train for the more effectual protection of the South western frontier will particularly evidence the interest which is felt for the security of those Citizens over whom you have been called to preside.

I enclose you several official papers which will serve to show you the critical situation in which we stand with regard to certain foreign powers, and the inimical practice of some of our own Citizens, and how important it is that all good men should unite their endeavours to avert the Storm which would seem to be gathering round our common Country, and to detect those concealed enemies whose projects would overturn its government or deluge a whole people in blood. The papers alluded to will bring particularly to your view the criminality of an old acquaintance who has rendered himself unworthy of the seat he held in the Senate of the United States from which he has been recently expelled. I am Sir
respectfully your Friend

Josiah Fox

Sir—

your most very sincerely
Samuel Hodgson

War Office 13. July 1797.

Sir,

I inclose Copies of my letter of the 9. Ultimo to General Wilkinson and mine to you of the 10 and 15. Ultimo.

I have also annexed the correspondence between Lieutenant Pope and Governor Gayoso and M. Elliott with a letter from the Minister of Spain to the Secretary of State dated the 11. Instant and published (as believed) by his direction.

You will I have no doubt duly appreciate and conform your conduct to my instructions, and take every necessary precaution in your military positions for the safety and protection of your command, and maintenance of a good understanding with the Indians and inhabitants, while you will at the same times, carefully avoid whatever might disturb the peace between the United States and Spain or afford ground for complaint or hostility.

You will be pleased also to pay particular attention to the Contractors department so as to have at all times a supply of provisions on hand competent to any emergency. —

I am Sir
with respect
Your obed<sup>t</sup>. Servant
James McHenry

Captain Isaac Guion

You will find this accompanied by a Pay Role of Captain Edward D. Turner's Company for April 1797 together with a Muster Roll taken for April May and June 1797 the amount paid for April two hundred seventy eight dollars which you will be pleased to place to my credit. The result of all my enquiry for Captain Duncan McClain is that in March last he had left a small improvement he had been making about 45 miles north of this place [strikethrough: with an intention &] he had reported of going to transact some business in Philadelphia & to return. But it now appears by tolerable good information that

instead of proceeding on the proposed Journey he had changed his rout and proceeded to Canada where it is reported he was employed as an Incendiary in concert with his Brother said to be a General in the Service of the Republic of France and that both Captain McClain and the General his Brother had been apprehended and imprisoned in Quebec, therefore I have now returned your Letter addressed to him enclosing your statement of accounts against him.

I am,
Sir

Such reports from the Officers engaged in Building th Ship affords room to believe that you have not been so assiduous in your exertions as the nature of the Service you are engaged in Required. I have therefore to request that you will use your utmost endeavours to have the Frigate finished and Launched with all possible expedition that no further delays may be imputable to you. It may also be proper to remind you that in carrying these orders into execution you are not to run into any unnecessary expense, but on the Contrary to be as frugal as possible in every part of the work.

You are likewise requested to Copper all the Bottom on the Stocks before the Ship is Launched to prevent her sinking down afterwards and a Consequent heavy exp—

W O<sup>r</sup> July 15 1797

[M<sup>r</sup> David Stodder —]

Receiv'd your letter of the 13 instant.

The plan that you propose of partially Coppering the Bottom of the Constellation I cannot approve; you will therefore be pleased to conform to the Instructions communicated to you in my letter of the 11 instant. You state that you launches her in such a manner that listing across her Keel cannot be cap— I have to remark on the above, that the Keel cannot surely be laid so very low as to endanger the Vessel in passing over the lower Blocks: but if such danger is likely, in your opinion, to happen on Launching, you will be pleased to State it by return of post together with the distance between the Keel and such Blocking, as it is my desire that every precaution may be taken by you in due time to ensure the safe Launching of the Ship into the Water; you are therefore not to neglect any measure that will conduce to that desirable end —

58501:
War Office 1<sup>st</sup> August 1797.

[No: ]

I have it in view from the president of the United States to lay before Your Excellency the act herein enclosed entitled "An Act authorizing a detachment from the Militia of the United States, passed the 24<sup>th</sup> of June 1797.

The object of this law being to provide and have in readiness a selected and completely equipped and organized body of Militia fit for action, at a moments notice, the President in pursuance thereof requests that you will be pleased to take immediate and effectual measures to organize, arm and equip, and hold in readiness to march, at a moments warning, this detachment required to be so organized, armed and equipped by the State of Connecticut, agreeably to the said law and the act entitled "An Act more effectually to provide for the national defense, by establishing an uniform Militia throughout the United States, passed the 8<sup>th</sup> May 1792.

With a view to expedite the completion of the said detachment the president has judged it expedient to authorize you to accept any independent corps of Cavalry, Artillery or Infantry, or part thereof, provided they shall voluntarily engage as corps in the service.

As it will be desireable to know the measures which Your Excellency may be pleased to adopt on this occasion, and from time to time the actual state of the detachment, it is earnestly requested that the Adjutant General may be instructed to make such returns and communications to this department, as may satisfy this object.

With great respect I have the honor to be
Your Excellency's obedient servant,
James McHenry
Secy of war

His Excellency
The Governor of Connecticut

o M<sup>r</sup> Josiah Fox,

Sir

Having employed all the Engine makers in the City to make Engines for all the Frigates as well the a Nigerian Ships from their conduct I am led to believe that all their promises are not worth a single Cent and as I can with propriety refuse to receive the Engines were they this moment ready for delivery. I certainly can have no objection to your displaying the Boston Frigate from any quarter
Signed F. Fenner

I am Sir &c    Josiah Fox

[William Simmons Esq<sup>re</sup> William D<sup>pt</sup> of War accp<sup>ts</sup> Philadelphia aug. 4]

Governor Mo[rris] Aug<sup>t</sup> 4 1797

Sir

Having understood that Cap<sup>t</sup> Littlefield upon his return from Oswego presented an acc<sup>t</sup> of expences he incurred to and from that place that were allowed. I request the favor to be informed whether it was the case, if they were allowed the rest of the officers on that command [strikethrough: were] equally entitled to theirs.

We did not take receipts as might have been proper, but as we clubbed our expences all the way on the marches they consequently must the each amount to the same

Further the subalterns may be said to have been at greater expence, for in consequence of their not receiving arrears of pay [underline: they] were obliged to

sir to raise cash to bear unavoidable expences, and received for their drafts half cash, and half goods which they had little or no occasion for — I suppose our reasonable expences to have averaged about a dollar a day but they can be best ascertained by Cap<sup>t</sup> Littlefield's account.

I have th request your answer as soon as convenient as I am under orders to sail immediately for Charlestrop or Savannah

I am Sir with respects
Your ob<sup>t</sup>. Serv<sup>t</sup>.
W<sup>m</sup> Morris L<sup>t</sup>.

M<sup>r</sup> Simmons Esq<sup>r</sup>

Pittsburg 4 August 1797

Sir

I have received your letter of the 28 ultimo accompanied by the news papers

The Secretary of War informs me that he has instructed you to forward immediately a quantity of Assurance Stores &<sup>ca</sup> for which I am to provide for transportation to Mafiac — an account of the weight of the Articles would enable me more accurately to estimate the means of transportation This information I have to request you to transmit by return of post

I have this day felt necessary to draw on you at 15 days sight in favor of R<sup>o</sup> Campbell H<sup>o</sup> for 1600 dollars which be pleased to pay and charge as usual. And I am at the very pressing importunity of Abijah Hunt and some of the 2<sup>d</sup> B<sup>t</sup> particulars friends induced to take up Daniel Hannagan's draft on the city for 1600 dollars and have this day drawn on you for that sum at ten days sight which you will be pleased to pay & charge to the 2 all B<sup>t</sup> particulars account and it is probable I shall be also induced to take up the two drafts mentioned to you formerly in favor of William and Michael Jones

I am anxious to know how far you have advanced in negotiation with M<sup>r</sup> Ebyuch for the boat hulls land — it is probable that M<sup>r</sup> Bects a business will call on you for information on that business and will assist you in it

I am Sir Your very obd Ser.

Samuel Hodgdon ag<sup>t</sup>
Philadelphia

J.C.

War Office August 7<sup>th</sup> 1797

Sir,

Your letter of the 31 Ult<sup>o</sup> was received last Friday.

I immediately wrote to M<sup>r</sup> Pennies to let me Know what Stores he had purchased for your ship and in answer he informed me all the Additional Stores were in a train of being completed. War office 8 Aug<sup>t</sup> 1797.

Sir

I have the pleasure to inform you that the Indians on the North western frontier give indications of their desiring to remain at peace and under the protection of the U States, notwithstanding the various efforts that have been made to detach them. They have consented that the line of Limits should be run, (with an exception by Little Turtle,) agreeably to the Treaty of Greenville and the Surveyors have accordingly commenced the work under the countenance of a small military guard.

The Creeks appear also to be well dispersed, and affairs in Tenisee to wear a favourable aspect.

The Commissioners who are engaged in establishing the boundary line between the Cherokees and the U. States, have proceeded to run the course 40 miles above Nashville where they have stopped, till they can make some experiments necessary to ascertain whether

if continued, it would touch the river called for in the Treaty of Holston. By their last letters of the 8th & 12th of July they were on their way to the Kentucky Trace in Cumberland, to run the line from Tinnee to Clinch and thence across the Holston to the S. Carolina Indian boundary on the North Carolina line. Here they proposed to halt till they had ascertained and marked every part of the line where intrusions might be apprehended within the present year.

L<sup>t</sup>. Col. Butler arrived with his command at Nashville on the 21 June, and on the 27th had advanced 32 miles in approaching Knoxville. This movement has been conducted satisfactorily and without accident. Cap<sup>t</sup>. Ransalains company of Dragoons reached Knoxville on the 5th July in good order, having performed a march from Fort Washington to that place in one month without the loss of either man or horse.

This detachment, I expect, will fully answer the several important objects for which it was intended. M<sup>r</sup>. Hawkins writes

[Private Confidential]

Phila. 17 August. 97.

Dear Sir.

When I passed thro' Brunswick on Tuesday last on my return to Philadelphia, I found a gentleman there, who from several circumstances, and recent information, have led me to suspect that his business there cannot perhaps be altogether proper — His name is Thomas Odiorne, a native of New England — of liberal education, and has lately resided in Philadelphia — Pray keep a watchful eye over him — Observe with whom he associates, and particularly when the passengers arrive in the Stages, if you see him intimate with any particular person (especially a foreigner) endeavor to get a sight of his Way bill and find out his name — I was informed he had been in Brunswick, eight or ten days [strikethrough: &] you do not know him, M<sup>r</sup> Vernon <sup>the Tavern keeper</sup> may inform you — But do not make any enquiry of M<sup>r</sup> V— that may cause suspicion — Communicate to me, as early as possible, any thing that may occur —

M<sup>r</sup> O — is a thin spare man — Wears a blue coat, and a round hat.

Yours very Sincerely.

[signed] J<sup>n</sup> Bragg Jun<sup>r</sup>

Ensign W<sup>m</sup> R. Boote.

P.S. Pray acknowledge the receipt of this letter — forward yours to me under cover to the Secretary of War — He has seen this — Take care not to lose it.

It was a Beautiful day in the visible world — only dull in my dull mind, But even that was somewhat vivified by the bright Sunshine, the Azure Sky marbled with white wreathy Clouds, the Verdant Earth of an emerald Green and the Blossoms profusely Scattered abroad. No one drank tea with me; but at night-fall Mary Regan came to Stay all night and tomorrow. Maria will not come.

Second Day morning may 21<sup>st</sup> 33.

Yesterday we were alone all day, only Mary and Gustavus and Dickinson were here. The Weather cool for the Season, but very Delightful to me. There has been an excitement in town about the coloured Gentry; but We hope it is allayed.

3<sup>d</sup> Day morning the 22<sup>d</sup>

[We have received an account of a riot which took place on Wednesday evening outside of the large new building called the "Pennsylvania Hall," lately opened in this city for scientific and political discussions and becoming particularly obnoxious on the question of abolitionism. As there is a part of the communication which it is desired to make about a recent and disgraceful scene, we shall omit its detail, giving in substance. Last evening the hall was crowded with about three thousand persons, to hear a lecture by Mr. Garrison and others. Of this audience about one half were females. It was promiscuously composed of white and black people.

At the close of Mr. Garrison's address, a mob outside was very noisy. Mrs. Maria W. Chapman, of Boston, then addressed the meeting for several minutes. She was followed by Mrs. Angelina A. Grimké Weld, Lucretia Mott, of this city, and Abby Kelley. In the mean time the mob increased and became more unruly and threw various missiles at the windows. No further injury was done than breaking the glass, as the blind fastenings protected the audience. A few minutes before ten the company retired amid the cries and shouts of the mob who blocked up the street on every side. One black man was knocked down with a club.

The proprietors of the Hall have applied to the city to pay the amount of damages done. The Police will, we trust, use every exertion to discover and punish the rioters, and in the mean time nothing should be done to excite popular outrage. For the riot in Philadelphia has been sufficiently disgraced by a single riot. — National Gazette.

27<sup>th</sup> We were, with extreme regret, as a disgrace to the city of Philadelphia, that at about eight o'clock yesterday evening, the "Pennsylvania Hall" was set on fire by a mob, and, with its contents, totally destroyed.]

I shall subjoin the newspaper account of the late disagreeable affair in town, which is thought to be pretty correct. I do not know Who Mr<sup>s</sup> Maria Chapman is — The Grimke's, are the Sisters of the respectable Judge Grimke, late of South Carolina; They are Women of good education, who professed to be proselytes to Friends and have been received into the Society. But Angelica has lately married out of it. Lucretia Mott is a fanatical woman of our own. It is a very disagreeable occurrence. Who is Abby Kelly? I do not know.
