58815:
[Lisbon, Augt. 24. 97, W<sup>m</sup> Smith.]

Lisbon, August 24. 97

Dearest —     I have the pleasure to inform you of my safe arrival here on the 20<sup>th</sup>. after a passage of 27 days from the Capes.   Near the Western Isles, we espied at day break on the 15<sup>th</sup> three Ships of War, which were standing to the Westward; but as soon as they saw us they tacked about & chased; they hoisted English Colors, till they came near & then they changed them to French & fired a Gun. We lay to & were boarded by two officers from the Foncorde, Frigate of 44 Guns, having on board the Commodore Papini, I addressed the senior officer in French, invited them into the Cabin, informed them who I was & shewed them my passport from De la Lombe; they enquired for the Ship's papers which they examined very minutely; they then took memorandums, & returned to their C[itoye]ns; as they behaved with the utmost politeness, I requested [strikethrough: them] a Certificate from the Commodore of our Examination to prevent our being molested by Privateers; they were about some time & on their return presented me the Compliments of the Commodore & a Certificate, setting forth that they had Examined the Ship & denying all French subjects from Buspect we The senior officer then with an apparent bashfulness (which I little expected) said he was charged with a little Commission which was to request a small supply of Sugar having lost their Stock by a loss; we furnished them cheerfully with half our remaining Stock, happy to get off so well. They wished us a bon voyage & took their leave, having behaved with as much

respectful politeness as I ever saw from French officers under the old regime.   She has their vessels was the Hercules of 44 & the Bruges of 20. They told us that they were bound eleven days from a Vessel down bound to the W. Indies, but we suspect they are cruizing about the Western Isles. Last night we were waited on by a formal gentleman in a full Suit of black who came to make some enquiries about this Squadron which report had informed [us] was left by a [undecipherable] in sight of the Portuguese Squadron; W[illia]m offered him it was a mistake, as we saw no Portuguese Ships; perhaps said he asking pardon for the liberty, you were a Sleep when the Portug. Squadron came in sight; he however went away at length satisfied that they were in no danger: there is a Squadron of five Sail of the line of Portugal cruizing on the Coast, & this curious Gentleman is [undecipherable] & [undecipherable] of the Ships.

The Passage was as pleasant & comfortable as being 27 days at Sea can be; I experienced every attention from my worthy companion, M<sup>r</sup> Bulkeley & am at present at his father's, whose house is in a noble situation on the great [undecipherable], command[s] an extensive prospect of the Tagus — Shipping which are and scattered in the river, here seen, noble views: his premises a prodigious bustle of navigation, employing a vast number of boats, incessantly in motion — Before my eyes are the four Spanish Ships, taken by Ad. Jervis; they are waiting for men. That Admiral is still Blockading Cadiz. Yesterday an account arrived here that Admiral Skelton with a small force from Jervis' fleet had made an unsuccessful attack on Teneriffe — retired with loss; the Admiral had lost an arm in the engagement with the [undecipherable], which was not happy for him.

I have made my bow to the Secretary of State M<sup>r</sup> Pinto who knew the President in London; I am to be presented next week to the Prince & when that business is settled I shall retire to Cintra for a few weeks. I have taken the House occupied by my Predecessor, who has left a great [undecipherable] of his furniture in the — I find the weather cooler than I expected; this may however be owing to my staying mostly within doors & to the very cool Situation of M<sup>r</sup> Bulkeley's house. Since my arrival, the weather has appeared much cooler than it was in Philad<sup>a</sup> when I left it.

This Govt. appears apprehensive of a war with Spain, & is raising troops for the defence of the Country; they are actually at war with France & have taken some French privateers; the French on their part have taken a great many of their rich Brazilmen & have done them an immense injury. There is an army in the environs of this City, paid, I am told, by Eng<sup>d</sup>. There is another on the frontier paid by Portugal.

I hope to hear from you soon; I was happy to see in an English paper an acc<sup>t</sup> of [undecipherable]'s arrival in Holland. — I rely on your friendship for advancing with the President the object I suggested to you the morning I left Philad<sup>a</sup>. as my wishes are fully known to you, I shall not trouble you with a repetition; I cannot omit this opportunity of expressing the pleasure I have had in your acquaintance & the gratitude I feel for your friendship which it will always be my anxious wish to cultivate — with respects to M<sup>rs</sup> M<sup>c</sup>Henry & assurance of regard for yourself I am D<sup>r</sup> yours

W<sup>m</sup> Smith
58816:
Lisbon, August 24<sup>th</sup> 1797

Dear Sir

I had the pleasure of writing you a few lines on the 20<sup>th</sup>, the day of our arrival, by a Vessel bound to Alexandria, which was under sail, immediately after we anchored in the Tagus. This goes by a Vessel bound from St Ubes to Philad<sup>a</sup>. — We landed here on the 21<sup>st</sup> & on the next day, accompanied by M<sup>r</sup> Bulkeley, Jun<sup>r</sup>, I waited on M<sup>r</sup> Pinto, the Secretary of State, was very politely received, & informed that he would make my arrival known to the Prince, & notify me on what day it would suit his Highness to receive my Credentials. As the Secretary was not in good health, & the Prince resides at some distance from Town, it will be some day next week before I am presented.

When this Ceremony is over, I propose retiring to the Country for a few weeks, the City being at present disagreeable. —

On our passage we were brought to by a small flying Squadron of French Ships; two officers came on board, examined our papers & after a detention of less than two hours, suffered us to proceed. They behaved with the utmost politeness & had very much the manner of Gentlemen. The Commodore, on my application, sent me a Certificate of our examination, to prevent molestation by Cruizers. The officers seemed very anxious for Peace, which they said would certainly take place during the Summer: - in this however they may be disappointed, the last accounts being rather unfavorable; but as the negotiations are conducted with secrecy, every report on this Subject must be founded on a slender basis; at one moment we hear that the pretensions of France are so extravagant that England cannot listen to them, at another, that Trincomale is the only re-maining subject of controversy. It is certain that both Nations are anxious for Peace & ill able to continue the war; I am impatient

to learn what part the new minister of foreign affairs, Talleyrand, will act in respect to England & the United States. You must have been as much surprized at his elevation as myself; in the present conflict of parties, by which that government is agitated, I doubt whether he will remain long in office; as he is a shrewd, & interested politician, he will probably pursue that course which he thinks, will tend to his own aggrandizement. — The Danes have met with a great loss in their able minister, Bernstoff: he is succeeded by his Son. The day after my arrival I had a visit from the Danish minister, Warnstatt, who expressed a desire to cultivate a friendship with me. He freely complained of the ill treatment his Country had sustained from the English & French during the present war, regretted much that the U.S. had not a navy, which he said was always the first wish of Count Bernstoff, that an alliance might take place between the neutral powers to defend their Commerce effectually in time of war.—

The government of this Country is taking active measures to defend their frontiers against Spain & to protect their Commerce against France: they have even made reprisals & have brought in here some small french privateers. They have a squadron of five Sail of the Line at Sea, & a considerable number of Troops, encamped in the neighbourhood of Lisbon, consisting of English, French Emigrants or Portugueze, besides an army on the frontiers. To support the extra Expences occasioned by these preparations (in which England has aided them with £ 300,000 St.) they have issued Paper Bills to the amount of 1.500,000 dollars, which are a Tender in law in all payments: I have seen one of the Bills, just come into circulation; it promises payment in one year at the royal Treasury with Six percent interest; I don't understand that there is any obstacle to their free currency; if they maintain their credit, they will be extremely useful in negotiations, there being no other paper in circulation. —

There was found on board one of the Privateers brought in here, a Paper, purporting to be an instruction to the Commander of the Privater designating the mode of distinguishing a genuine American Sea-Letter & Register from counterfeit ones: this came into the hands of M<sup>r</sup> Bulkeley's father, & he has permitted me to send you a copy of it. We may infer from this Paper, that there is a practice in England of forging these [underline: Paper Documents] to some extent, which requires instant remedy, either by calling in old Sea Letters & Registers or by such devices as may guard as effectually as the nature of the case will permit against these frauds: We may [underline: likewise] infer, from the great pains & accuracy with which these Papers are described that there is an intention to respect Vessels having real bona fide Papers, & that some Captains may possibly be attributed to a detention of forged ones. Captain Dohart tells me he has been several times boarded by French Cruizers & that after a strict examination of his Papers (which has been sometimes done by an exact admeasurement of the Seal &<sup>c</sup>) he has been always released.

The Consul, M<sup>r</sup> Bulkeley, informs me that American Sea Letters, supposed to be forged, have been sold for a Trifle, & that he has no doubt of the practice. —

Col. Humphreys quitted Lisbon about the beginning of this month; his arrival at Madrid was announced by the last Gaz<sup>te</sup>. M<sup>r</sup> Adams was daily expected here & I am told some of his baggage is actually arrived. — As your Son writes by this Vessel, I need not inform you that he is in good health, but I cannot with hold the pleasure of assuring you how much I am pleased with him: he more than realizes the account you gave of him & exceeds my most sanguine anticipations. — He suffered greatly by the voyage for the first week, but from his looks he now appears to have been benefitted by his sea-sickness. —

As this then appears, from the circumstance I have communicated, respecting the Sea Letter, an intention somewhere to respect Vessels having genuine documents, conforming to the principles France has assumed with respect to us, yet it is but too true that some of their Cruizers have captured [strikethrough: American] Vessels without any pretext whatever; an instance has lately occurred of an American being carried into Spain by a French Privater [strikethrough: [undecipherable]] for having on board [underline: the Colours of three different nations]; she was cleared however; but it is said that by an order from the Prince of Peace she was restored to the Captor. I am promised the particulars of this Case by the Consul, which I will forward to you: — the owner of the Vessel is, I understand, now here. —

I request you will present my best Respects to the President & I beg leave to recall to your recollection the Subject of our conversation the day of my departure from Newcastl. Presuming on your friendship, I shall make bold to rely on your Services, where not incompatible with the public good.

With my respects to M<sup>r</sup> Pickering I remain Dear Sir

very respect[ful]
Your most ob<sup>t</sup>

W<sup>m</sup> Smith

Pleas. to send me the acts. of Congress of the last Session, — the entire Session.

[W<sup>m</sup> Smith Lisbon August 24. 1797. rec<sup>d</sup> Nov<sup>r</sup> 14.]

58988:
Philadelphia 7<sup>th</sup> Septem<sup>r</sup> 1797

S<sup>ir</sup>

I duly received your letter of the 23<sup>d</sup> Ultimo. Any others that may arrive by the post due to day, I cannot expect to receive in time to reply to, as the Post Office is removed, and the [strikethrough: penny] Post; no longer carry letters. I am yet at my post in Water Street, & must here remain or the Public business must cease, or suffer. Harris is gone, and two of my Clerks, one only remains with me, yet I hope to keep business going on. My house in Arch Street is nearly finished, and I expect soon to inhabit it. The City wears a melancholly appearance; more houses being shut, and more persons removed than in ninety three. Yet in my apprehension the danger has at no time justified the fears of the inhabitants; the frenzy is occasioned by a review of former scenes. I have received Capt Crawfords letter, and power of Attorney, I will attend to his business because you request it, and because he is a poorman,

Corporal Nevells letter shall go forward safely & soon. I do not think it adviseable to send the News papers, as I have no means of getting them franked, & therefore conclude they may be too costly to you. Enclosed you have this days paper —

I am

Sir,

Your most Obedient Servant

Samuel Hodgdon

Lisbon, Sep. 29<sup>th</sup> 1797.

Dear Sir          3

Since my last I have spent a very agreeable fortnight at the Country Seat of, M'Bulkeley a few miles from hence, delightfully situated on the Tagus. Finding that my audience would not take place immediately I not daring to venture far from town until the presentation was over, I was happy in having an opportunity of spending the intermediate time in a pleasant & cool retreat, where I could be ready on receiving notice to repair to town & prepare for the Ceremony. This took place yesterday; a new minister having arrived a few days after me from Russia, we followed the Danish Ministers Chariot & four Servants having had Six Mules we proceeded in great State in one Chariot & Six to Queluz, about 8 miles from Town. We were first presented: I was then introduced, made the proper reverences at the proper distances & delivered to the Prince of Brasil, who represents the Sovereign, the President's Letter, making him a very concise address, [interlined: in terms as gracious in them] to which he replied that he was very glad to see me & would acquaint his Mother of my arrival. I then made my Bows, retreating with my face to the Prince & withdrew; had I not rehearsed this Ceremony with my friend the Dane, a very good natured friendly man, I should have probably committed some faux pas, as I did afterwards at my audience of the Princess, respecting which (there having been some doubt whether I sho'd see her Highness) I had not been so particular in my inquiries; being suddenly ushered into a large room—

where I beheld a splendid sight of Ladies in large hoops, arranged along the [undecipherable] in solemn silence, as cold & awful as the wax-work; I was a little discomposed at first, but recovering myself approached the Princess, whom I discovered by her Jewels, & told her [interlined: how] happy I sho'd be if I sho'd be honored with her favor & protection during my residence at this Court, to which she made some very gracious reply, which I did not understand not having heard it. I then wishing to be abundantly polite, & to bow to the Ladies who were paraded along the wall on my way out, unfortunately was so indecent as actually to turn my side to the Princess & indeed very nearly turned my back; when I approached the door, I recollected my crime & to expiate it, suddenly faced about & made her Highness a most profound reverence & withdrew. But when we got into the antechamber I found that I had omitted a very essential part of the Ceremony, which was, making a complimentary Speech to the Prince's suite & his daughter, a child of four years, a circumstance I had not been apprised of. I was however consoled on learning from the Russian Minister that he had committed the same blunder; this he attributed to the neglect of the proper Officer, in not having accompanied & introduced us; as the Russian Minister is Chamberlain to the King, has lately been presented to the Empress, the Directory, & the Court of Spain, I was comforted by his blunder, & he was comforted, after some fretting, by the blunder of the Master of the Ceremonies. He told me he had prepared a very pretty speech for each of the Ladies, but he could not [undecipherable: distinguish?] them, & to add to his chagrin he altogether

forgot to deliver to the Princess a message from her mother the Queen of Spain with which he was charged. — On our return from the Palace, we paid some visits to the Officers of State & then dined with the Corps Diplomatique at the Danish Ministry.

In the Evening I went for the first time to the Opera; the House is a fine one, large & commodious; it has five rows of boxes; the Music & Singers are excellent, but there are no women allowed to appear on the Stage at Lisbon: this is done by the Queen to preserve the morals of the young Gentry: the female parts are performed by men in women's cloaths: the thing which performed the first female character made a very good Serafina, it has a remarkably fine Voice. —

The day after tomorrow I set off for Cintra for a few weeks. To morrow I dine at a Fidalgo's (nobleman.)

The late Treaty with France is ratified here. The English government is said to be very much offended with Portugal for having entered into Stipulations, injurious to England; we hear nothing decisive from Lisbo. —

I wish to make an Excursion into Spain — is it not probable that Spain will expect an Envoy Extra? or a Commission of two or three Envoys to settle our differences; should any arrangement of this kind be thought of, it will be extremely agreeable to me to go to Madrid in that character; there will be no expence attending it. I am learning the Portugese language & can soon acquire the Spanish. —

With repeated thanks for your friendship, I remain my dear Sir
very sincerely Yours
W<sup>m</sup> Smith

59029:
Philadelphia Sep<sup>a</sup> 11<sup>th</sup> 97

My Dear Sir.     I received your obliging favors of Aug 19<sup>t</sup> report you on the first information that a serious state of things existed in the city. It gave me pleasure to find that yourself and family have moved. I hope you have found a dry and healthy situation; here I imagine we are exposed to the fever and ague. The yellow fever or the the-ter to both together have baffled poor Dennis your messages. I have entreated by a worthy old man Mr Berrent the messages to the Comptrollers office to recommend a relation of his, William Chartworth who lives nine or ten miles from the city. Berrent is one of the most exemplary men of my acquaintance and he speaks of Chartworth in decided terms as an honest, sober, and diligent man. I could not and ought to express conveying his wishes to you, though I have been careful not to raise his expectations. By friend I have not been for a week, and you'll see from out that living alone in a small room in a tavern, with a prospect of a confined river running through to myself, and occupied alternately with desk full of business or conversation, my along the destruction of a full city, is far from being in a state of perfect happiness. The contrast between our present situation and that which I have hitherto felt is most impressive. I have been lately too happy to expect that I should experience some reverse. Please to present my respects to Mrs. McHenry and believe me your esteemed friend.

Oliver Wolcott

James McHenry, Esq.

Trenton Sept<sup>r</sup> 12. 1797.

D<sup>r</sup> Sir

I duly received your letter of the      mentioning Mr John Caldwell for the office of Treasurer of the Mint; and altho' you referred to me to say what appeared proper concerning him, I chose to forward your letter to the President, to the contents of which I with pleasure subscribed. The only circumstance that would excite any hesitation as to the fitness of the appointment— even his near connection with the [underline: Secretary of War], which might give rise to disagreeable remarks among the enemies of the Government— to excite the disapprobation of its friends. This circumstance a sense of duty led me to intimate for the President's consideration. But I had better give you all that I wrote concerning M<sup>r</sup> Caldwell. It here follows.

" Altho' M<sup>r</sup> McHenry, on account of his connection with M<sup>r</sup> John Caldwell (the brother of M<sup>rs</sup> McHenry) did not think it proper directly to make known his wishes to you, yet all that he has written in his letter to me appears so correct, I thought it best to inclose it. M<sup>r</sup> Caldwell is by profession a Lawyer: yet having some fortune he has very little engaged in practice. I have known him these ten years. He is a sensible, well-informed man, a decided federalist and supporter of our government, with a fair moral character. He has an increasing family. But with entire fitness for the office, perhaps the expediency of appointing the brother-in-law of the [underline: Secretary of War] may merit consideration."

All this I hope will meet with your approbation, which the confidence and candour that ought to subsist between us have induced me frankly to lay before you.

There are many other candidates, some of whom have revolutionary merit, for their services in the american war. I forward all their applications to the President, accompanied with remarks, where I have knowledge of the characters.

My family is comfortably situated in this place. We moved in good time to save ourselves from the rage of the Philadelphia fever.

The President highly approves the letter to Lynis. I ordered M<sup>r</sup> Shumo to send you 30 copies, agreeably to your request.

Truly yours T. Pickering

[James M<sup>c</sup> Henry Esq<sup>r</sup>]

My dear Sir.

The bilious fever with which I have been attacked has left me weak and subject to feverish returns that affect both my sleep and spirits. I flatter myself however that a little care and time will enable me to enjoy the beauties of this part of the country which are far more cheering various and interesting than the dull damp sedgy serpentine sorrowful river whose banks have become your residence.

What obstructs my recovery is the business which I am obliged to attend to. Tempee and Cox have a good deal disturbed me, but I expect (as my nephew has informed you, that the measures which I have taken will prevent any insurrection in that quarter and defeat Cox's project. It is true that Blount has still influence in Tempee.

I am S. great respect
Your obed Servant

S<sup>ir</sup>

On the 25 July 1794 Captain Pike executed a relinquishment of twenty dollars per month of his pay from and after the first of October 1794. to be received at your office, and I obligated myself to Stop the payment here; In november 1795, Captain Pike was put to Command at Macpas, and then represented to me that all his debts were paid in the atlantied States, and wished to receive his whole pay here, upon which, I desired him to with draw his Relinquishment and my Obligation from your Office, as a necessary Step towards obtaining his whole pay here. I have continued notwithstanding to make the Stoppage until the 31 day of October 1796. — but in Consequence of his letter to me of the 24.<sup>th</sup> of October 1796 of which the following is an extract. ("I am not a little "Surprised at the detention of your certificate or Obligation for the relinquishment of my pay, for which "I have wrote to the accountant in the most "pressing manner, Stating the necessity of receiving "my Stipend in this country, however I shall not "unless compelled by necessity, continue to importune "him. — and that in the meantime should you "have an interview with the accountant, you will "be able to obtain your Certificate".) I have just him his pay in full by Lieu<sup>t</sup> Sterrett, from the 1 November 1796 to the 31 October 1797. and therefore requests that you will be pleased to enclose to me by the next post, the abovementioned Certificate which I have given relative to the Said Stoppage, and that in any event you may recollect the circumstances of his being paid in full for the period before mentioned.

I am Sir
your m<sup>ost</sup> ob<sup>t</sup> Ser<sup>vt</sup>

Near Downingstown 13 Oct<sup>o</sup>. 1797.

My dear Sir.

I have been kept so very busy since I received your letter of the 4<sup>th</sup> between the affairs of Blount, Cox, and the Mississippi, (the current of which Calls river you know is not easy to stem) as to have left me no time to reply. particularly to a part of it; and even now I can do no more than signify my intire concurrence with the line of march which you have suggested for the troops. Nothing has come to my knowledge either of a domestic or foreign nature that would make a change in it either prudent or politic. I long to get into winter quarters.

Yours Affectionately
James McHenry

Oliver Wolcott Esq.

Fort Wayne 15<sup>th</sup> October 1797

Mess<sup>rs</sup> Leith, Shepherd & Duff

Gentlemen

Your Application of the day is before me and I will reply to it in brief.

The General Orders regulating the Trading houses within the Military Reservations explain the Motives which direct to it M<sup>r</sup> to prevent frauds & abuses and to preserve tranquility with the Natives.

The Regulation touching the Pawa Town was calculated to drive out M<sup>r</sup> M<sup>c</sup>Donald who has been represented to me, as a man mischievously disposed towards the Government of the United States, and who had continued the purchase of Stolen Horses from the Indians, the preference to M<sup>r</sup> M<sup>c</sup>Dougall was founded on the presumption of his Services to Government, his expences incurred in establishing the Town in question and the manifest confidence reposed in him by my Predecessor in command and the Acting Governor of the Territory.

But Gentlemen, while I avow the determination arising from a sense of duty and justified by the usage of Nations to give a preference to the Citizens of the United States in all cases; I beg you to believe me incapable of entrenching on the rightful pretensions of any foreigner whatsoever; much less, to offer wanton Injury to an Individual. Although I feel myself authorized to regulate within the Military Reservations,

Near Dawnings Town 16<sup>th</sup> Oct<sup>r</sup> 1797 —

Sir

Should this find you at the Natchez you will immediately dispatch a messenger to the Commanding Officer at the Chicasaw Bluff to inform him of your situation and as far as you know, the situation of things at the Walnut Hills. It is expected that the three posts below the Ohio viz that of Chicasaw Bluff, Walnut Hills and Natchez will assist each other in emergencies as far as can be done consistent with their respective safety.

You will husband them as much as you can consistently with circumstances and endeavour before you bestow them, to have some knowledge of the person and they will not be thrown away, whether given to abate enmity or confirm friendship.

59480:
Near Downings Town 16<sup>th</sup> October 1799.

Sir,

Having been called upon, to perform the following services— viz.

1<sup>st</sup> To facilitate the progress of two detachments of troops, to a station on the Mississippi; the one, from Tennessee which is to rendezvous at Majac, and the other, on the Oba board and now on its march to Pittsburg— 2<sup>d</sup> To achive a letter which you will receive from Brig.<sup>d</sup> Gen.<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson, to the Governor General of Louisiana at New Orleans— 3<sup>d</sup> To transmit the said Governor's answer to the Department of War— 4<sup>th</sup> To resume the functions of agent for the department of War in the State of Georgia.

You will be pleased to proceed 1<sup>st</sup> to Pittsburg and immediately on your arrival there, call on Col. James O'Hara the army contractor or his Agent, and inform yourself, within the requisitions in my letters of the 28.<sup>th</sup> July, 29.<sup>th</sup> September and 6.<sup>th</sup> and 10.<sup>th</sup> October with copies of which are annexed, have been duly complied with— 2<sup>d</sup> If you find that provisions, conformably thereto, have only been partially forwarded, you will observe and see, that immediate measures be taken to send forward or supply the deficiency. 3<sup>d</sup> You will call on Mr. Wilkins the D.M.G. or Mr. Isaac Craig [undecipherable] Q.M. to learn whether the military and other articles ordered to be sent to Majac, have been all forwarded— and obtain a list of the same and their quantities— These are intended for the detachments mentioned above—

4<sup>th</sup> You will request the B.<sup>t</sup> D.V. Master, to have in readiness for the detachment on its march to Pittsburg, a sufficient quantity of tents, for its accommodation, and boats for its removal to Majac, with its baggage and provisions— 5<sup>th</sup> You will see that the Contractor is prepared to furnish the Provisions as well for the detachment during the Voyage, as for its supply agreeably to requisition after

after their arrival at [undecipherable] station— 6<sup>th</sup> The necessary besides, that the B.<sup>t</sup> D.V. Masters be directed to hold in reserve as and forward sufficient quantity of tools, to the detachments— more transmitted to Majac, being too inconsiderable to be useful— 7<sup>th</sup> You will see that the detachment is provided with an Acting Commissary by the Contractor—

This Point answered and settled, you will proceed to Majac to prepare for the expeditions departure of the detachments from thence.

There you will 1<sup>st</sup> Ascertain that the articles mentioned to have been sent by the B.<sup>t</sup> D.V. Master arrived and their State and condition— 2<sup>d</sup> You will see that the boats, destined to transport them, are in good order— and will fail everything on the best consideration for the removal and safe keeping— 3<sup>d</sup> If you should find the detachment from Tennessee in any part of it at Majac, you will hasten its departure to the Chickasaw Bluffs or Iron Banks on the Mississippi— 4<sup>th</sup> If that from the Sea board arrives first, its departure is to be facilitated in the same manner, with a proportion of the artillery, without waiting for a junction with that from Tennessee— 5<sup>th</sup> Should Brig.<sup>d</sup> Gen.<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson be at Majac on your arrival there, you will deliver to him my letter, shew him your instructions, and commence under his directions, your superintendance as aforesaid— 6<sup>th</sup> Should he be at a distance, you will send my letter to him, by a trusty person or officer, request the favoured with your dispatch to the Governor General of Louisiana, and in the mean time occupy yourself as aforesaid—

7<sup>th</sup> You will besides these particular duties, with respect to the detachment in question, consider yourself authorized to do every thing necessary and required to facilitate their safe, transportation, and that of their artillery and provisions—

8<sup>th</sup> Should the detachment from Tennessee have reached from Majac—

Majac before your arrival there, You will after making such arrangements as may in your opinion be proper to facilitate the expeditions junction with it of that from the Sea board, hasten after Brig.<sup>d</sup> Gen.<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson for his letter to the Governor of Louisiana—

9<sup>th</sup>. Should you find the General at Mashakias or on the Mississippi you will dispatch thence for New Orleans, without returning to Majac—

Having finished these duties and received General Wilkinson's dispatch for the Governor General of Louisiana— You will proceed to New Orleans, without stopping at any port on either side of the Mississippi, except that of the Chickasaw Bluffs, if in possession of our Troops. This precaution is to prevent delay in its delivery or in obtaining an answer, which might happen were you to be prevented from proceeding to New Orleans under some frivolous protest—

Having delivered the General's letter to the Governor General of Louisiana and obtained his answer, you will take the nearest route to the State of Georgia where you will resume The functions which you have heretofore exercised in that State under the denomination of Agent for the Department of War. If then is a Vessel at New Orleans for Philadelphia or New York, you will send the Governor's answer by it under cover to the Secretary of War, taking a receipt from the person to whom it is intrusted for its safe delivery at the Port office of the Port to which he may be destined. Should... none offer, you will send it, by the next Mail for Philadelphia on your arrival in Georgia.

With respect to your Salary, appointments and extra expenses as Agent for the department of War— These will remain on the same footing as heretofore, and be settled on the same principle, as governed in the late settlements of your account as Agent—

As to the expenses of your present mission— These will

will be paid by the Public— It is however expected, that Vouchers will be produced to substantiate your expenses in all cases when they may be attainable—

It may be proper perhaps to notice, That your pay as Agent for the Department of War is not intended to affect in any wise, your pay in the line of the Army. Neither is your Agency to prevent you in case circumstances should require your military services in Georgia, from rendering them, in which conjuncture it is permitted you to appoint a Deputy, who is hereby authorized to discharge the functions and duties of Agent for the Department of War— Your Agency to commence from the 18<sup>th</sup> of October instant—     with respect &c.

J. McH—

P.S. It is ordered that you are to command the detachment under Cap.<sup>tn</sup> Pierce, till its arrival and departure from Majac—

59484:
War Departm<sup>t</sup>. 16<sup>th</sup> Octobt 1797

Sir

The company of Artillery and Infantry under your command, are to be marched to Pittsburch. There you will have them mustered and paid by Isaac Craig Jr D. M. who has orders for that purpose, and will in conjunction with the Captain of Infantry, appoint provisionally from among the soberest and most intelligent privates, the necessary number of non commissioned officers, giving those thus appointed to understand, that the confirmation of their offices will depend entirely on their good behaviour and attention to duty on them Pittsburch - you are to descend the Ohio, to Mafsac and thence to the Chickasaw Bluff on the Missisipi.

The practise to the French and Spaniards, to alienate from the U.S. the affections of the Indians residing on the east side of the Missisippi, and some recent attempts to convert them into actual enemies, renders it absolutely necessary, that you should use all requisite diligence to gain possession of the Chickasaw bluff. You will not therefore wait at Mafsac for information from the Bluff, or any of the Spanish Posts, or be deterred from proceeding with your detachment by any accounts of the intention of the Spaniards to dispute your passage, a firmness on our part to be stopped by any thing short of superior force applied in such manner as shall demonstrate unequivocally their determination to shut up the Missisippi.

It is not however supposed that they will proceed to such an extremity, as that you will be opposed by force or other means, than seemingly friendly requests, and such pretexts as they have already used, and may conceive calculated to induce you to suspend the undertaking. Should you therefore be only interrogated in passing New Madreid, or dissuaded from it by any Spanish Officer not to proceed, you will clearly that your destination is for the Chickasaw Nation, which is within the territory of the U.S. that in navigating the Missisippi to carry you thither, you are only exercising a right secured to the U.S. by Treaties. Caried that on no occasion have for their sole object the execution of the Treaty between the U.S. and Spain, to strengthen the bonds of amity between the two Nations, and preserve peace with the Indians within the territory of the U.S. on the east side of the Missisippi.

Artillery ammunition and provisions have been sent to Mafsac for your detachment, and for a mortar that has been ordered from Tennefee. The Artillery and ammunition left Pittsburgh's own time since, and hopes no accident will have prevented the Contractor or those from providing in reason the latter - if however the full quantity of rations should not be found at Mafsac, you will borrow from that Garrison what will enable you to proceed. You will also take such proportion of the Artillery ammunition and stores, as may quadrate with the force under your command. - The remainder to be left for the detachment expected from Tennefee.

On your arrival at the Bluff in case Capt. Guion (who is said to be a post there) has fallen down the Missisippi, you will send a trusty Indian or non-commissioned officer to [undecipherable] the information of your arrival, and your strength.

But should Capt. Guion have left no party at the Bluff, and the Spaniards have reoccupied it, you will in that case, [undecipherable] at the iron banks or any other fit place for a fort short of the Bluffs on the Missisippi. From this place you will give information to Captain Guion as before directed. You will also dispatch a commissioned officer to the Bluff, to request the immediate evacuation thereof, signifying to the Spanish officer your surprise at its having been reoccupied and the unnecessary policy this extraordinary procedure lays you under to take the most instant measures to preserve entire to the U.S. the attachment of the Indians within our territory, which this usurpation of the rights of the U.S. if not remedied by their immediate removal within their own territory, is calculated to disturb.

You will instruct the Officer who may carry your remonstrance, to ascertain the strength of the Spaniards at the Bluff, and if found inferior or only equal to yours, will immediately remove your detachment to their neighbourhood, and fortify yourself, but not so near as to insult them or be insulted by them. This step is necessary to preserve our influence with the Indians, ought to be pleasing to them. You will therefore inform them, that your coming there, has appeared to their father the President indispensible to preserve them against the designs of false friends, to afford them protection against enemies, and to counteract the ambiguous policy of the Spaniards, who have not fulfilled their treaty with the U.S. tho they still say, they will comply with it.

You are not to mention at Mafsac or on your route the object of your detachment, or to what point destined, except to Brigadier Gen. Wilkinson, should you fall in with him. Every other person is to be left to his own conjectures respecting it, and the Spaniards to theirs.

As a General rule — It is to be understood, that in all your intercourse with the Spanish officers, you are to appear them of your sincere desire to unite with them, in every measure calculated to preserve peace and lasting friendship between Spain and the U.S. consistent and conformable to Treaty.

I have given instructions to Maj. Freeman to make such arrangements at Pittsburch and Mafsac as may tend to facilitate your voyage and [undecipherable] in us the power to do every thing, that can in any way promote its object.

You will write me immediately on your arrival at the Bluff, sending the dispatch by a faithful Indian runner to Knoxville, to the care of the Agent for the Department of War, and another by the way of Pittsburgh - You will also keep me duly informed of every circumstance and occurrence necessary for me to know, by the same or any other equally or more expeditious means of conveyance.

Annexed is an order on Captain Turner and [undecipherable] Butler for as many privates as may be wanted to complete the two companies under your command, and for a Subaltern to the Infantry if deficient in Officers.

It is indispensibly necessary, that you should pay particular attention to the Contractors department; so as to have always on hand, salted provisions and flour competent to any emergency - You will of course make the necessary regulations from time to time to keep a due supply.

Annex for your Government is 1<sup>st</sup> Rules and Regulations relative to Munitions and frontier posts or fortified places, [undecipherable] the 28<sup>th</sup> March 1797 - 2<sup>d</sup>. Regulations relative to discipline, and the defense of fortified places dated the [undecipherable] July 1797 - and 3. Regulations for [undecipherable], dated 1<sup>st</sup> July 1797.

With respect be

Cananadeaguas Oct<sup>r</sup> 15 1797

Sir

By our last mail I expect you red. letters from the Post Niagara by which I suppose they informed you something of their Apprehensions, from some danger that might arise from the Indians. During the Summer past I have been watching their movements & have detected several speeches that originated from the Caykin savages that live near Montreville, being sent by them to the Indians, and by the Indians to the Onondagas who live a little west of them to forward the same to the Senecas and others who live west of this place. The runners gave me to understand something of their business, which was enough to learn me that the Cannada Indians were not well disposed.

I suppose the French at the Northward & the Spaniards at the Southward have endeavored to distract the minds of the Indians, and to prevail on them to be hostile towards the United States & I believe have had some success untill of late. I not long since has an interview with some Seneca Chiefs who lately returned from Montreville who had a talk with Sir John Johnson — Sir John told them that their Indians something wrong owing to wrong stories which has been circulated among them by wicked men.

I have taken pains to inform the Six Nations that nothing more could contribute to their happiness than to attend to the voice of peace, that the United States would save them harmless from War if they would remain quiet, and not listen to the wrong stories which were spread by wicked and designing Men. I cannot discover any thing among the Six Nations but a peaceable disposition and believe the American Posts have had nothing to fear from them. The Six Nations have sold most of their land — (excepting those of them who remain at Grand River) which has united their interest materially with the United States, which we conceive & circumstances will render us more secure from difficulties that might arise from them.

I am Sir with every respect your Obedient Serv<sup>t</sup>

You see by the Pittsburg paper of last week, that my letter of Aug. 3<sup>d</sup>. to [undecipherable: probable reading "Gruye"], is [strikethrough: undecipherable] prematurely publishing. I must charge some of your military friend with the communication; as I have sent no copy to that quarter, and wherever I have handed it to my friend, it has been with an explicit caution against such a publication. But I do not know that it is to be regretted: it is an anticipation of but a few weeks, for I doubt not that Congress would have directed its publication, as usual with documents before [strikethrough: presented] to them on the same subject. And as one of my friend has lately written to me, "Since the policy of France has dragged our Executive into the forest, it is best to make the people who are there understand that we are wholly right, and our accusers altogether wrong." This friend then begins his letter. "I am greatly obliged to you for the pamphlet [letter of Aug. 8. to Ky.] you sent me, as I felt a strong desire to see the argument which should prove conclusively that the [undecipherable] would be a Knave if he were not by nature a Fool."

It is a good while since I heard from you or of you: how are you? is your health restored? I shall be glad to learn; being very truly yours,

James McHenry Esq<sup>r</sup>                                                        Timothy Pickering.

Trenton Oct. 25. 1797.

Dr Sir,

The inclosed letter from Kentucky I received last evening, covering one from Walter Evans to James Harris, relative to Cox's project of a forced settlement at the Muscle Shoals. The 1000 men mentioned as ready to proceed must be a monstrous exaggeration: such villains always exaggerate, to encourage & fortify their deluded partisans, and with such decoys to lure others into their snares.

I do not consider the letter of much consequence: but it may afford some evidence against the writer this friend addressed, should the scheme be prosecuted.

I am respectfully yours
Timothy Pickering

James McHenry Esq:

[Post]

Fort Wayne, October 31<sup>st</sup> 1797

Sir

I have this day received your letter of the 18<sup>th</sup> of august 97. It gives me great Inquietude when I am informed in your letter that I stand charged with monies unaccounted for on the Books of your Office.

I received by order of the late Secretary of War, General Knox, which will I think appear on the War Office book, six months advance pay, with six months Subsistence in the year 92. — as Conductor of Military Stores at Thirty dollars per month, and two rations per day; this money I am Confident I have accounted for; my next payment after I left Philadelphia was paid to me at a place called Hobsons choice in Cincinnatti; Colonel O'Hara late Quarter Master General paid me at that place three months pay, as Conductor of Military

Stores, twelve months after I left Philad<sup>a</sup>. I then informed the Colonel that General Knox Secretary of War, had advanced me six months pay, and my first account made out for pay; in this Country, did not take place untill I had performed twelve months services; then my account was made out for three months Wages, at Thirty dollars per month, & two rations per day, & I receipted for the money on Colonel O'Hara's Books. All the money which I have received, as Conductor of Military Stores in the Western Country, has been paid me by Colonel O'Hara late Quarter Master General, John Belli late deputy Quarter Master General, & Daniel Haragan late Deputy Quarter Master General in quarterly payments; their Books are upwards of 100 Miles from me, or perhaps in Philadelphia. I have no Vouchers, nor no account of the money, I have received of either of these Gentlemen;

When three months pay was due me, I had my Account made out, receipted for the same, received my pay, paid my debts, & never took any Account or memorandum of the same, to keep or retain in remembrance; what monies I am indebted to your Office I am totally in the dark to know how to account for, may you be pleased to State or have Stated to me the Account, I have too great a regard for my Name & my Country to do an Action unworthy of either. I have never in all the business I have done, been so unhappy, as I am at the present moment. every particle of money which I have received, I gained by hard service before I touched it, & thank my Gods, I never received any Public Money only my Wages. If I have taken of this, more than my due, I am very sorry for it. But Sir I assure you I am as ignorant of this transaction as an unborn Infant.

I will thank you to make

sensible of what I owe your office, on Public Account, I shall be Stationed in this Garrison this winter, Write me Sir if you please; by night or day I will attend to your letter; if necessary let me be ordered to Philadelphia; let any thing take place with me, I will not wrong the Public, if monies is due from me, I will repay it. If I cannot refund the money, will serve them faithfully until the debt is paid.

I shall forward Sir to you, a duplicate of this letter, & hope this may speedily Arrive to you.

I am Sir

Your very respectful
humble Servant
Samuel Henley
Comm<sup>t</sup> M. Stores

William Simmons Esqre
Accomptant
War Departm<sup>t</sup>

voucher missing through all the Business done by me in the ordnance department in this Country, to answer your question on the Quarter master department I have enclosed to the Secretary of War a return of Quarter Master Stores. I hope Sir that my own information to the Secretary of War will support my honor and that it

may not be doubted in my own hand writing to him,

I am lone in the department and this season have attended dried and aired the powder in the magazine it is now in good order with all the public property under my care.

I arrived in this Garrison the 19<sup>th</sup> of June last took a new account of the public property committed to my charge by Generals order, to Captain Matthew Ernest assistant Quarter master General on the business of that department give me leave in future to refer you to him, as I am only an assistant in the business. and not a bad heart,

[Copies of a letter to James McHenry Sec<sup>t</sup> of War Phil: Nov: 10: 1797]

Philadelphia Nov. 10. 1797

Sir

I take the liberty of laying before you a statement of the Frigate United States together with her appurtenances So far as comes under my knowledge [redacted]

The Ships hull is completely finished except a few small Carpenter Jobs which may be done in a few Days and some Black Smiths work which will not take above three or four weeks, the Iron Ballest is all on Board and in its proper place, the most part of the Water Casks stowed and filled and the remainder will soon be ready, the Masts all are end and riged; the Boats built and in compleat order, Anchors all on board except one which may be got on board at a short notice, the Cables all made some of them on board and the remainder ready to take on board, It may not be amiss here to observe that whilest we have a Number of Men employed in geting the Cables on board, if She is to lay up for the Winter She ought to be put into a Safe place to keep her clear of the Ice in the Winter, and as there is but one Such place that I can find along shore, Should the Winter Set in soon and that place be occupied there may be Some trouble to get it, but if She is to be put to Sea this Winter, She ought to be Moored in the River at the lower part of the town to take on board her Store and then in either of the above Cases I ought to have your Orders, the Yards are not yet finished but in hand and may be completed in ten or fifteen Days,
Signal and other Colors not in hand except —

Continental which is nearly finished, one Suit of Sails finished and the other in hands Riging all made — waiting for the Yards to compleat his Rigging and fit her for Sea in a Short time —

You will have herewith a Statement of the Guns on the Island from M<sup>r</sup> Duvster and my Self, and I am very sorry to say it is [strikethrough: very] disagreeable one to me as we have them in a very bad State, the Powder I am informed is all ready to put on board, the other articles for the Great Guns are some ready and the remainder in a fore way, the State of the Provisions and Slops for the Men I know nothing of, It may be proper to appoint a proper Person not only to pay the Officers and Men now on board and has money Due them but all such as may be employed hereafter,

It is much to be regretted that one of the most material articles for equipping the Frigate is at this time not to be had nor do I know where you can find thirty, twenty five pounders for such a Ship, for it is very clear to me that a Ship that has cost the United States so much Money ought not to be Sent to sea With out a Compleat [undecipherable] and well Maned whom that is the case make it Death for any Commander that will not do Justice to his Ship and Men and Honor to him Self and Country, I need never to go to Sea in a better Ship on any other terms
on any other terms

I have the Honor to be with Esteem
The Hon<sup>ble</sup> James McHenry Sec<sup>t</sup> of War                       Your Ob<sup>t</sup> Humb<sup>l</sup> Ser<sup>t</sup>
                                                                                                 John Barry

Your letter of the 8<sup>th</sup> instant together with one directed to the Gen. G one to Brig<sup>t</sup> Beavins and one to Captain Crawford is received. With every Sentiment of respect & Esteem

I am D<sup>r</sup> W<sup>m</sup> most obed<sup>t</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup>

War Office  November 27  1797

Sir

Your having been appointed as Clerk to the Navy Yard Philadelphia, it may be proper that you pay close attention to the additional instructions following.

In the first place you will carefully examine all the books proper to be kept in the Clerks Office on account of building and equipping the Frigate United States, and in case there should appear to be any Omission in the said Books, or any articles entered erroneously you will correct them without any cost —

Secondly, you will be particularly careful in the examining of all accounts of articles received into the Navy Yard & issued therefrom, and as soon as you have fulfilled this part of your instructions you are to make out a complete return of every article received into the Navy Yard and from whom, and what articles have been issued and to whom since the commencement of the present building which said return you will deliver to Samuel Hodgson Esquire Superintendent of Naval and Military Stores and a copy of the Same to the Secretary of War.

Thirdly, you will also make out one exact Statement of what articles remain on hand belonging to the Public of every denomination whatsoever particularizing their by name, Length, Breadth, and thickness together with the number of Superficial feet they Contain, & Weight. Also what Buildings may have been erected & of what materials they are composed and their dimensions. A Statement you will be pleased to deliver to Samuel Hodgson Esquire and a Copy thereof to the Sec<sup>y</sup> of War.

Dear Sir.

I forwarded your letter to M<sup>r</sup> Hemsley whose son had gone to England previous to my receiving it, and who has no doubt waited upon you. The young gentleman is well qualified for the station you contemplated for him. His father is rich extremely respectable and esteemed.

My poor Indians are very clamorous for their medals, more so indeed than for their plows.

I have very Lately seen a penny of the new British copper coinage, the edge or rim of which is considerably thicker than the plate part that contains the figures or devices. I should think were the Indian medals to be so formed, it would add to their strength without requiring any increase in the quantity of medal. It occurs also, should the work be still in a state to admit of alteration that one side of the medal might exhibit figures of a warlike nature, and the United States as protectors of the Indians. I should wish in this case the Legend to be Presidency John Adams 1797. The medal would then comprehend

both Presidencies.

I have written to Mess. Savage & Bird for a book intitled "Rules & regulations for the formation, field exercise and movements of his majesty's forces." as this work has been printed and distributed to the officers of the British army only, and is not to be purchased it may require a special application to obtain it from the war Department. If so, may I request you to procure it for me. I am engaged in digesting regulations for our army and stand in need of such lights as this compilation must afford. Philadelphia Dec<sup>r</sup> 6. 1797

Sir

I have perused with pleasure the Rules of Regulations for the Discipline of our Army, and confess they appear to me a great improvement to any hitherto established in this Country.

My experience in the Revolutionary War I am convinced for the want of such the discipline never was what it ought to have been, we had nothing but great outlines to be filled up by discretion or Caprice— hence there was nothing like System consequently when ever Corps were to act together their organization, their Supplies and every thing else so discordant that no harmony could exist nor could discipline be preserved —

Permit me to observe that as you have gone so far as to digest a plan for the management of the Army I take the liberty to suggest the propriety of

T.O

of your prosecuting your labours still further. It will be useless to have a small tho well regulated Army in so extensive a Country as this, without forming the Skeleton of one on a much larger scale in future exigencies should require it— hence I take the liberty to remark that a System should be formed for organizing an Army of say fifty thousand Men, apportioning the General Officers, detachments, Divisions, [strikethrough: Legions] Brigades, Legions, Regiments, Batallions, with the necessary Cavalry, Artillery, Grenadier, Light Infantry, Engineers, Sappers, Miners &c. having regard to the Nature, [undecipherable: extent] of our Country, the War most likely to be engaged in, and the Enemy to contend with.— Here we should as Stop, we have wasted large Sums of Money on Fortifications, in many instances they have been injudiciiously planed & more shamefully executed, the plan adopted by General Knox was to apply to the Governors of the different States who without regard to any general plan, followed the bent of their own inclinations & the persuasion of

— others, and so mistaken has been the opinion in one instance that in case of an invasion of Troops by— supported by a Naval Force that the works may with little address of the Enemy be made usefull to them tho hostile to us.

I take the liberty to advise that a skilfull engineer should be employed to lay down a plan of defence by Fortifications for the U. S. a great Skeleton to be filled up as prudence should advise for the protection of the Frontiers— and that no Fortifications or works be built at any other place or places to be permanent but at those, and that there Should be finished from time to time as might be found necessary to begin the great chain, that at some time within it may be necessary to finish.— as if we do not proceed in some regular & Systematic plan we may find it necessary to incur as much expence in vageing works

T.O

which may be found to be improper, as we have been or may be at the expence of erecting from Caprice without Judgment—

It has been in consequence of the honor you have done me in presenting your plan for the discipline of the Army which I highly approve, that I have taken the liberty to give you some crude opinions relative to an Army & a permanent defence of our Country in Case of Foreign invasion —

I have the honor to be with much respect & esteem. your friend
J Parker.

James Mc Henry esq<sup>r</sup>.
Sec<sup>y</sup> of war.

Dear Sir

I shall not trouble you again for some time with my enclosures, for to morrow morning I leave this place — do therefore send the letter for M<sup>rs</sup> Freeman to her as soon as possible.

Capt. Lewis has arrived here, and paid me the money I lent him on the road you will not [strikethrough: notice] therefore take any of what I have written to you respecting it.

I am induced to believe from a letter I have received from Eaton that he intends to publish either his tick or something to exculpate himself and injure the reputation of those officers whom he calls his enemies when he was in Georgia — He will do me the honor to rank me among the number and may says some things for the purpose of injuring me — I have to request my dear Sir, that, you would, should this be the case, do me the justice, to acquaint my friends, to convince others is of no consequence, that as far as my duty or business has been connected with your office, I have given entire satisfaction; to which you may add whatever praise I may in your opinion be entitled to, and which would be improper in me to dictate —

I am greatly at a loss whether it would be best to send my trunk of papers immediately to Georgia

I may be detained on the route — I would wish you would not send them until you hear from me again. I hope you will be so kind as to call and see your old acquaintance M<sup>rs</sup> Freeman keep up her spirits until I can see her again — She has written to me that she has exacted a promise from you that you would use your influence with the Secretary that I might be permitted to come for her — If it can be consistently done it would be agreeable to me.

My [underline: best compliments] to M<sup>r</sup> Simmons, M<sup>r</sup> Hayner and all my friends & acquaintances — You may see by my writing that I am in a great hurry —

I am with great regard & Esteem
Dear Sir
Your obl'd & hum<sup>e</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup>

Wm. Freeman

P.S. I have also enclosed a letter for my father and one for M<sup>r</sup> Seagrove which I will thank you to forward —

REGULATIONS
To be observed in the delivery and distribution of

FUEL and STRAW

*To the Garrisons on the Sea Coast, and Recruiting Parties.*

FUEL.

1. To every Lieutenant Colonel, and Major, is allowed, one cord and an half cord of wood per month, from the 1st day of October, to the 1st day of April every year.

2. To every commanding officer of a garrison, one cord and an half cord of wood per month.

3. To every officer commanding a recruiting party one cord of wood per month.

4. To every other commissioned officer, one cord per month.

5. To non-commissioned officers as hereunto by eight non-commissioned officers, soldiers, musicians, and privates, one cord of wood per month.

6. To a garrison barrack guard, half a cord of wood per month.

7. To officers, and Soldiers, half of the aforesaid allowance of wood from the first day of April to the first day of October in every year.

8. To the Sick in hospital, the allowance of wood is to be regulated by the Surgeon.

STRAW.

1. One truss of Straw, weighing thirty-fix pounds is allowed to each private soldier, per year. At the expiration of fourteen days, each person may be refreshed with eight pounds. At the expiration of thirty-two days, the whole truss is to be removed, and a fresh truss of one truss is to be furnished, and so on every succeeding period of fourteen and thirty-two days.

2. The Store quantity of Straw is allowed for Servants or barrack non-holders, and for wollor-women attached to each company in the proportion of one woman to seven laundry brewmen non-commissioned officers and privates.

3. The Straw is to be changed for the Sick in the hospital as often as may be deemed needsary; this needsary to be determined by the Surgeon, or Surgeon's mate in the absence of the Surgeon.

Requisitions for Fuel or Straw.

1. Requisitions for wood or Straw, shall flate the number and rank of the officers, the number of non-commissioned officers, and privates; laundry-women barrack non-holders, and of wollor-women for whom demanded, and be certified by the commanding officer of the garrison, or recruiting party.

2. No wood or Straw shall be drawn for officers, or wood or draw for Soldiers, which on furlough, or any allowance made to them for this time.

3. Whenever it shall appear that more wood or draw has been drawn, than there were officers, Soldiers Servants or barrack non-holders, and in that manner dfully gotten and certified thereto; the commanding officer signing the Requisition, shall be held responsible for the value of the article drawn beyond the quantity allowed by their regulations, and shall have his name and the circumstances of the case, reported to the Secretary for the department of war.

4. Requisitions thus signed, and the receipts given by the officers, to whom the articles are delivered for combustion, shall be produced as vouchers by the Contractor, Agent, or Quarter-master, in the Settlement of his accounts.

5. In auditor quantity of Fuel the Soldier for the garrison and recruiting parties, having received their allotment by their regulations, their commanders are not allowed to regulate the demands for this article by any former ufage or custom.

Given at the War-Office of the United States in Philadelphia, this twenty-fifth day of December, A. D. 1797.

By order of the President,

[*A.S. Galatin PB*]

War-Office of the United States.

May 4, 1796.

*The following RULES, explanatory of those published the 15th February, 1789, are to be observed by all persons entitled to lands in pursuance of Resolves of Congress.*

EVERY certificate of the acknowledgment of a Deed, or Power of Attorney, either before a Notary Public or other Magistrate, must, in addition to what is usual, set forth that the person making the acknowledgment is known to the Notary or other Magistrate; for which purpose words of the following import must be inserted in the Certificate.

*"And I do moreover certify that the said A. B. making this acknowledgment, has been for personally known to me."*

If the Notary or other Magistrate has reason to believe that he is the person he represents himself to be, he will also certify it.

And if the proof be made by a witness or witnesses, he or they must swear to some general state of their knowledge of him, which matter must be set forth in the Certificates; and the Notary Public or other Magistrate before whom the acknowledgment is made, must also set forth that the witnesses or witnesses have been for upwards of                    personally known to him.

If a Justice of the Peace is employed, the clerk of the court of the corporation or county must certify that such person is a Justice of the Peace of the county or corporation, as the case may be, and that full faith is due to his acts as such.

JAMES M<sup>c</sup>HENRY,
*Secretary of War.*

War-Office of the United States.

January the 1<sup>st</sup>, 1798.

WHEREAS frauds have been practised, in obtaining warrants for Bounty Lands, due to the Officers and Soldiers of the late Continental Army, by the production of forged instruments. To check in future such impositions, it has been thought adviseable; that all persons, having claims for Bounty Lands, whether in their own right, as legal representatives, or by virtue of any instrument or deed of transfer, be required to forward their respective claims to the War-Office, on or before the first day of January, 1799, in order that such claims may be duly examined, adjusted and determined upon.

To substantiate such claims, a strict observance of the rules heretofore issued from the War-Office will be indispensable; and in addition to what is required by the said rules, the certificate of the acknowledgment of a Deed or Power of Attorney, must also set forth the place of residence and occupation of the claimant or person making such acknowledgment; and when the proof of personal knowledge is by a witness or witnesses, their place or places of residence must be set forth in like manner.

JAMES M<sup>c</sup>HENRY,
*Secretary of War.*

Sir,

The Committee of the House of Representatives, appointed pursuant to the inclosed resolution, have directed me to request, that you would, as soon as convenient, furnish them with such detailed accounts of the expenditures therein referred to, as will enable them to perform the duties of their appointment. What must be my feelings— and what my Relief now She is Safe at Sea— the Wind Stills continues to blow N. W. It is with diffidence that I have taken the liberty of changing, or adding to the regulations which you have been so kind as to send for my consideration: I have altered such of them as will in my opinion render their observance more subject to responsibility, and their execution more faire

I have endeavoured to conciliate the Alterations, with the spirit of each of the articles altered, and if I have erred, I hope you will be pleased to pardon me; if they are approved, it will afford me great Satisfaction; but it must be observed that the General in Chief has in the course of last year made a number of arrangements in the Army, many of them amounting to those contemplated, with perhaps some difference in their execution. Would it not be best, in order to remove all ambiguity, which frequently arises in the construction laid upon orders, (more so when given by two different persons) to consolidate both, so as to give a clear Idea to all Officers of what is expected from them: whatever may be the final Theme of the regulations will I assure you, be obeyed with punctuality on my part and enforced with those under my Command

Mount Vernon 28 Jan<sup>ry</sup> 1798

Dear Sir,

Knowing that the War Office has an agency in the Western Lands, I take the liberty of putting the enclosed letters to General Putnam and Col<sup>o</sup> Sargent under cover to you, open. — By doing so, it supercedes the Necessity of a repetition of what is therein mentioned. — Another occasion for giving you this trouble, is, that if M<sup>r</sup> Massey is a Surveyor in the Northwestern Territory, it is highly probable that his business in Philadelphia is with your Office. — In which case, it me pray you to obtain what information he can give respecting the claim upon my land, & transmit the same to me, — and to request, after sealing my letters to the Gentlemen abovementioned, that you would be so kind as to put them into the safest channel of conveyance, that is afforded from Philadelphia. —

What means this calm, & apparent harmony in the Representatives body? Is it because no collusive subject has come on? — or does it proceed from a change of sentiment in the opposition members? — Are there no accounts yet from our Envoys? — I ask, to what is their silence attributed, when the News Papers are filled with accounts of them, as late as the middle of November, from Paris; where they must have been at least six weeks?

What, as far as it can be guessed at, is the public sentiment relative to Monroe's voluminous work? — which I have not yet seen, but have read of: — and what of Fauchet? — Another elaborate work, I presume, will appear soon, from the late Commissioners of the Revenue; — the cause of whose dismission has now (that I have seen) been noticed at in the Gazettes. — What has been, or is it supposed will be done, by the House of Representatives in consequence of the extraordinary application which was made to them on that occasion, by the Ex-Commissioners —

I have exhibited a long string of questions, but if you have no leisure, or any of them are embarrassing, I require no answer to them. — M<sup>rs</sup> Washington & Nelly Curtis unite with me, in every good wish for M<sup>rs</sup> McHenry, yourself & family, — and I am always, and

Affectionately Yours

G<sup>o</sup> Washington

[James McHenry Esq<sup>r</sup>]

Sir,          Philadelphia 29<sup>th</sup> Jany 1798.

In consequence of the presentment of your Draft on me dated the 1<sup>st</sup> inst. for 450 Dollars in favour of Mess<sup>rs</sup> Evans & Sibby, and by them and a subsequent endorsement made payable to Mess<sup>rs</sup> Baker & Commegys of this City, I immediately called on M<sup>r</sup> Simmons the Accountant to know the State of your Accounts, as he had undertaken their adjustment; the result of my enquiries you will learn by the enclosed Statement of your Account, and by the other which the Accountant informs me he has sent to you. It is plain, according to your apprehensions signified in your letter that accompanied your Draft, that there is a mistake somewhere & of course your Draft could not be honoured. It is possible some of your Accounts and vouchers may not have got to him, but in whatever shape any mistake may have occurred, you will have it in your power by perusing the two Statements, you will receive to set all right. You will recollect that Leonard Davis's receipt admitted in the enclosed Statement, is not a perfect Document, and that in answer to a former letter on that subject you promised to obtain such an one as I requested, let it be done, and sent in your next communication. Also a special order on Mr Simmons, to pay me the balance due you on his adjustment of your Accounts. Your letter to that effect, he does not deem sufficient.

The sooner you attend to this business the better, as it is desirable to have it closed with the business is fresh in all our memories. I am very sorry that your Draft under circumstances could not be honored.

I am Sir
Your most Obedient Servant

Major C Langham.          Samuel Hodgdon.

Sir

This day James Hamilton Waggon leaves this City for Pittsburgh laden with the articles inserted in the enclosed Invoice. It was at first thought best to address the Goods to Fort Stayac to be forwarded from thence, but it struck me that you may have other Stores for these Parts, and that the whole might go through together without being subject to any detention. And I accordingly wish you to mark them answering to the Invoices & send them forward as soon as possible as it is of importance that they get speedily to hand. You will please to write to each of the Commanding Officers, when you forward the Goods and enclose the invoices now sent to you, as they may be of use in making the distribution. Hamilton has the other invoices with him as usual. On examination it is found your disbursements are adjusted as are all others alike circumstanced to the 30<sup>th</sup> June 1796 inclusive and placed to the credit of Col<sup>o</sup> O'Hara's all subsequent will be credited to the present Quarter Master General. The Comptroller will Prospect write you on the Subject.

I am Sir, Your m<sup>o</sup> Ob<sup>t</sup> Servant,

Samuel Hodgdon

Major D. Craig.

I have added Copies of all the Invoices of Goods forwarded by Hamilton. General Wilkinsons Wine is in another Waggon that you on to day under Hamiltons care, the other part of the load is for the public.

I also sent you a Statement of Hamiltons Account, for his last Load, that you may adjust and pay it on the spot: which I think the best mode under circumstances. I have accordingly carried the advances made him say 362 Dollars to your debit, of course you will take his receipt in full.

Samuel Hodgdon
