61082:
Speech of the Little Turtle, to the President of the United States, on the Seventh day of February 1798.

Father,

I thank the Great Spirit for the opportunity which he has given me this day to see you and speak to you, I am now going to express to you the wishes and opinions of the nine Nations, with whose knowledge I have come here. I was at the treaty which was formed at Greeneville. I as well as my people had felt and experienced the inconveniencies of War. I and some others did not like all the parts of the Boundaries, which were proposed by General Wayne for that treaty; but weighing the evils which might have been expected from the continuance of War and the great advantages held out by other parts of the treaty, I considered them to outweigh the inconveniencies, which we might experience from the boundary not being entirely satisfactory and signed the treaty. We know the boundaries established by this treaty cannot be easily altered. We do not wish them to be so altered as that less land should belong to the United States, than what we have relinquished to them. We wish therefore only to propose that a parcel of the land relinquished to the United States at the Great Miami may be restored to the Indians for an equivalent parcel between the Ohio and Mississippi, which we are disposed to give in exchange. If this can be done it will add greatly to our comfort and may prevent the inconvenience of having the white settlers so near to our principal Towns and hunting grounds.

It is proper that I should mention to you that a number of White people have been marking land at and in the neighbourhood of Post Vincennes. We know the United States have obtained a reservation in that quarter, and we wish the quantity so reserved to be ascertained and marked. Part of this is to consist of lands said to be sold to the British and the French Governments. Let whatever has been thus sold be ascertained and the whole reservation marked, that the Indians as well as the Whites may know what belongs to them respectively.

The goods allowed by treaty to the several nations may not always come of the kinds which would be most acceptable to them. To obviate this inconvenience each nation will make out each year an invoice of the different kinds they wish their stipend should consist of for the succeeding year, and send it to the Secretary of War. This will enable him to order those kinds of goods which we most want without its being more inconvenient to the United States. It is desirable also that the stipend for each nation should be in a package and directed to each separately, accompanied with the invoice or account of the kind and value of the goods.

It would be agreeable to the Indians to have a person appointed an Agent, who should reside with them and of whom they should approve. They would on their part grant to such a person a tract of land for his trouble and to render his stay among them comfortable.

My Brothers frequently experience inconveniencies respecting necessary articles, which the Traders have not, or from the great prices they are obliged to pay for them. The treaty promises to establish trading houses to supply us with goods such as we want and on the most moderate terms. The Secretary of War has told us that these should be established as soon as circumstances would admit. If they do now admit of it or when they do I should recommend Fort Wayne as a good situation for one.

I am sorry to have it to mention to you that an Indian Chief and another Indian were killed in the Streets of Vincennes last fall. we have not heard that the perpetrators of that crime have been punished. It is natural to wish that they should. We have as yet restrained the Indians from Retaliation and hope the Criminals will be punished by the United States.

We perceive that the numbers of our people are much diminishing and we consider one of the principal causes to be the quantity of liquor sold to them by traders and others. As far as it is possible to remedy this evil, we entreat it may be done. We find that Stills have been also erected within the reservations from whence much of this mischief must issue. We see also that as the settlement increases more of this mischief is to be apprehended. How far it is in your power to check this evil we do not know, but we rely that whatever can be done in this case will not be omitted.

We have acknowledged by the treaty and I now again acknowledge in the name of all the Indians whom I represent, that we are under the protection of the United States and claim from them to extend that protection to all cases to which it applies.

We see that it would be a good thing to learn to cultivate our land, but as we are young and ignorant in such a matter it will be necessary that we should have Ploughs and Steers and a man to teach us to use them. It would also add to our convenience were a Blacksmith to be sent among us to help us to those things which are become indispensable to our wants.

Although at present the state of the Indians might not be much benefited by the residence of a person capable to teach our Children to read and write, yet as the prospect of our receiving advantage from such instruction is daily increasing it is hoped that in a few years, our Father may think proper to send such among us. —

We know that agreeably to the treaty no sales of land can be made to Individuals without the consent of the United States. This is a wise and just part of the treaty as respects us. We are too much disposed to sell our land and Whiskey is a great Tempter. We hope therefore that this wise provision in the Treaty will preserve us, under the regulations of the United States from such temptations.

I shall not trouble you with other matter of less moment, which I shall mention to the Secretary of War, who if he thinks them deserving your attention will no doubt communicate them to you. I have only further to observe that if any part of what I have said should require the interposition of Congress, that I submit it to you at such time as you may think proper to call their attention thereto.

61117:
Philadelphia, 10 February 1798

Sir,

Relative to the claim of D<sup>r</sup> Smith, who was appointed Judge Advocate to the Army by the commanding Officer Gen<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson in General orders, and who for sometime as it is stated to me rendered services in that capacity to the United States, it is my opinion he is equitably entitled to compensation for those services. Though Gen<sup>l</sup> Wilkinson does not in my opinion possess the power of appointing the Judge Advocate as I have seen no act of Congress vesting such a power in him, yet as the President of the United States with the advice of Senate has omitted to make the appointment, which omission has been supplied by the commanding Officer for the good of the public service, I think the Judge Advocate sho<sup>d</sup> be paid for his services as in any other case not expressly provided for by law, where in justice compensation is due from the United States. For adjusting the quantum payable to D<sup>r</sup> Smith for his services as Judge Advocate, no better rule can be suggested than the allowances fixed by law to this Office and the contingent fund appears to me to be the proper fund for paying this claim. —

The same principles apply to the case of D<sup>r</sup> Webb of the Cavalry, who formerly a Captain of the Cavalry and during [undecipherable] took the command of a company of Cavalry by the orders of Gen<sup>l</sup> Wayne, when there was no other Officer holding a commission where the Company was. He ought to be paid as Captain during the period of this extraordinary service out of the contingent fund.

The Sum of twenty six thousand four hundred and thirty five Dollars is included in the amount of the whole expenditures, but allowing the Buildings &c as Stock on hand and admitting the other charges which makes up this Sum, it may be proper to Subtract it from the whole amount of expenditures, which proceeds divided by the whole number of Muskets made will prove each to have cost twelve Dollars & thirty two Cents

It is not possible to procure documents to ascertain accurately the annual expenses of the post as they relate to the Workmen these with others of a trifling nature may be omitted, exclusive of these the foregoing statement will probably be found pretty correct—

An Establishment of this kind in its early stages must necessarily be subjected to many embarrasments they arise from the difficulty of obtaining experienced workmen, the want of Machinery and proper accomodations, and many other causes which will readily occur to those conversant with such Establishments. These difficulties are in a great degree

degree surmounted, and the expense in future will be proportionably reduced. The boring Machinery is nearly completed, the Workmen are better acquainted with their business, and are now well accomodated, the most important Tools are made by the Workmen although they do not appear to the credit of the Post. Labour in consequence of the numerous private Contracts is considerably raised while the Wages allowed the Workmen at the Post remains as they were— a circumstance in favor of the Works for the present, and by the time these engagements end it is probable private contracts may cease and labour of course become more reduced—

The past time has afforded no opportunity for a fair experiment to determine the utility of the Establishment but the time is now arrived— the present year will certainly determine the propriety of continuing the present and augmenting the number of Posts for procuring the Supplies expected from them— The cost of a compleat Musket in future probably will not exceed twelve Dollars the Superintendant is sanguine in his opinion that he can turn them out at eleven Dollars— The Situation of the Works is favorable in every point of view— All articles necessary for the Works may be conveyed by water & landed at a distance not exceeding half a mile from them— The water Shops for plating the Barrels, boring and polishing them are well constructed and eligibly situated— Provision may be purchased at as low a rate as at any place in New England— or probably in the United States— large Tracts of Woods suitable for Coal and other purposes is found in the vicinity of the Works which may be obtained at a very low rate— Coals are delivered at the Works at the average of four Dollars the hundred Bushels they cannot be furnished cheaper any where—

The situation of the Works is such that they may be encreased to any extent, and they will be always safe from sudden invasion and destruction; the adjacent Country being full of hardy veterans and disposed to support the Government they have chosen and from which they have experienced a degree of happiness not known till since its operation—

It ought again to be observed that in the Outset of the business of the Post, very few persons could be procured who were perfectly acquainted with the business of making Muskets— Many are now expert in the Work even Apprentices have been taught who are now compleat Masters of the business— For many months after the commencement of the business all the labour was performed by hand which was painful and slow, and greatly enhanced the price of the Articles made or repaired; this will also account for the small number of Muskets made in the first years— the Superintendant confidently expects after three Months from this time he shall be able to turn in three hundred Muskets per Month into the Public Stores, with the means that he will then possess— considerable advantage would arise to the Public if the necessary foreign articles for the Works were purchased in larger Quantities, both Money and time have been lost for want of a more early and generous supply, I might and perhaps I ought in justice to the Post, inlarge, but enough I trust has been said to satisfy your enquiries, & more you have not time to attend to— I therefore forbear and subscribe myself—

Your Most Obedient Serv<sup>t</sup>
Samuel Hodgdon

James M<sup>c</sup>Henry Esq.
Secretary of War

War Office 15 February 1798.

Sir,

I have received by todays mail your Excellency's letter of the 24<sup>th</sup> of January.

The prompt step which you have taken to discover and bring to punishment the person or persons who shot the Indian Commissioner and wounded two other Greeks in their Camp on Little River, cannot fail of being satisfactory to the President, while the cause for it has excited serious apprehensions and leaves it extremely uncertain whether it will be possible to prevent retaliation. Every measure has been adopted that appeared calculated to soothe and pacify the Indians and induce them to wait the operation of the laws.

The money appropriated for the pay of the Georgia Militia for past services has been directed to be lodged in the Branch Bank at Charleston subject to the orders of Major Freeman who has been advised thereof and instructed to proceed to pay it as soon as possible after his arrival in Georgia where he may be

daily expected. It is out of my power to give you any satisfactory information touching the probability of what Congress may do respecting a further appropriation for the Militia.

With great Respect

I find by this Mitchell, that he is concerned with Foo & his party, that finding it impracticable to pass the Military Posts upon the Tenesee, they have altered their route, & mounted thro' Kentucky, in part, where they are assembling at the falls of the Ohio, from whence they intend to embark for the Mouths of Cumberland River, where a Town was to be laid out for their temporary accomodation; Mitchell is to be, as he says, the principal Surveyors & that his business at this place was to know from Captain Pike, where the Indian line, particularly ran, that he wished to know as they intended to move as near it as possible; however I am well assured that all this enquiry of M<sup>r</sup> Mitchell, is nothing more, than finesse; I think his real object was to discover what number of Troops the Garrison consisted of, & to know the disposition of this detatchment — his Kentucky Corps of Artillery consists as I am informed, of Small pieces which

he has pack'd on Horse back to Kentucky & will embark them at the Falls. —

While I labour under much pain from the accident I met with on the day I left Philadelphia, in addition to it, I have been regularly attack'd by the Ague & Fever, how long it may continue, is hard to tell; I fear it will not be [strikethrough: shortly] remove'd & on this account I beg leave to observe that the sooner I am able to get out of this county the sooner I shall be able to have my health restored.

Have the honor to remain with great respect & Esteem your mo.
ob<sup>t</sup> Hble Servant

[signature]

Gen<sup>l</sup> Mc Henry
